div.head: "Dr. Williams' Pink Pills gave me back my health."
div.p: "Dr. Williams' Pink Pills gave me back my health."

Thousands of men to-day are doing their work with difficulty. Their chests are weak, their legs ache after any exertion, they are nervous, have dull pains in the back, frequent headaches, and food does not do them any good. They have too little energy to master work or enjoy recreation. There is a prompt cure for this wretched state of debility, for the rich, red blood that Dr. Williams' Pink Pills create, makes men well and gives them new strength. This good, red blood invigorates the muscles and strengthens the nerves, dispels rheumatism and makes all the difference between an enjoyable life and a miserable existence. Thousands of men, young and old, owe their present splendid health to Dr. Williams' Pink Pills. An instance :

Mr. Robert Clarke is a tall, powerfully-built young man, and, to use his own expression, "as hard as nails." Yet only a few years ago he was on the verge of Decline. When interviewed at his home, 120 Leta Street. Walton, Liverpool, he explained that this transformation was due to Dr. Williams Pink Pills, for they built up his constitution and made him a robust man. "Just when I was looking forward to taking a man's part in the world." said Mr. Clarke, "my health began to break up. Sharp pains attacked my chest and sides, and when I hurried I was troubled with shortness of breath. "At nights I could not rest properly, but was bathed in perspiration. As time went on spasms of coughing nearly shook me to pieces. My appetite failed me, and anything in the way of nourishment had to be forced on me. "I expectorated a lot, and the pain in my chest and sides became almost unbear- able; the night sweats seemed to drain all the strength from me. " A doctor said there was every indication of Decline. I had treatments, still I waitel away until I was little better than a walking skeleton." Mrs. Clarke, who was present, explained that she persuaded her son to give Dr. Williams' Pink Pills a trial. "Yes." resumed Mr. Clarke, "and after taking a few boxes of the Pills, I could eat heartily, and enjoyed my meals; food nourished me, and my strength increased. "As I persevered with the Pills my breathing became regular and the night sweats disappeared. Steadily all pain left my chest and sides, and before long the cough ceased to trouble me. I put on weight, and in time my cure was complete. Dr. Williams' Pink Pills gave me back my health." Study your Blood, Reader.—Never neglect the early signs of Weakness. GENERAL BOOTH'S VISIT.
REPLY TO CRITICS OF THE SALVATION ARMY.

General Booth, the veto:an head of the Salvation Army and one of the greatest figures in the religious and social work of our time, visited Warrington on Sunday and addressed two meetings in the Hippodrome. Although he has just attained his eighty-third year, the General still enjoys a remarb- able degree of activity, and his presence inspires his soldiers with enthusiastic devotion. There is some- thing pathetic in the knowledge that he is not able to see a single member of the huge audiences he addresses, for one of his eyes has had to be removed and there is a cataract in the other. At the end of this month the General is to undergo an opera- tion which, in his own words, is to restore his vision and make a young man of him With characteristic cheeriness be gave his word that Ile had made up his mind to live as long as he possibly could and when Alderman Tinnion, in proposing a vote of thanks, made allusion to the General's " declining" vests, the veteran rose and deprecatingly interjected the words " Steady, now ! " With his flowing white hair end long beard, he looked a picturesque, venerable leader of men, and, although his voice teems to have got a little WE aker since last he visited HP, he spoke with all his wonted fervour nod conviction ?bout the splendid work of the mar- vellous orpardsation which he brought into being. The Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph) presided at the afternoon -fleeting and amongst thove on the platform were ! Aldermen A. Bennett, W. Pierpoint, D. Tinnion, James Evans and J. Smethurst, Councillors W. H. J. Jenkins, J. Dickenson, T. S. Steel and J. T Locker, Mrs. Garnett (renketh), Mrs. Withinshsw, Mr. and Mrs. J. A. Ransome, Mr. W. H. Woo-'ccck and Mr. T. Prince. The MAYOR said the organization which General Booth had instituted and built up was highly valued as a great influence in the many countries to which it had penetrated. He would liken the Salvation Army to those whom the Master, in the parable of the Feast, sent out into the highways and byways to compel the lame, the halt and the blind to come in. It was the function of the Army to shed the light of Christianity upon those who would never think of attending a place of worship. The recent Titanic disaster, by the heroism and self-sacrifice which it called forth, had shown how men were capable of living noble and use- ful lives and if E 0 many heroes were to be found amongst a concourse of 2,000 people how many inore i potential heroes must tly.re be n the world, waiting for a body like the Salvation Army to induce them to make the best of their lives. (Applause). General BOOTH, who was warmly applauded on rising to speak, said a great change had come over the public mind during the last few years with reference to the work and character of the movement, but some very peculiar notions still prevailed. It was not long since the General of-the Salvation Army was commonly repre- sented as an autocratic despot, ruling his people with rod of iron. Those who Mile such statements failed to tell them that the General was perhaps the best beloved leader of any religious or philan- thropic movement on the face of the earth (Applause.) It was commonly believed that General Booth was a splash adventurer, piling up a colossal fortune for himself and for his family. Those who made that statement failed to say that General Booth during the forty-Enven years the Salvation Army bad existed had never taken a shilling from its coffers for his own support. (Applause.) Much was mid of the magnificent mansion in which the General reAded and the splendid motor car in which he rode about the world but no witness was ever produced who had ever seen the mansion or the motor. Then there was a great deal of talk about tbe want of prope- accounts and balance sheets, although as a fact there was perhaps no religious or philanthropic movement on the face of the earth that took so-much pains and spent so much labour on its statements as to the income and expenditure of its /nods. lie cure heard a man who complained "What a pity General Booth does not issue a balance sheet."

He (the General) told his informant : " Next time you see that gentleman, give him my compliments and say that if he will only send a £5 note to our headquarters, he will get a balance sheet every year of his life, if he lives to be as old as Methuselah.' (Laughter.) The battle of the Salvation Army soldiers was difficult and often very discouraging, but as a rule they were fight- ing it with a bravery which was the admiration of the angels of heaven. Referring to the possibilities which opened themselves to Christian enterprise, the General said they had long been looking beards China with longing eyes, yearning for that great nation. Great things might be done if they could only get a proper entrance into the country, but they wanted men and women and money to enable them to grasp the , opportunity. People frequently asked " What will ' happen to the Salvation Army when the General is dead and he was always replying " Don't worry about that. The General is not dead yet." (Laughter and applause.) When that event did occur, however, there was no need to fear that the Salvation Army would come to grief. The perfection of its organiza- tion, the effectiveness ot ;ts methods, the devotion of its officers and their intelligence and consecration assured him that the Salvation Army would go forward. (Applause.) The object of the Army was to deal with masses of humanity who were ignorant of God's claim upon them, and who were outside the pale of all ordinary benevolent and religious effort. A river of souls was roll i rg onward to the precipice which overhung miserable eternity and the Army was doing a great work in rescuing them and changing their modes of life. the General then sketched the rise and progress of the Army, point:ng out that to-day its flag was flying in 61 different countries and its message was preached in over 40 different languages. It had created no fewer than 9,000 societies of its adherents ; it bad 10,000 officers entirely supported by the Army, assisted by 5,000 employees who did not carry any rank and by 100,000 unpaid local officers. Each week there were 52,000 indoor meetings, attended by 1,500,000, people. The Army also went out to the people who would not ei.me to them and conducted 30,000 out& or meetings, attended by 2,000,000 people, every week. They fed 270,000 hungry men, women and children and sheltered under their roofs 200,00 homeless people every week. The General made special reference to the marvellous work of the Army in the world of arunkenness and pointed out how its assistance in the work of reformation had been enlisted by the governing authorities in several countries. Instances mere also given of the usefulness of the Army in finding employment and of the success of its emigration scheme. The first thing the municipalities and governmental authorities ought to do for the Salvation Army was to inquire into it, and give an independent judgmett as to the value ot its work and how far it was wortky of being sustained by the com- munity. (Applause.) Alderman TINNION, in proposing a vote of thanks to the General, said that in his opinion General Booth was the finest man in the public life—religious, political, or social—of England to-day. (Applause). Councillor JsNKINS seconded. He said that however, they differed on matters of religious opinion they were all able to agree most cordially in paying a tribute of regard to a great end goodman. (Applause.) lit- hoped the good work which had been done by the Army in Warrington and district might be renewed with greater enthusiasm and veater rewards. (Applause). The vote was warmly accorded and the General in replying proposed n similar compliment to the Mayor. In the evening the General preached to a large gathering.

X 'GOOD CASE. The 'appreciation of the public, the com- mendation of doctors, and the support of the Press make' together a very good case in favour of margarine as a food. Those who have ,never used margarine before would do well ' to cast all prejudice aside and just try 'Stork,' by far the finest Margarine obtainable. They ' will discover, no doubt to their surprise, that they can detect no difference in flavour or appearance between ' Stork ' Margarine and choice country butter. In the certificate of merit awarded for 'Stork' Margarine by the Incorporated Institute of Hygiene, there is sufficient evidence of quality; medical testi- mony proves a standard of food value as high as that of butter; and the economy is obvious—indeed, it means a saving of half.

div.p: THE WORST RECORD.

Review of Season 1911-12. By " Ovallst." I suggested a year ago that Warrington had touched rock-bottom in a playing sense, but in the season just concluded they have gone a step further down and their record is the worst since the formation of the Northern Union in 1805-6. For the first time the percentage of League points has fallen below the 50 per cent, mark, and one has to count the position of the Wirepullers from the bottom instead of from the Itop of the League. They are much nearer the last four than the first four, and the percentage of 43 75 for 32 matches indicates uncommon feebleness. The trouble is the same rid trouble—a team which requires new blood. But we have gained this much from the season just cicsed—the worst is knoan and has been boldly faced. The slow process of building up a new team .has begun, and only needs to be continued with enterprise. and determination to once more raise Warrington football to the proud level maintained for so many years. It will take more than one season to make up the leeway, for there is still a strong contingent of veterans in the service of the club, and new men are not found as rapidly as the old ones drop cut. Still, something has been done, and if the advance is too small to he apparent in the table of results it exists nevertheless. The record of tha season is, to some extent, misleading, for I think it must be generally admitted that the Club finished the season with a stronger thirteen than they began it. The pro- gress made in the cup-ties is one sure indication of this. Warrington did something to justify their reputation as cup-figlitets by twice drawing on their opponents' territory, and winning at home, while their feat of playing each round twice is one not likely to be equalled 1-; any other club. The greatest advantage was in gate money, which received a good lift from the six hotly contested cup-ties. Warrington ceitiinly finished strongly, for in addition to the advance made towards the cup, they put up their record score in League matches for the season with the last fixture of all— Salford at home. The season before, they never once ran into the thirties of points for, while th. 4 have during the past eight months beaten Barrow by 33 points, and Salford by 31 points. Another curious feature, and one that goes to the credit side of the season's work, is that the points for and against in the League table are both a shade better than they were a year ago, even through the percentage on results is less. Coming to the play and the players, what adranoe Warrington have made as a team has been in pace At the close of the campaign they were playing a speedier and cleverer game than at any time during the previous 18 months, and this fact gives one cause to hope that things wi'l show a more marked improve- ment in the season to come. Not many new players have been enrolled, but some of them have proved of inestimable value. The introduction of those three young and speedy local players, Fearnley, Tranter and Skelhorn, has worked wonders in the forwards, and bar a slight lack cf weight the vanguard is good enough to bear the brunt cf the sternest struggle. Shugars and Thomas are showing the effects of wear and tear and time, and it is obvious that further acquisitions are necessary to keep the forwards up to the reluired strength. In the back division there is less improvement to record, and more required. Woodburn was the first acquisition, but after a promising start he proved disappointing in a scoring sense. Bradshaw was the best wing, but on the whole the extreme men were the weakest links in the attacking forces, and here, at least, something will have to be done. Waywell and Clare can only be looked upon as reserves. In the centre George Dickinson has once again performed wondrous well, and made light of the many seasons of heavy football behind him. But even "Dicky" cannot last for ever and had it not been for the advent of Renwick in December the club would have been in a parlous state. The New Zealander has proved the best investment War- rington have made for many years, and his sterling play saon made him a favourite with players ard spectators alike. The most urgent reform, in my opinion, is required at half hack. Brooks's injury seems to have shortened his career by a year or two, and with no one else to fall back upon but Daintith and Jordan, the club is seriously handicapped in a vital position. There are possibilities about Jolley, the smart youth from Ruacorn, but unless a really class half back is secured for the opening of the next season, Warrington's advance will certainly be problematical. At full back Mclntyre has worthily filled Tilley's shoes, and at times shown promising form in the three-quarter line. Probably the most disappointing feature of the season now under review, is the poor quality of the young players who have been performing in the" A" team. Scarcely any can he looked upon as reliable reserves, and very, very few show any signs of "training on." There is a dearth of junior talent at present, and the keenest look-out will need to be kept among the various leagues to maintain the supply of new blood in the Warrington ranks. div.head: SCHOLARS' INSURANCE.
div.p: SCHOLARS' INSURANCE.
IS THE EDUCATION COMMITTEE LIABLE?
Important Point Discussed.

The question of liability for the insurance against accident of the children attending the schools of Warrington was raised at the monthly. meeting of the Education Committee on Monday evening. The follow. minute of the Finance Committee was submitted for approval :—The Committee again considered the question of insurance against risk of accident to children attending the non-provided schools, but in accordance with the opinion of the Law Clerk it was decided to take no action in the matter.

The Rev. JAMES DAVIES inquired if any explanation could be advanced with respect to the Law Clerk's views. He thought they were running a great risk in not having the children in both the non-provided and Council schools insured. As a matter of fact the soholars were attending the non-provided schools because the Education Authority insisted upon their being present and not because the managers required their attendance. Therefore the authority was respon- sible for them when they were in the building and the question of insurance ought to he faced. Mr JOLLEY explained that the views of the Law Clerk were simply to the effect that the authority had not the power to defray the necessity expenditure. It was purely a legal question over the interpretation of which the Committee did not presume to set themselves up against the Law Clerk. There was some difference of opinion on the subject. but they accepted the guidance of their official legal adviser in the matter. Would not the expenditure necessary for insurance be exceedingly small ? _ .

Mr. JOLLY : it is an illegal one, the law clerk advises. Councillor WlLiciresox : In case of an accident to a child should not we, as as authority be liable? The CHAIRMAN said he could not pretend to answer that question. The Law Clerk advised that it would be illegal to pay for insurance and presumably he was of the opinion there would be no liability. Mr. FAIRCLOUGH said the managers of the Church of England schools had insured the children against accident, and if they were liable in the matter, he should say that the Education Committee was responsible for the Technical School and the School of Art as well as the Council schools. The CHAIRMAN : Gentlemen, you have got the decision of the Town Clerk, who is our legal adviser. I don't think you can go behind it. Councillor PEMBERTON thought that in he circum- stances the wisest course would be t 3 refer the minutes back and get counsel's opinion. It would be rather awkward if some calamity were to occur and the Courts held that they were liable. Canon STEVENSON: Do I understand you to say that the managers of a school are not liable ? The CHAIRMAN : No, sir, don't understand that. I said that as the Town Clerk had advised that we could not legally incur the expense of insurance I presume he is of the opinion that we are not liable. lam not referring to managers at all. Alderman TINNION thought it WR3 admitted that the authority was liable for the 'children attending the Council schools. The risk, however, was so small that it was thought hardly worth while insuring He under- stood the question was not a legal one but one of policy whether it was worth ehie taking the risk or not. He thought if the risk was small the premium would be small, and it was much more desirable that they should he covered. He therefore proposed that the minute should be sent back for further consideration. Ihe Rev. JAMES DAVIES seconded. The CH AI RIIAN suggested that the amendment should be drafted in terms asking for the written opinion of the Law Clerk on the question ; but Alderman TtmoN observed that his amendment was hardly to that effect. It involved the question of policy. Mr JOLLEY again explained that the opinion com- municated to the committee was that the authority had not power to spend public money in insuring against risks in non-provided schools. Mr KING DON : Do 1 understand that to mean that the children in the other schools are insured? Mr JOLLEY : No. The CHAIRMAN : I think we must confine ourselves to the resolution, which only refers to the children attending the non-provided schools. Mr FAIRCLOUGII said he did not Agree with the ruling of the Law Clerk. (Laughter.) The managers of the Church of England schools had had advice on the matter and it was held that the managers were only responsible for the children while they were in the playground and not when they were inside the schools because the authority had charge of the buildings. The CHAIRMAN : I think, having regard to the views expressed, that the matter had better go back for full reconsideration. This course was agreed to.

div.p: M- 10: MEE
[BY REDCAP:
BUFF ORPINGTONS.

The subject of this week's illustration is that of a pair of Buff Orpingtons. These ever popular fowls continue to hold their own and rightly so; for they are a most useful variety. When lin d solely for utility purposes they are amongst the best as winter layers. They are a sitting breed and when used for this purpose they make good sitters and mothers, often rearing their young with great care The Buff Orpington has played a very important part in proving the fact that a pure bred can be made more useful than a mongrel. One does not hear so much nowa- days about the special qualities cf the common barndoor fowl, and as I before stated, the Buff 'Oro ' have had a great deal to do with removing this prejudice; for you scarcely find a farm yard where a few buffs are not found. All honour then to their originator (the late Mr. Arilliam Cook), for with the advent of the Orpington came a new era in the breed- ing of pure bred poultry. Before he made the Orpingtons, Mr. Cook claimed that what we wanted was a good all-round fowl, and it was to this end that he worked and succeeded ; for who i there who des not say that the Orpington is not a good all-round fowl? They are beautiful to look at, as well as being extremely useful ; they are quick growers and with their white shanks make very desirable fowls for culinary purposes; they are good layers and what is more they lay a good-sized :egg.

div.head: BUFFS FOR EXHIBITION.
div.p: BUFFS FOR EXHIBITION.

_ My weekly remarks are generaily written on behalf of the amateur, and I can scarcely advise such to take up Buffs for exhibition purposes. At the present time you would have to run up against something "very warm" in the Buff fancy so I would ask you to wait awhile before embarking thitherward. Of course if you are keen on them and have a " bit " of money to spend then you may try your hand, but you will find some good men amongst them and all the more credit to you if you beat them. A rough outline of the show standard is as follows : —Clear, sound even buff throughout to skin, the body should be deep, short and cobby, short on leg, tail rather short (a bit like a cochin's tail) and compact,the general carriage should be bold and upright as in the illustration, legs ivory white and beak white or horn colour, comb, face, earlobes and wattles blight red, the comb should be evenly serrated but not too large. There are several shades of buff, but providing the colour is even throughout it matters little, never show a bird that is patchy what I mean is they must not chow two or three distinct shades of buff.

GENERAL. As you are well aware we have marl other cilours in the Orpington family; but I refrain from writing separately on these, as I may have an opportunity of doing so later on, and also of giving illustrations of them to accompany the remarks. Meanwhile let me say, that if it is your intention to breed a few Buffs this season, no time should be lost, so get your eggs down at once. CHESHIRE FOR POULTRY. A business engagement took me right through the heart of this most beautiful county last week. lam a Cheshire man and have lived in it all my life, but I was never more struck with ideas for the future of the poultry industry before. Cheshire, this most adapt- able cuunty,!and yet, what a dearth of poultry farms! I cannot imagine a county more suitable for poultry farming, well wooded, giving natural shelter, and rich in all with natural bmbiage. Still further it is adjacent to some of the finest markets in the world. Stoke, Birmingham, Liverpool, Manchester and a host of watering places in North Wales. Surely there must be a big demand for borne produce, but I am perfectly certain not half the demand is supplied.

div.head: FUTURE DEVELOPMENT.
div.p: FUTURE DEVELOPMENT.

now can the industry be developed? We often talk of developing and supporting our colonies, and yet at our very door we have English counties abso- lutely in a state of dormancy in respect to the poultry industry. We might well have to spend 32-8,000,000 per annum rn foreign eggs and poultry, instead of which, with proper development we could easily export as much, or if we did not, we could at least keep 3:8,000,000 at home. To I eturn to my journey. As I wheeled through Cheshire I noticed lots of large farms with just a few fowls running in the yards, and, in some instances only a pen, which from all appear- ances, were there E imply to supply eggs for home consumption. What ought I to have seen? Why, acres of poultry pens, of course ! well laid out farms, with a stock from two to five hundred head of poultry on hand. And why did I not see these things? There is an answer, and one which is easy to explain.

div.head: RAILWAY RATES.
div.p: RAILWAY RATES.

Under present 3onditions, the people who occupy the farms—while they are within reasonable distance good markets—are, however, too far away to make the conveyance of produce a reasonable item in the business. Another cause for lack of develop- ment is the high rental of ag,icultural land, these together with the lack of organisation, are the chief I causes why we as a nation spend eight millions annually on foreign produce. I am not a keen politician, but I have sufficient reasoning power to know that if you taxed foreign eggs you wculd not create a greater output of home produce. No, the draw backs to greater developments ;n the poultry industry are caused through difficulties inside our own borders. You may teach the art of tcientific poultry raising as much as you like ; but until you remove the main obstructions (as pointed out) you will never create a much greater development. Until we can get these difficulties removed we shall have to adopt the co-operative system of the National Poultry Organisation. Fix up collecting depots and arrange for the proper dispatch of produce to the best markets. At present no proper rule exists. The farmers simply take what eggs they have on stock, and if di.), think they have too many male birds on band, or if a few of the hens go broody they kill them and take them to the nearest market town, and get the best price they can. The whole business is haphazatd ; and so long as our Board of Agriculture sus nothing and does nothing, I suppose we shall plod on in the same bad old way.

OTItElt ITEMS. Here lies a great field for development ; and once fairly under weigh oothing but success can follow. For instance, if we had a greater output of home produce in eggs aid dead fowls, we should hear less of ptomaine poisoning, often the result of .food stuffs, so much inferior to a nice new laid egg. Again, poultry could be so extensively bred that it would be easy for the working classes to obtain this class of flesh meat in. preference to so much foreign meat because the price would tule so much less. Then again, it would increase rural employment, and here I think you will agree there is a great need fu. this. The more people you get working on country farms, the less need we shall have for sanatoria. And still further, it would greatly increase employment in the manufacture of poultry farming utensils and the construction of fowl houses, coops, incubators, etc , etc. By the way, I noticed a correspondent in the

div.head: BOWLING NOTES.
div.p: BOWLING NOTES.

Fine weather again prevailed on Saturday when the first round of the Works' Bowling Association Competition was continued on the Horse and Jockey Green, which looked in excellent condition ; and some g )ocl games were witnessed.

A ONE-I'OiNT VICTORY. Undoubtedly the most exciting match on Saturday was the one in which the Lead Works beat Fennell- street Tannery by the odd point. 'I he victors were conceded 40 points and their opponents received 65 and this proved a very even hanuicap. Rigby started off well for the Lead Works by beating his opponent six points. It was only at the tenth end that Boyle got the bowls going at all, he having been beaten eight ends out of the nine and the game then stood at 11-3 in favour of the Lead Works man.. From the tenth to fourteenth end Boyle got an additional six points and the remaining three ends were in favour of Rigby. The Lead Works got a very severe set- back when J Griffiths was beaten by J Carter by I 15-1. Gritaths won the first end by one point but his opponent had little difficulty in attain- ing his majority of points which feat he accomplished at the tenth end. However the Lead Works men did not lose heart after this rebuff and W Smith and G Ward beat their opponents /11 Glover and J Kirkham by 9 and S points respectively. The game between Unswortb and G Lunt was only decided by a brace of points in favour of the Lead Works man Unsworth. After twenty ends F Clerno, Lead Works, beat C little by 15-10, the game being very slow up to the tenth end, but subsenuently Cletno' added his eight points for game to his opponents four, making his score 10 points. From this juncture the game was fairly even,eacb side winning in turn,but a very Pxcit- ing finishing game was witnessed between W Shaw, Lead Works, and R Kly. _ The Corporation team have every reason to congra- tulate themselves on their magnificent win by 47 points and should have plenty of confidence for the next round. F Shaw gave the first impression that the Corporation team were "out for blood" when he beat W Povey at the twelfth end by 153. The latter only won two ends, the third and eighth. However the fate of his predecessor did not in any way deter H Williamson (Beam Shed) from beating G Hall by 13-9. It was a deserved victory and well earned by fine play. E Hayes was successful in beating C Povey (Beam Shed) by 15-9 after a good game. Clarke however, succumbed to G Howarth (Beam Shed) with 13 points to his credit. W Swan (Corporation) put up a keen struggle with R Howarth, and indeed he led by 14-13 at the 19th end, but in the ensuing length Howarth added a pair of good woods and won by a solitary point. After this the games were fairly even. except for the one in which W Beresford beat T Bibby by 15-4. Corporation, 215 ; Orford Beam Shed, 108.

"PETER PEACOCK" CHALLENGE CUP. Given a fine day, the competition for the " Peter Peacock" Challenge Cup, presented to the Liberal Association by the popular chairman of the Executive, will make an auspicious start to-day. The first game will begin on the Bowling Green, Bank Quay, at 2 o'clock. The draw for the first and second re und will be found in another column. Each member will be I notified by the Secretary (Mr E A Sanders), seven i clear days before the time he s expected on the green. The first game each Saturday will commence at 2 o'clock. Should any of the matches be postponed on account of bad weather, or any other unforeseen circumstance, the committee will re-arrange them after the remaining games have been played. Non- competitors will be admitted to the green at a charge of one penny each.

div.head: TRIUMPH OF ORGANISATION.
div.p: A TRIUMPH OF ORGANISATION.

The Ideal Home Exhibition has closed its doors, but the lessons, of at least one section, will live long in the memory of its many thousand visitors. Those who were not privileged to visit Olympia, or were prevented by the constant crowd of waiting spectators from seeing Virol's exhibit, are likely to obtain an erroneous impression. Its unparallelled success was not only due to the magnificent show of babies of forty diffe,ent nationalities that had been brought up upon " Virol," but also to the firm's perfect organisation. The beautiful hall in which Virol s guests were accommodated, represented the courtyard of an Indian Rajah. Here one hundred and forty children, and the nurses of the various nations that furnished the children, who had never before met, played together in conditions of perfect health and happiness. The children crawled about and made friends at vill or amused themselves with toys according to their varying moods,and never was it necessary to administer punishment to any one of them. Such health and happiness under normal conditions, is the most eloquent testimony to the perfect arrangements made by" Virol" ' for their guests, and the value of their speciality as an infants' food.

div.head: FARM SHOOTING AFFAIR.
div.p: FARM SHOOTING AFFAIR.

At the Warrington Occasional Court on Monday, before Mr F A Frost, William Harrison, Cuerdley Hall Farm, Cuerdley, was charged on remand with shooting with intent to do grievous bodily harm to four men named William Griffin, Edward Shannon, Anthony Griffin, and John Griffin, on Sunday morning, April 21. Superintendent Strickland said two of the injured men were unable to appear at the court, as they were yet inmates of the Widnes Accident Hospital. A further remand for a week was ndcessary. It was alleged at the first bearing that the men were stealing potatoes from a corner in the stackyard when the accused, who was on watch, fired at them from close range. The accused stated that the gun went off by accident. A remand was granted, bail being allowed.

div.head: TRIBUTE TO CHAS. DICKENS.
div.p: A TRIBUTE TO CHAS. DICKENS.

The annual meeting of the Manchester Dickens Fellowship was held on Monday night. The Dean of Manchester, the President, was the chairman. They honoured Dickens, he said, as a humorist, a social reformer, and a moralist. De had been instrumental by his writings in mitigating, and, to some extent, in abolishing, evil practices and systems that were taken for granted when he began to write; and out of his writings had sprung a new feeling of sympathy. a feel- ing or sympathy between social classes who had long kept apart. ile had made, as no one else had done, the poor intelligible to the rich, and, to some extent, lie had made the rich intelligible to the poor. Like Addi- son, he combined wit with purity. Ilia life had a permanent value ; and so long as his writings were read, so long would the great heart of the English people be true.

div.head: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
div.p: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.

LATCHFORD WORKS MEDAL COMPETITION. There was a large attendance at the final in the Wolics Medal Competition promoted by the Latchford Foot- ball Club, which was played on Saturday on the Thelwall-lane ground between Crosfleld's and White- cross, and resulted in a victory for Crosfleld's by one goal to nil. At the conclusion of the match, gold and silver medals were presented to the winners and runners up by Mr Harold Smith, M.P. Mr. Edmondson, as the representative of the Whitecross team, said they had had a bard fight but would nevertheless probably fight again. The Competition was a good omen for Association football. Forty teams entered the competition and that , indicated the progress of Association football in War- rington. (Applause) The captain of Messrs. Crosfield's team congratulated the Latchford Club upon their endeavour to foster Association football in Warrington and wished their opponents better luck next year.

div.head: RUGBY FOOTBALL.
div.p: RUGBY FOOTBALL.
NORTHERN UNION CUP FINAL.
Oldham Beaten by Dewsbury.

There was a surprise in the N.D. Cup Final at Headingley, Leeds, on Saturday. Oldham were strongly fancied against Dewsbury, who made their first appear- ance in the final and had an inferior record for the season. The Yorkshire team, however, showed that their victory over Halifax was no fluke by beating the ex-League champions 8 points to 5 points. As against Halifax, the Dewsbury men got the winning points in the last two minutes, and owed much to their strong finishing powers. Oldham played far below League form, and were deservedly beaten. For a Cup final the gate was disappointing, the attendance being 16,1A0 and I the receipts £854. Teams : Dewsbury. -Jackett, back ; Rhodes, Ware, Ward and Sharpies, threequarter backs ; Milner and Nearey, half- back ; Richardson, O'Niell, Garnett, Hammill,Abbishaw and Evans, forwards. Oldham—Wood, back; Cook, Deane, Davies' and ' Williams, threequarter backs • Anlezark and Louise, half-backs ; Ferguson, Avery, Smith, Wright, Wise, and Wiltshire, forwards. Referee, Mr B Ennion, Wigan. The game opened very evenly, loth sides keeping the ball close. Oldham were the first to score, a flagrant piece of off-side work by Richardson giving them a penalty after sit minutes' play, from which Ferguson landed a neat goal. After Dewsbury forwards bad forced a scrummage near the Oldham line,Milner passed the ball to Nearey,wbo coolly dropped a goal. Anlezark next got possession from a scrummages at the centre and fine work by the Oldham tacks gave Cook a try at the corner. Wood failed to convert. The Dewsbury forwards played with rare dash and determination, and certainly had the best of matters until the Marvel, but Oldham defended keenly. Half-time :—Oldharn, one goal and one try (five points) ; Dewsbury, one goal (two points). The second half was full of incident, although the football could never be considered high-class. Wise missed a certain try for Oldham, and for the last twenty minutes of the game Dewsbury were handicapped by the absence of one of their forwards, Hammill, who had to be carried off with an injury to his knee. The Tykes forced several scrimmages near the Oidham line, and at the break-up of one of these an altercation ensued, in the midst of which Avery, the Oldham forward, was ordered off the field. Anlezark, on getting the ball from a scrummage, punted to Rhodes, who cleverly fielded the ball, and with a strong run managed to score a try at the corner. Ware failed at goal, so that the teams, with about seven or eight minutes to play, were then on level terms. Immediately upon the restart Oldham forced a scrummage near the Dewsbury line and an ill-considered kick by one of the Dewsbury backs enabled Davies to make a fair catch on the "25" line directly in front of the posts. Wood sent the ball just wide of the goal. Dewsbury pressed, and lslilner whipped the ball out to Rhodes from a scrummage and the winger just managed to ground the Fall over the goal-line only a few inches from touch. Ware failed to land the goal Result :—Dewsbury, one goal two tries (eight points) ; Oldham, one goal one try (five points). In the absence of Lord Derby (President of the , Union) the Cup was presented to the Dewsbury team by Mr. A. H. Marshall, ALP:, for Wakefield. Two spectators from Dewsbury collapsed from excitement during the match, and died later in the day This incident cast somewhat of a gloom over the heavy woollen district, but there were great rejoicings in Dewsbury when the Cup holders arrived home with the trophy.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIELD.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIELD.
Rylands Recreation Win the Trophy.

Congratulations to Rylands' Recreation team on their victory over Flixton on Saturday in the final tie for possession of the handsome shield presented by the Manchester and District Rugby League. The match took place at Cadishead, and attracted a good crowd, many making the journey from Warrington. The Recs. lost the toss, but played so well uphill that they soon bad the Flixton men in difficulties. From a free kick by Leah the Recreation forwards followed up smartly but Mears saved near the line. The Flixton forwards made excellent use of their weight, and at times tested Bramhall, who was not found wanting in pluck or skill in relieving his lines. At half-time the defence remained intact.

Turning round with the slope in their favour Rylands' made excellent use of their advantage and it was not long before the Recreation vanguard showed splendid footwork which led up to Hennessey scoring at the corner. The success had its effect on the Flixton men and losing heart they were constantly on the defensive. Fine back play led up to Hennessey again scoring at the corner, and the point not being improved upon Rylands' Recreation thus won a keen game by two tries (six points) to Flixton nil. The shield was afterwards presented to the captaia of the winning team, Mr Leah, by Mrs Marks, wife of the president of the Manchester and District League. The Vrarringtonians were heartily congratulated on their success.

We are still a nation of THE SHOP shopkeepers, at any rate to WORKER'S an extent that makes an Act CHARTER. affecting the many thousands of workers in our shops a matter of general interest and importance. It is pleasing indeed to note the very general welcome which has been accorded the new I Shops Act which has come into force this week. Dealing as it does with a great body of workers, the very nature of whose duties tends to long hours and irregular meal times, there is little doubt that the Act will do much to brighten the lives of a consider- able section of the workaday world, and to improve generally the condition of health which their trying work imposes upon them. The outstanding provisions of the Act—the securing of one legal half holiday in every week for all shop workers, and the provision of regular intervals for meals—meet with general approval. They are long-called-for reforms in the life of the shop worker against which it is impossible to raise any objection. Much good must come out of this half holiday and meal time charter, and it is pleasing to find a general disposition on the part of shopkeepers to accept it as a necessary development, and to administer it in a generous and considerate spirit. At the same time, one cannot ignore the severe criticisms of details of the Act which are being made in many quarters. It cer- tainly seems as if the lack of elasticity in some of its provisions may give rise to a considerable amount of confusion and incon- venience in quite a number of cases, and it is not surprising to hear grumbling about the interference of the law on the part of many of the large firms who already provide the half holiday and regular meal hours for their workers, although not quite in the manner which the Act demands. Then there are innumerable cases in which the hour fixed at which the employee must start his half holiday and the times during which relief must be allowed for meals will cause very serious inconvenience. There are the cases of the caterer and the hairdresser in particu- lar. The Act does not seem to take much account of the fact that their assistants must begin their half holiday at 1-30, when work is at its highest pressure, and have a meal hour also during the busiest period of the whole day. Another case which illustrates the disadvantage of the too rigid fixing of the rules laid down by the Act: the small shopkeeper who deals in a variety of goods will find himself faced on certain days with the proposition that he may sell certain articles but not others. Clearly such a situ- ation must lead to a great deal of confusion, not only to the shopkeeper but to his cus- tomers as well.

On these and other points we think the Act, the principles of which have been so generally welcomed, errs on the rigid side. .There seems to be no good reason why the , concession made in one or two cases should not be made in many others. The objections which are taken to details of the Act are, however, insignificant in comparison With the benefits it confers upon one of the largest and most deserving working classes of the nation. We may hope that in actual work- ing a way out of the little problems which present .themselves on its first application will not be very difficult to find. That the great mass of shopkeepers are prepared to tackle them in the proper spirit we have already good promise, and in the circum- stances we are convinced that it will not be long before the Act is brought into com- plete harmony with the various conditions which exist in our shops. In short, the Shops Act, despite its little disadvantages and the inconvenience it must cause until conformity with its rules becomes a cus- tom, is fundamentally an excellent one. It will put the stamp of better health And greater efficiency upon the life and labour of a great mass of the workers of this country about whose lot Parliament ,and the public have not been as thoughtful in the past as they ought to have been.

On the occasion of SHAKESPEARE the Tercentenary of COMMEMORATION. Shakespeare's Birth in 1864, amongst other celebrations, a great banquet was given in London and Lord Carlisle delivered a most eloquent oration commemorative of the genius of the poet. But there are always some people so unhappily constituted that they must needs take a perverse and disparaging view of every cause which stirs the enthusiasm of their fellows, and from this odious spirit of destruction it would appear that even generous boyhood is not altogether free. In "The Tyro, " which was the school magazine then current at Harrow, there appeared the following ill-conditioned ditty. It is some satisfaction to the principles of literary justice to know that " The Tyro" perished early and unwept.
COMMEMORATION ODE TO SHAKESPEARE.

William Shakespeare! could not fame Dim the lustre of thy name ? Spelt, re-spelt, mis-named, corrected, Etymologised, dissected ; Painted, sculptured, carved and printed, Photographed, and drawn and tinted, Scribbled, pencilled, chalked and etched, Biographically sketched Born again, and schooled, and married, Re-located, killed and buried, Hymned, and sonneted, and toadied. Deified, adored, exploded. Essay 'd, epigramm'd, discussed, Talkedfand written, cried and fussed,— Is not thus thy fame abated? Then thou must be celebrated ! Bard Immortal ! Avon's Swan! Is not all thy freshness gone? Copied, folio'd, quarto'd, dated, Altered, edited, collated, Prefaced, published, dedicated, Versically commendated, " Read," misprinted, vitiated, Supplemented, innovated. • Blotted, glossed acol punctuated, Added to, interpolated, Supervisedapd expurgated, Purified anremendated, Criticised and annotated, Accurately regulated, COD truverted, commentated, Substituted, fabricated, Now restored and vindicated, , Beautifully illustrated, Bound, embellished, decorated, Learnt by heart and imitated. Garbled, la retchedly translated, Quoted and misquoted, prated, Acted and impersonated. Derogated, agitated— Still are not thy plaguers sated— Thou must be Commemorated!
The . Opposition is

TORY MANNERS: certainly making great THE NEW STYLE. progress in the "new style" inaugurated by Mr. Bonar Law (says the" Daily Chronicle.") Its two main characteristics are a grotesque wildness of statement and a lamentable lack of manners. Lord Claud Hamilton, in Wednes- day's Home Rule debate, for instance, was pleased to refer to Mr. Birrell as "a distin- guished literary scribbler." That is from the gentlemanly party! Then Sir Robert Finlay, who also belongs to the party which prides itself on its high respect for law and order, stated that the case of Ulster was ten times stronger than that of the American Colonies in the eighteenth century. That means, we presume, that the Protestant Tories are in danger of treatment ten times worse than that against which the Americans rose, and that they have, therefore, ten times more right on their side in resisting. What weary nonsense, what muddled history, what absurd insinuation that is!

It is impossible at this WARRINGTON'S stage to form any SLUMS. trustworthy estimate ' of the practical out- come of the local observance of Health Week, but if it has only succeeded in concentrating attention on the slum problem the experi- ment will have justified itself. Many of those who took part in the Corporation visit to some of our courts and alleys on Wednes- day, were probably surprised to find that such plague spots existed within easy reach of our main thoroughfares—suggesting the Mayor's simile of "whited sepulchre." The inspection will, at any rate, have opened their eyes to the most appalling side of our town life and a true realization of , the actual conditions in which the sub- merged classes exist is.an essential preface to any effective remedial measures. Dark, dismal hovels, cramped, fcetid back passages, repulsive and unhealthy sanitary arrangements—all the worst features of slum life were seen in the course of Wednesday's tour. What most impressed one was the unhappy fate of children destined to be brought up in such unwholesome surround- ings. It is for their sake that something drastic must be done, but how to grapple with the situation is a problem which -calls for courage and strenuous endeavour On the part of our local rulers. Educational work can do an:immense amount of good, and it is some satisfaction to know that the Warrington Health Committee is already proceeding on those lines. Finally we would urge the necessity for co-ordination of the various departments of the Corpora- tion which have to deal with the public health. At present there is undoubtedly over-lapping and confusion,and it is essential that the health department should have a voice in such work as the scavenging of back passages.

A salmon in the Mersey at Warrington a fortnight ago, a porpoise at Twelve Arches on Tuesday. Shades of Isaac Walton ! what next? A whale? * _ _

"Why should the fireman attend to the fires in the bakehouse?" asked a barrister of a "trade" witness at the Warrington Courty Court on Thursday. "Because it is a classical job" was the illuminating reply. *_* *

Why does the Member continue to leave the unravelling of "the wire tangle" in the clumsy hands of "Workman Jim " ? He knows how to. give a plain answer to a plain question, and we have yet to learn that he is " 'ard of hearin " !

• * The" Liverpool Daily Post" says " Mr. Harold Smith seems to desire that he should be taken very, seriously, but that would never do." Personally, we think he ought to be " well shaken before taken," and then taken CU77I grano salis. * * *

It is suggested that One practical outcome of Health Week in Warrington should be an "open window" campaign. As Dr. Hibbert, in his useful lecture last night put it. "We want fresh air not merely during an hour or so during the day when we go out fora short walk, but during every hour of the day and night." * * *

There is apparently no prospect of friction locally in putting into operation the Shop Hours Act. Most of the tradesmen have already fallen into line—Thursday afternoon being selected for the half-holiday--but, apart from the closing of the cafés, this will mean but a slight departure from the exist- ing Order of things. * * * Councillor Lindley has already been placed on two of the most important Corporation committees, the Gas Committee and the Electricity and Tramways Committee. Most new members have to serve an apprenticeship in less important departments, but the weight and worth of the new member for Town Hall Ward have found early recognition.

Is it true that there is small chance of the Howley foot-bridge being completed and in use this year? The last excuse for delay was the strike. Perhaps one of the repre- sentatives for Howley or Fairfield will elicit some definite information at Tuesday's Council meeting. Residents in the neigh- bourhood are getting reasonably restive.

* * * Councillor Pemberton will move an important resolution at the Council meeting on Tuesday expressing the Council's alarm at the growing increase in the 'contribution to be borne by the ratepayers towards the cost of education without adequate provision being made by the Government for an equitable contribution from the Imperial Exchequer. It has long been considered that the apportionment between imperial and local charges for education operates very hardly on municipalities like Warrington. In brief, the State is not believed to be doing its fair share towards meeting the national bill, and Councillor Pemberton is taking the right step in drawing attention to the matter.

n * More than one member of the corporate deputation, headed by the Mayor, which made a round of the Warrington slums on Wednesday, found himself in places the like of which he did not previously believe existed in Warrington. The Health Committee and the Medical Officer have done much in recent years to improve and remove many of these plague spots, and their crusade should receive a valued stimulus from the re-awakened consciousness and responsibility of those Aldermen and Councillors who saw for them- selves on Wednesday. One half of Warring- ton (as well as the world) has a very hazy idea of how the other half lives. The Corporation ought to be taken periodically on such a tour of inspection. It would do more good than hours of argument and reams of statistics about tuberculosis and infantile mortality.

div.head: VOICE OF WALTON ! Harold and Horatio in the Commons.
div.p: THE VOICE OF WALTON ! Harold and Horatio in the Commons.
A SNUB FOR THE MEMBER.
" The voice was the voice of Warrington, but the language was the language of Walton."

_ Mr. Horatio Bottomley, M.P., has made history before, of sorts, but we are sure he has never said or done anything in his curious career which will be so long remembered in Warrington and Liverpool, as the phrase quoted above, which he uttered in the House of Commons when replying to a speech by the Member for Warrington. It was a very happy hit, provoking uproarious laughter in the House, and a rather sallow and sickly smile on the face of the gentleman thus " pinked " by the swashbuckler of South Hackney. Mr. Harold Smith, M.P., had, with characteristic pushfulness, taken the oppor- tunity afforded by the "ten minutes rule "to ask leave to bring in a Bill to amend the Parliament Act of 1911. Under this rule private members may bring forward a Bill which they deem worthy of the advertise- ment, and apparently the privilege is one which is greatly appreciated by the Member for Warrington. The fact that he was only allowed ten minutes for the explanation of so weighty a proposal did not deter Mr Harold in the least, and we doubt whether anyone else could have packed more cheap sneers and vulgar abuse into the time: Hi § speech reminded the House of his more famous brother in his worst style. The preamble to the Bill, he said, " had done its dirty work," "the fraud had so far prospered," it was "a shameful and notorious falsehood." Then followed a series of truly Smithian jibes in the worst possible taste at the expense of. the Irish party, the Labour party, and the Prime Minister. He suggested that Mr. Asquith might take the 'opportunity of saying "we have perpetrated a 'dishonest trick; . . . we did not die with a lie on our lips." And so on, in a vein of uncultured sarcasm which came ill from 'so young and undistinguished a member of the House of Commons. The Premier ignored this snapping at his heels, and the House I showed its appreciation of so gross an abuse of the "ten minutes rule" by refusing Mr. Smith's request to introduce the Bill by the big majority of 233 votes to 147. Such a rebuff under the circumstances is rare, and it is to be hoped (though it is scarcely believed) that the Member for Warrington will be wiser in future. Mr. Bottomley is neither an admirer of the Parliament Act, nor a notable exponent of the courtesies of debate, but even he pro- tested against the abuse of the rule, and gave the younger Smith a "Roland for his Oliver" in the pointed allusion to the voice of 'Warrington and the language of Walton.

div.head: BLUE FUNK.
div.p: BLUE FUNK.
By the Cynic.

The official Mascot of the Order of the Tub had got it badly. I waited for him to appear at his usual place in the park, and was on the point of writing the editor of the " Examiner" that we had not had our usual interview, when I observed the dwarf slouching along in a most dejected manner. He eat down with a sigh and turned his dull eyes upon me, then groaned as he assumed a most resigned attitude. I suggested a visit to the infirmary, but the elf would have none of it, so I asked him what had gone wrong. "Everything," he replied, "the May Festival at Parr Hall is a greater success than ever, the promoters are popularising temperance principles, and if they succeed, what is to become of our glorious Order? That is not the worst of the business either. One of the members of the Board of Guardians has had the audacious effrontery to insinuate that men interested in,' The Trade ' ought not to be voted to positions of honour." "And is be not right"? I ventured. The Manikin glared at me for a moment and then resumed his plaintive wail. "The 15th of July is getting dangerously near." " What of that" ? I queried. " Why the Insurance Act comes into operation on that date, and then, 0 Lor !" " But why dread the Insurance Act? " "The August order of the Tub have tried to keed people in ignorance of its blessings, they have treated it with contempt, criticism, scorn, and sarcasm, and yet the people have not risen against it ; it's on the Statute Book and comes into operation on July 15th." "Perhaps the poorer people suspect it may help them, and certainly the rich do not require much more help than they have already received." "That's it," groaned the:mascot," the poor do stand to profit by it, andiwhen they discover that in practice, what is to become of us, who warned the public against this atrocious measure ?" " But the Member is doing a little better," I suggested. " Humph! He was put up in the House to move some gim-crack motion cr other, and nobody took him seriously. You see the party at Westminster is terribly hard-up for brains, so they have to fall back upon any apprentice who chances to be handy and wishes his name to appear in the press. I mean—that is—l wish he had left that resolution alone for his own good." " What about the Town Hall Ward election ?" An unguarded expletive escaped the Manikin, then ha apologised and resumed the conversation. "You see, it's this way, against the wishes of some of our best members, our party decided to make this a party contest, though what the House of Commons and Welsh Disestablishment have to do with our Town Council surpasses my comprehension, Well, as you know, everything went wrong and our party had a • set-back which went down badly both at Walton and in Sankey-street. " " Perhaps the ratepayers in that ward have been thinking ?' " That's what makes ms feel so ill. Oa all these great issues such as Tariff Reform, Home Rule and Welsh Disestablishment —and even ward elections a few of our leaders can think for the party without the public troubling its head at all." " Then why should people be troubled with brains if they are not to use them"? " 0 you go to—anywhere you like, only I am going home, it only makes me feel worse while I talk to you."

div.head: 2aa,mmer, Sattifday, May, 4 1912.
div.p: The 2aa,mmer, Sattifday, May, 4 1912.
CROWNING THE MAY QUEEN. PRETTY SPECTACLE IT THE PAKR HALL.

Stately ceremonial and old-time revels attended the Crowning of the May Queen at the Parr Hall on Wednesday and Thursday evenings. It is not too much to claim that the Band of Hopo festival riders the most picturesque specthcle seen at the Parr Hall in the course of the year, and its remarkable popularity shows that even in this prosaic, bustling age, the people like to hark back to the simple pleasures and pretty pageantry 'which trnditionally heralded the incoming of May. This year one felt that there was a special appropriatenes3 in the rejoicings, for they began on May Day itself, and Warrington was to some extent brought into line with Knutsford in crowning its May Qmen at the very opening of the " merrie month." Although cur I, dal festival follows on much the same lines each year, it never lacks a freshness of. charm. The childrenniominate the scene and there is nothing forced or mechanical where they are concerned. They gloty in the parts they have ti play and throw themselves into the events of the even- ing with a buoyancy and zest which their elders may well envy. But even the " children of a larger growth" seem to be rejuvenated by the happiness and , delight of the little ones and view the ever-changing picture with almost PS much pleasure as if they .too had a share in it. • When the festival opened on Wednesday. evening, most parts of the hall were well filled. The platf ,rm I with its large gallery wa, however, unocxupied and it was in the massing of the 409 children who were to take possession of this spacious area; that one of the most fascinating features of the whole display was witnessed. At a call from the bugle a procession, impressive by its numerical strength and the beauty and variety of the costum-s, began to piss round the hall and on to the platform. 'I he moving wealth of colour made a picture of kaleidoscopic brilliance and

their parts with rare confidence and the I.all resounded with laughter. A series of national 53ttas and dances gave still another touch of variety to the entertainment ThP youthful performers, who had been trained by Spink-, went through some beautiful dances, characteristic of the f or sections of the United Kingdoot, with charminggrac and dignity and the delight of the spectators was evidenced by the rounds 'of applause. The solos were excellently stingily Irene Cunningham and Percy B )wers. Altogether the festival was worthy of the" merrie month," of the tempt ance cau-e, and of the organiza- tion which has promoted such a long and successful series of celebrations. A spPrial word of praise is due to Mr. Spruce for his t ificient management of the chorus. It was a joy to listen to the fresh, young voices as they rang forth in unison, and the various pieces were given v ith a whole-heartedness and full realization of the spirit of the compoeitions which betokened, very painstaking preparation. Mr. A. W. Clatworthy was a tactful organist and made as ef4ctive use as possible of an instrument which is the despair of musicians. The pianoforte accompaniments were shared by Miss Spruce, Miss M. Huston, Mr. C. Mills, Miss Fellows, Mr. H. B. Mellor and Miss Noden. Mr. G. Whitfield, as platform manager, is to be congratulated upon the complete success of his supervision. He had a capable assistuat in Mr. C. S. Fellows, who marshalled the procession. Mr. F. Gandy was, as usu .1, reap nsible for the impojtant duties of hon. secretary, and his as,istants were : Messrs. T. H. Elliott, It. Fell ,V4s and J. E. Pardee.

div.head: MRS. DODDS' SPEECEL.
div.p: MRS. DODDS' SPEECEL.

In her address at the opening of the festival, Mrs. Dodds described the occasion as " Warrington s Temperance Birthday." She hoped the children would grow up and keep the pledge which they had hitherto kept. all their lives. On saw a rosy vision of what War.ington might be if all the children who came under the inflience of the Band of Hope continued in the rauks of total abstainers and worked ent`iusiastioally for the cause. Warrington would be a very cliff rent place, as far as the drink question was concerned. (Ay plause). div.head: :E QUEEN, THE RETIRING QUEEN, MAIDS OF HONOUR AND ATTENDANTS.
div.p: :E QUEEN, THE RETIRING QUEEN, MAIDS OF HONOUR AND ATTENDANTS.

as the long line of notabilities in history and nursery rhyme, representatives of seasons, fl vvers and nationalities unfolded itself, the audience was repeatedly moved to expressions of admiration. Last of al), escorted by guards with drawn swo ds arid attended by maids of honour and train bearers, the retiring queen (Amy Spencer) made a stately progress to the thrcne wLich had been set up iii the centre of the gallery. When she Lad taken her place, the glow of many-lined electric lights added to the effectiveness of the ensemble. The children and audience then joined in singing the stirring hymn "S ,und the battle cry," after which the Rev. H. Ogden offered prayer Brief but well chosen words from the President (Mrs Dodds) followed, and then the entertainment was carried through without an interval and with a smoothness which did infinite credit to its organisers. The chorus "Hurrah for merry Maytime " aptly expressed the sentiment of the occasion and went with fine verve Mrs. Owen, on behalf cf the British Women's Temper- ance Association, having handed a haLdsome bouquet to the retiring Queen, the ceremony of choosing a a succesor was entered upon. A group of rollicking children on their way to the village green gave the keynote of joyousness to the proceedings. Jack Frost (Arthur Harublett),reluctant to resign his sway to genial sunshine, was banished from the scene by the Fairy Queen ( \laud Kirkland) and her followers who afterwards tripped a gracerul measure, for which they had been trained by Miss Monks. Then we had a successim of children ingeni- ously representing the various months. Thus January was on roller skates, February was armed with umbrellas, March appeared with motor veils, and April was decked with primroses. In order to decide between the respective claimants to the Throne, the plan of drawing lots was resorted to and Flora (Amy Littlewood) was successful, her good fortune being hailed with great satisfaction as promising good things for the temper- ance cause. While preparations were being made for the Coronation, George Tanner, who staggered beneath the weight of a huge j am pot, sang a delightful little comic song in praise of the cupboard " where the jam j»ts grow" with true boyish gusto. The pro- cession of the new Queen and her escort was carried out with all the pomp and circumstance of a regal function The two queens met on the platform, where the retiring ruler resigned her crown, sceptre and garland which were bestowed upon her successor. A lusty " hurrah " from loyal subjects broke forth on the completion of the ceremony, and her Majesty having ascended the throne, delivered with force and distinctness a short address of thanks. She was afterwards the recipient of a gold brooch, presented by Mrs. Dodds. Then began the revels which are indispensable to a true celebra tion of May Day. A. chorus "Queen Flora," with a tuneful melody and a captivating rhythm, was very tastefully sung. Then a troup of lads and lasses in quaint, old-time costumes, tripped gaily on to the platfor m to perform the maypole dance. Dexterously were the many-hued ribbons plaited in many different ways and the dance was executed in a finished manner which spoke well for the instruction received from Mrs. Whitmore. Britannia (R Fletcher), and John Bull (S Pemberton), accompanied by a detachment -of Jack Tars, next entered to do obeisance to the Queen. Following them came representatives of other nation- alities,who were introduced by &ha Bull Percy Bowers then gave a very creditable interpretation of that popular patriotic song Motherland," the chorus being taken up with enthusiasm. A delightful diver- sion was the action son " His Majesty the Baby " by the junior girls (trained by Misses Ireland and Baker). The little maids, clad in nightdresses and nursing dolls, gave the item with charming sweetness and simplicity, but the vigour with which some of them handled their precious charges was highly amusing. A chorus " We'll sing you a song ' introduced a pleasing duet by Ada Hamer and Florrie Watson. A contingent of boys, trained by Mr. D Plinston, went through a club drill with neatness and precision and fully merited the applause which greeted their efforts The voices of Ada Hamer and Florrie Watson again blended nicely in the duet " S r‘e the child " which they sang with •surprising feeling for such young vocalists. A number of girls dressed in while, and carrying dainty white umbrellas then sang a bright "Umbrella Song." rhe item proved one of the most novel, picturesque and admirably arranged of the programme. At the second verse maids from Japan, with paper parasols, appeared on the scene and they were succeeded by Dutch boys and girls with clatter- ing sabots and red umbrellas. In the finale, when the different coloured umbrellas were whirling round, the picture was one of sparkling animation and beauty.' The performers had been trained by Miss M. Isherwood. Sprighty servant .gills, with caps and aprons, sang of the joys of "Our night out " in piquant style. Their instructors were Misi J. Ellison and Mrs. Davenport. From the musical p •nt of view special interest centred in the part songs o e"bybot e body `s-'ePSliecchtneehi do choir. s Bmarn d" an d ‘ Spruce Summer's h‘ad his r of voices under perfect control and their crispSummer'se'ws well Come" chosen and finished interpretations of the pieces were not wanting in the finer details of taste and expression which are so essential to adequate treatment of part songs. In "Summer's Come 'the solo was most effectively given by Eva Tanner. For sheer merriment the palm must be awarded to "The Local Volunteers," an item which afforded the usual nondescript corps opportunity to indulge in weird and wonderful manoeuvres. The boys, who bad been trained by Mr. G. Shaw, took

Pa id of Hope, for obtaining 25 recruits. Silver medals for 15-24 recruits were awarded to Reginald Gallop Elsie Whitfield, Maud Kirkland and Pollie Fletcher Bronze medals for 10-19 recruits were received by Joe Macarty and Olive Ratcliffe, and white metal medals for 5-9 recruits were presented to Doris Owen, Ethel Owen, Hilda Wainwright, Thomas Brooke, J Sutton, May Barber, Albert leherwood, Flurrie Sandford, Harry Samson, Harold Pembertor,Utred Claric,,Wal ter Patin, Fanny Fisher, Evelyn Roberts. Band of Hope Diplomas were ginen to the following Bands of Hope which tad increased their membership by 50 pr Independent Methodists (Stockton Heath), Hill Cliffe and Stockton Heath United, and Cairo-street and Saukey Bridges Wesleyan Band of Hops. THURSDAY S PROCEEDINGS. On Thursday evening the hall was crowded and the performance was thoromOly enjoyed by all present Mr CE Parker presided and prayer was offered by the Rev W Cooper The CHAMMAN said he was glad to be associated with them in the work they were doing. The Band of Hope U.,ion had won all along the line. When he was younger it was thought Oat no one could be happy unless they took drink, but now they knew that those who did not drink were stronger and lived longer (hear, hear), ar.cl were far happier. He had been to the Garden City of Letchwonh, where there were no public houses—(applause)—and one result of that, along with better housing, was that the general death rate was only about one third of that of Warrington and the infant mortality was also about one third of the Warrington figures. During the evening the Queen-elect was presented with a handsome box of chocolates by Miss Parker and the retiring Q teen receive I a gold locket at the hands of Mrs Gandy on behalf of the National dand of Hope Union. div.head: EVELYN-STREET HEADMASTERSHIP. Warrington Teachers' " Disappointment and Dissatisfaction. " Memorials to the Education Committee.
div.p: EVELYN-STREET HEADMASTERSHIP. Warrington Teachers' " Disappointment and Dissatisfaction. " Memorials to the Education Committee.

At the meeting cf the ih'so rington Education CAmmittee on Monday evening the Director (Mr. J. Mo ,re Murray) read two numerously signed memorials from the teachers of Warrington with reference to the recent appointment of an outsider (Mr Alexander N. B. Appleton, of Wolverhampton) to the headmaster- ship of the Evelyn-street Council school. The that was born healteachers in the borough and read as follows :—We, the undersigned headteachers of Warrington, respectfully neg tolsapress our deep regret that, in the recent appointment of a head teacher in the boys' department of the Evelyn-street Council school, your committee has not seen fit to restrict the appintment to those already serving under the local authority, especially in view of the fact that among their number many are included whose experience and qualifications would fully entitleothem to consideration for the highest appointments 'under any education authority, and some also by long and arduous service in the interest of the public of Warrington have earned a right to preferential treatment. . The communication was signed by Mr. John W. Parker (president), Mr. Thomas W. An (secretary), and thirty-two other head teachers.

TLe Certificated Class Teachers' Association for- warded the following memorial signed by 237 teachers : —We, the undersigned certificated teachers of Warring- ton, regret that the School Management C Anmittea has decided not to recommend a Warrington teacher for the headmastership of Evelyn street Council school. This failure to recognize tin claims of the local teachers has caused intense disappointment and dissatisfaction. Our position has been placed before you both in committee and in the local press, and we desire to take this opportunity of once more bringing the question of local appointments before your notice. No comment was made upon either of the communi- cations, and the come: ittee formally confirmed the following resolution of the School Management Com- mittee :—That Mr. Alexander N. 13. Appleton be appointed Head Master of the Boys' department of the Evelyn Street Council school, his commencing sakry to b at the rate of £250 per Annum up to the 31st March, 1913, and to be increased or reduced after that da,e, in accordance with the Committee's scale of salaries, upon the average attendance of the department during that period ; his engagement to commence on a date to be hereafter fixed, and to be subjeA to the conditions set forth in the Committee's scale of salaries and the regulations governing such appointments attached thereto, together with the con- ditions of employment conjained in the Board of Education's code of regulations for public elementary schools in force for the time being.
