div.head: SHAKESPEAREAN COMMEMORATION PERFORMANCES. IMPRESSIONS AND REFLECTIONS. [By Alfred Perris].
div.p: SHAKESPEAREAN COMMEMORATION PERFORMANCES. IMPRESSIONS AND REFLECTIONS. [By Alfred Perris].

In my account of the ornate representations of "Richard III" and Jnliva Crrsar " given at the Royal Court Theatre on Thursday, Friday and Satur- day in last week, published in the " Examiner " of Saturday, I endeavoured to give some idea of the care and labour that must have been devoted to the accomplishment of the courageous if somewhat ambitious undertaking the amateur Shakespeareans— ' under the regis of Mr. Charles Law —bad imposed upon themselves. Oaly when engaged in as a labour of love can such devotion be sustained and it is gratifying that their efforts met with a substantial I measure of success. So far as regards the spectacular effect produced by the mounting of the plays, and the pageantry which was made such a strong feature in both drama., all was in the highest degree admirable. But in viewing the representations as in intention commemorative of our estimation of the genius of Shakespeare we cannot but recognise the fact that much greater prominence has been given to pictorial illus- tration, with all the modern aids to nhat is known as realism, than to the attainment of a cultured interpre- tation of the plays by a thoughtful, earnest and thoroughly exhaustive study of the text. In saying this I must not be understood as inferring that the entire cast gave evidence of inadequate study. There were notable exceptions, where the capacity of the a Aor and actress to evolve from his or her own con- sciousness a right and just rotion of the character impersonated, was conv;ncingly shown, and in some few cases there was also the ability to express adequately the conception so formed, but the lack of this power of expression in many of the members— ladies and gentlemen alike—detracted very largely from the effect of otherwise meritorious performances. There are, of course, physical limitations in every organisation which absolately prevent adequate expression of what is in the mind, but within the limits which are assigned by nature to every individual the success of the personation depends upon the vividness of the actor's sympathy and his honest rsliance on the truth of his own expression, in pre- ference to the conventional expressions which may be accepted on the stage. The conventional actor, either because he does not feel the sympathy, or feeling it, has not the power to express it, or has not sufficient energy or self-reliance to trust frankly to his own expressions, cannot be the part, but tries to act it, and is thus necessarily driven tp adopt those conventional moans of expression which have become traditions of the stage. But I must not stay to enforce my own opinions on natural and conventional acting. The point I am anxious to direct attention to is this. The import- ance attached to the elaboration of detail; and the infinite care and pains (not to speak of the expense) so lavishly bestowed on the spectacular effects have ben quite disproportionate to the attention which has been given (judging by the speaking and acting of the impersonators of the minor parts) to the render- i ig of the play in a manner according with the object and special province of a Shakespearean Society—that is to say, showing such an intelligent comprehension and illuminative expression of the text, in every psi t, that it shall be obvious to the auditor that the Society has a proper appreciation of its functions and that the fulfilling of those functions constitutes its raison &etre. Has this prime object been kept in view, and has the other important object—namely, the raising of funds—as an ourcome of these performances, in aid of the Infirmary, been allowed sufficient consideration in making arrangements for such corilly accessories, which may possibly absorb the greater part of the proceeds? I fear neither of these questions can •be answered affi matively, and it is to be regretted that the beauty of Shakespeare's poetry and the influence of his wonderful philosophy should be in:any degree sacri- ficed to the modern•craze for sensational effects, many of which are obtained at the cost of mutilating the plays and emasculating the sense—resulting only in mystifi- cation to the onlooker—and distressing the loving disciple who desires the pure milk.tof the word and resents the abstraction of any portion of cream. I have before p'eaded for a careful study of each play before any attempt is made to prepare it for representation on the stage, and I am quite sure that only by this means can it be hoped that a worthy presentation of any play may be given. The great difficulty in elocution is to be slow, and not to seem slow. To speak the phrases with such dis- tinctness and such management of the breath, that each shall tell, yet due proportion be maintained. Hurry destroys the effect, and actors hurry, because they dread, and justly dread the heaviness of a slow utterance. The art is so to manage the time that it shall not appear slow to the hearers ; and this is an art very rarely understood even by professional actors. With amateurs, nervousness accentuates the desire to hurry, and so it happens that when they have to express excitement or emotion of any kind they seem to lose all mastery over the rhythm and cadence of their speech.lf they would but study the style of really great speakers they would find that in passages which seem rapid there is a measured rhythm, and that even in the whirlwind of passion there is a strict regard to tempo as in passionate music. The acting of Mr. Law, lam constrained to say, creates the impression that be is giving us a good imitation of a bad m, del—ratler than a poor imitation of a good model. He mistakes violence for emotion, and tears a passion to tatters. The entire tendency of Mr. Law's acting and soeaking, as Richa-d and as Brutus, was to convince his most e ithu&astic admirers that he allows the craving far sensational effect to herd him into a use of unnatural means of expression. It would be much more congenial to my. taste had I been able to bestow the same commendation upon Mr. Law's acting, that I have already done in respect of his ability to organise and arrange productions of the character we have just had examples of, but those who know me will credit me with a willingness to do justice impartially. I am somewhat afraid, however, that the high pitch of Mr. Law's voice which is habitual with him, whether natural or acquired, will remain a bar to his entire success in t-agedy. Let me, before concluding these reflections on Mr. Law's performances, call attenticn to a feature in his acting of Brutus. To me it was most noticeable that Mr. Law's Brutus in one speech (the address from the pulpit in the Forum) was, metaphorically speaking, head and shoulders above his Brutus of any other scene in the play. Why? It can only be that more study had been given to this one speech than to any other portion of the play. I will not attempt to contrast the acting and declaiming of Mark Antony's part by Mr. Harold Smith with that of Mr. Law, in Brutus. Suffice it to say Mr. Smith's rendering of Antony's lines—those of them he was permitted (by the arrangement of the play as produced) to deliver— was as nearly as possible perfect. I think the example should be followed by every member of the seciety. They could not well have a better model for wise dis- cretion in action or well balanced tones in declamation, and his words are so clearly pronounced and nicely accentuated that it is a delight to listen to him. The difference between true and faulty elocution is that the one is convincing in its effect—every word with its full meaning sinking deep into the consciousness of the hearer—whereas the other has but a transient effect on the mind and in time becomes absolutely wearisome to the listener. The absolute control which Mr. Smith exercised over the modulation of his voice, and his careful conservation of energy and power, enabling I him to preserve to the end of his long and most exact- ing scene in the Forum an undiminished force for I the final sentences which are delivered to the excited citizens between their stormy outcries—culminating in the firing of the funeral pyre—exhibits him as a con- summate exponent of one of Shakespeare's greatest characters. I cannot say that I agree with the way in which the Forum scene is ended, or with the omission of the opening scene in the last act between Antony anG Octavius. The rendering of the part of Cassius by Mr. John Lowe showed conscientious study and an appreciation of the true spirit of the character which stamped him as the possessor of an artistic sense very much above the average. His mental grasp of the impulsive nature of Cassius was shown most explicitly, and the temptation to rant and whine which is very often yielded to by actors in parts of this kind was by him wiselywa sa t 0 resisted.ned frb y his His i ndheefirceine dignity, more especially in physical stature whets in repose. He has not so perfectly acquired the art of moving with dignity and grace on the stage, but he will improve, no doubt, as he gains experience. Mr. Harvey Adams gave a most distinctive rendering of the regal characteristic in Cm Bar, though he appeared to be obsessed by the idea that it is necessary to maintain throughout all his speeches the same slow

div.p: measured tones. There are moments, however, in which I think Cirsar himself might relax a little. There is a danger of the frigid monotone taking on an air of pomposity. It was apparent that Mr. Adams had given very careful study to this part and it was one of the most successful impersonations in the play. Mr. Victor Roberts, as the cobbler in the Ist scene of "Julius Cxsar " displayed a fair amount of appre- ciation of the humour of the part but showed a mistaken understanding of its subtlety by instituting laughter at his own utterances. If he had reflected be would probably have decided that such behaviour in the presence of two Tribunes would have resulted in rigorous punishment. The humour of the cobbler's part lies in his answering all the questions that are put to him with a semblance of respect for his interlocutars and in an almost deferenti el manner which precludes offence. Regarding the female characters in "Julius Ciesar'' though in both cases the ladies appeared to have formed good conceptions of their parts, they lacked the power to express the emotion which is necessary to produce the effect shown on their husbands. Miss Fairclough was much too cold and formal in her acting and Miss Tunstall did not manifest sufficient animation in her appeal to Ctrs ir, or evince the satisfaction which should have been apparent when it succeeded. • It really would be invidious to single out for special mention any of the a inor parts. There was a uniform desire shown by all in the pieces to do their best to make them successful, and success has followed.

div.head: CONVIVIAL FINISH.
div.p: A CONVIVIAL FINISH.
Presentation to Mr. C. D. Law.

At the King's Cafe, on Tuesday night, the wh, le of the acting members who took part in the production of "King Richard III." and "Julius Cirsar "sat clown:to an excellent supper to celebrate the _successful production. Mr. ARTHUR BROWNE was asked to take the chair, and with a few opening remarks congratulated Mr. Law upon the excellent acting and finish of all three performances.

An excellent programme was then proceeded with, and in an interval Miss Elsie lunstall presented Mr. Law with a tantalus in token of their appreciation of his successsful piloting cf the two plays, and the Chairman supplemented her remarks. Mr. LAW in reply said that he was exceedingly grate- ful for the beautiful present, and he should for ever hold it in remembrance of the happy period that had just concluded. He also said that when he had finished the six weeks for the production of Macbeth last year he thought it was the happiest six weeks of tis experience, but now the six months had elapsed for the production of "Richard lll."and "Julius Cinsar" he bad to confess such period was far happier, and he had thoroughly enjoyed it. He thanked all the ' members for their loyalty to him, and for their obedience to his ideas, and he was proud so say that he did not think that any Shakespearean production of an amateur description had ever been produced in England with more loyal assistance than he had had. He desired to thank Sir Joseph I3eecham for the loan of the theatre for rehearsals during the past six months, and Mr. Loader for the valuable help he had given him for dramatic hints whenever he felt himself in trouble. He also thanked the Chairman for the care which bad been taken to keep the production within financial bounds, and he more specially desired to thank Mr. Bullen, the hon. secretary. upon whom the "donkey work "of the front of the house had fallen, as he had spared no pains and no time in helping to bring the show" to a successful issue. In conclusion, Mr. Law said he desired in the future to have the pro' duction of the Shakespeare Production Society put on a proper basis before next year's Commemoration, and he had talked it over with the committee, wh) also agreed with him, and further that the committee should be enlarged, as there was too much work for such a small number, and he had no doubt before very many months passed a meeting of the members would be called with that object.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

Again patrons of the Hippodrome have had a real treat in this week's show and have manifested their appreciation by crowding the spacious building- nightly. "The Bargain" is the title pen to the realistic Western American sketch presented by Frank Ilayo and Company, which is fun of thrilling incidents and typically American. One gets an ides of the rough-and-tumble life led by our over-13(a cousins, and the brusqueness of the actot s is truly consistent with the general run of the sketch. J. H. Scotland greatly pleases with his old dialect songs which he gives in a deep, round bass voice. Albert Rees does justice t his title as "the eminent entertainer with the phenomenal voice" in a very clever turn. Not only has he a good tenor voice, but he can also mimic various musical instruments and impersonate musical stars in a most entertaining style. The Menzies greatly amuse in their absurdity, " The Suffragette " and some quaint witticisms are well received by the enthusiastic audience. Frank Powell is a comedian with an original style, and cleverly com- bines song and patter. His "make-up "too, is smart, and not over-done, as is often the case with comedians of this character. A very good instrumental turn is provided by Eunice and Zena, who manipulate the cornet and bugle in a musicianly style. Kitty Smart keeps the audience in a good humour by her character male impersonations, which she gives in a clever manner. Her songs are decidedly humorous and well chosen. Gladys Wingrove appears in a song and dancing turn with marked success, her dancing being very acceptable in iew of the fact that it is not accompanied by the usual "flip flap" banging, but it is done on more classical lines. The Sauteron Wonders give a neat and entertaining performance of jumping, kicking, dancing and singing. Some really remarkable high jumps are made by the male actor, and the lady proves a most able assistant. SPECIAL PERFORMANCES.

The performances on Thursday evening we!e in aid of the Titanic Distress Fund. In addition to the usual list of artistes, the well known Warrington soprano, Miss Marie Houghton, also appeared and delighted the audience by her cultured singing. Her rendition of "Nearer my God to Thee" was very expressive.

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

Next week's "bill" bids fair to excel it predecessors for in addition to Russell and Held the popular American entertainers there will also appear Fred Shepard, versatile comedian, Felix and Fisher in a phenomenal comedy gymnastic act, Burnell's Crazy Golfers, and Richard Finberg in a host of character studies aud other turns.

div.head: Girls' Club.
div.p: The Girls' Club.

The closing evening of the Girls'- Club, West-street, for the winter season, was marked by an enjoyable tea last Monday. Nearly seventy girls sat down to a substantial meal at 7 pm. Afterwards a concert, which was presided over by Mrs. Garnett, took place. Prayer was offered and a hymn sung. Songs were most ably given by Miss Jones and Mr Harry Griffiths and a reading by Miss Brown, while Miss Turton was the accompanist. Perhaps the most notable feature of the programme was a part-song "Swinging" most tastefully given by the girls of the Club. In response ta an encore they rendered a round " Humpty Dumpty." Mrs Garnett spoke cheerily to the members, and expressed the gratitude of the managers to Miss Beswick, the untiring and self-denyingj secretary, and to Mrs.Marchment the popular matron, also to those kind friends who had given long continued help to the work. Miss Dutton distributed the garments made and. stockings knit 'luring the season. Oranges were distributed at the close of the proceedings.

div.head: Warrington Woman's Word
div.p: Warrington Woman's Word
There is not a drop of pure blood in the body until it has passed through the kidneys.

For the kidneys are the blood-filters. From birth to death the blood is con- stantly flowing through them to be filtered. The heart pumps the blood, but the kidneys purify it. They strain out the uric acid poison and waste water and dispose of it through the urinary system. When the blood reaches the kidneys it is dark and poisonous, when it leaves the kidneys it is the purest blood in the body—all its impurities and waste water have been filtered out.

Every twenty-four hours the kidneys remove about 500 grains of urinous poison and three pints of water from the blood. But when they are weakened by a cold, ovenvoik, or excess of any kind, they begin to lose their power of separating the urine from the blood.

Then the poisonous waste they leave in the blood begins to make you feel heavy, dull and drowsy; you suffer from backache, sick-headache, dizziness or rheumatic twinges ; you have to be careful what you eat and drink,for meat, pastries, alcoholic stimulants, or too much tea are bad for weak kidneys. The water left in the system collects under the skin and causes the swellings of dropsy. There are urinary disorders and gravel. div.head: Borough Police Court
div.p: Borough Police Court

MoNnAr.—Before the Mayor (in the chair) Aldermen Evans, Bolton end Smethurst and Councillor Wilkinson, T Locker, Messrs W Furness, S Wright and W Roberts. A VIOLPST PRISONER..—MyIes Walsh, lodging house, Cloth Hall-larfl was charged with having been drunk, and also with refusing to quit the Higher Angel Inn and assaulting the police.—Mr. Cheadle, the licencee of the Higher Angel, said that about 7.40 on Saturday night the prisoner had refused ts leave hia premises and he had to call in the police. He had declined to serve the man because he was drunk and used the roost abominable language.—P.C. Kenwright said the prisoner struck him in the jaw and kicked him cn the shins and also kicked the publican. P.C.'s Shelton and Armstrong came to his assistance and in evidence P.C. Shelton said the prisoner was kicking like a madman.—Prisoner said he did not know what he was doing. He was very sorry but lately when he had had a few drinks he 'lost his head." He was tined 20s. including costs or one month's imprisonment. A LODGING-lIOCSE BRA WL.—Patrick Byrne, 9, Hill- street, was charged with unlawfully wounding Patrick Lovell on Saturday evening. The Chief Constable stated that at. 10.35 on Saturday night the prisoner went to the lodging-house No. 7. Hill-street under the influence of drink. Be had some bother with Lovell and went back to No. 9 where he 'mid it was his intention" to do" for someone before 12 o'clock. He picked a quart bottle off the table and struck complainant across the nose. The injury had to be treated at the Idirmary.—The case was adjourned for seven days. WIFE ASSAULT.—MichaeI Melia, 4, Platt-street, was charged with being drunk and assaulting his wife on Sunday.—P.C. Burton said about 12.45 on Sunday he heard a disturbance in Platt-street. lie found the prisoner lying on the ground and using very bad language.—Mrs. Melia, wife of the prisoner, said he come home about 1.30 on Saturday under the influence of drink and refused to give her any money. He went out drinking all Saturday, and when he returned he pushed her against the table. She fell and hurt her head. Her son came and put the prisoner out,. Melia, who made his 34th appearance, was tined ss. and costs. CivursN'S TIMELY ASSISTANCE.—Peter Murray, 53, Oliver-street, Mae charged with having assaulted Arthur Monks in Pinner's-brow on Sunday.—Evidence showed that the prisoner was drunk in Pinner's-brow about 9.15 on Sunday night. He was making use of bad language to some little girls. He became violent and Menke, hearing a policeman's whistle, went to the spot and found the prisoner kicking an officer. He struck both Monks and the officer. He tripped them both three times and topped Monks on the nosa. Monks' face and suit were covered with blood and his suit was ruined.—Murray was sent to prison for one month with hard labour.—The Mayor said the bench were of opinion that Monks had taken a very good course in assisting the officer in the performance of his duty. They were sorry for the manner in which he bad been maltreated rnd recommended that he should have a grant for the damage to his clothes.
TllE`,DAY.—Before Councillor Roberts (in the chair), Lieutenant Colonel Edelsten and Councillor Jackson

Holmes. WINDOW SMASIIINCL—John Marrat#, of 2, Lomax- sard, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and also with breaking eleven panes of glass at 2, Lomax- street, doing damage to the amount of 10s.—Marratt pleaded guilty to both charges.—A constable said he saw prisoner drunk and shouting in Lomax-yard, and heard he had broken the windows in the house. Prisoner refused to be quiet and he arrested him.—A fine of ss. was imposed in the first case and 10s. and costs in the second case.
THURSDAY—Before Mr A 3 Jolley (in the chair), Dr

Naden and Mr W Williams. A WINDOW SMASHER —Alphorsus Cullen, of no fixed abode,was charged with wilfully breaking windows to the value £ll at the Lion Hotel, Bridge-street, on Wednesday, and also with assaulting Samuel Worthing- ton. The Chief Constable said the prisoner was ono of the men in Warrington who were refused drink at the Lion Hotel Vaults. He had been refused the previous night and had smashed the windows with atones. He asked for an adjournment of the case for ssven days.—The application was granted. . - •

FRlDAY.—Before Mr S Wright in the chair and other magistrates. WIFE DESERTION.—Ernest Llewellsn, Liverplol- road, Sankey Bridges, was summoned by his wife Eliza for desertion and she asked for a separation order. Complainant said her husband turned her out of the house about eleven weeks ago and told Ler not to come in again, and her clothes were put out in the street. She got a situation in Lymm and her husband came to Fee her and suggested they should live together again. Mr. Steel, who defended, said the wife went away of her own accord.

div.head: INFIRMARY.
div.p: THE INFIRMARY.

A Visit From The Workingmen's Committee. It is a very happy idea on the part of the Board of Management of the Inlirmary to invite the members of the Workingmen's Committee and their wives to pay an annual visit of inspection to the institution, for it gives them an opportunity of judging for themselves of the practical usefulness of the work which they are so willing to support. The 150 visitors who were con- ducted through the wards on Saturday afternoon were much impressed by all that is done for the comfort of the patients and expressed their admiration of the devoted work of the medical and nursing staff. On entering the institution the guests were welcomed by the Mayor (Councillor Dr Joseph, one of the hon consulting surgeons), Mr J H Smethurst (the recently appointed chairman of the Board of Management) and Mrs Smethurst, and among others present were Mr Roger C Parr (honorary treasurer), Dr E J Fox (honor- ary surgeon), Mr John Fairclough (one of the vice- presidents), Alderman Burton (chairman of the Working Men's Infirmary Committee) and Miss Burton, Mr George Walker (vice-chairman), Councillor Jackson Holmes (hon. auditor), Mr fledley Taylor (hon dental surgeon), Dr Mason,Mr H Collin, Mr William Daintith, Mr N Cook and Mr J H J Hampson (secretary of the Institution). The visitors were escorted through the wards by members of the Board of Management, Dr Edward Fox, Mr Taylor and Dr Manson. At the close of the inspection all assembled in the large voicant ward at the top of the institution, where tot was served, under thedirection of the Matron (Miss Hammond) and where Nurse Tomlinson provided some pitno forte music. Several short speeches were de livered by Mr. J H Smethurst, the Mayor, Dr E J Fox, Alder- man Burton, Mr. G. Walker, and Mr N Cook.

£lO,OO FOR CHARITY, On Monday, May 13th, the Tenth Annual Volume of " Printer's Pie," edited by Mr W Hugh Spottiswoode, will be published by " The Sphere and Tatter, Ltd." The first Trustees who have kindly consented to act under the " Printers' Pie Trust " are Sir T Vezey Strong (late Lord Mayor of London), Cecil Harms worth, E.g., M.P., and Peter Keary, Esq., .I.P. Under the Deed of Trust GO per cent, of the income received from the £lO,OOO shares handed over to the Trustees will be paid to the Printers' Pension Corpora- tion, 15 per cent, to the other Charities which have benefited by the profits in the past, viz. :—The Royal Literary Fund, the Booksellers' Provident Institution, the Newsvendors' Benevolent and Provident Institu- tion, the Newspaper Press Fund, and the Artists' General Benevolent Institution. The remaining 25 per cent will be re-invested in other securities until the Trust Fonds accumulate to a certain figure, when the whole of the income will be divisable among Charities

div.head: ONE WOMAN AND ANOTHER.
div.p: ONE WOMAN AND ANOTHER.

Here is a letter, pitiable in its simple wording, and doubly pathetic because it might have been written by any one of thousands of Englishwomen. Mrs. Adams writes: —" I would rise in the morning, feeling more tired than when I went to bed. I was suffering from extreme lassitude and the all-gone feeling." How many women, if they had to deFcribe their bodily condition, would say just the same ? The pitiable thing about it is, that all this suffering, the backache, sick-headache, cold feet, sleeplessness, and general sense that life is not woith living are all useless, and could all be avoided by a little knowledge, which has been embodied in a book of private information for women, called Mrs. Lydia E. Pinkham's private text book. It may be had free of all charge from the address mentioned below. Contrast Mrs. Adams's description cf her misery with this :—" cannot tell with pen and ink what good Lydia E. Pinkham's Vegetable Compound did for me. Before I had used two bottles, I began to fell the buoyancy of my younger days returning. It is indeed a boon to sick women and I heartily recommend it." Is not this a contrast? And yet these statements are from the same woman. The medicine which made such a difference to her in a short time can be bought of, or will be obtained by any chemist--Lydia E. div.head: Examiner, Saturday, May, 4, 1912.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, May, 4, 1912.
HEALTH WEEK. WARRINGTON'SI3ART IN THE CAMPAIGN AGAINST DISEASE.

Warrington has taken a worthy part in the great national campaign against disease which, under the title of "Health Week," has been proceeding this week in many of the cities and large towns of the country. The object of the movement is to impress upon the public conscience the appalling tale of unnecessary suffering and loss of life, the need and ease of its sprevention, the fact that each person's health is mainly in his own hands, and the delight and power of perfect health. Although this is the first Health Week that has been attempted, forty committees have been formed in towns and villages and individual organizers great work in 150 other centres. Lancashire and Yorkshire have taken up the idea warmly, and doting the week there have been a variety of meetings, lectures and "health talks" in the big towns. Considering that there has been no past experience on which to rely, the celebrations in Warrington have, on the whole, been very creditable but if, as is hoped, "Health week" becomes an annual event, more enthusiasm will doubtless be dis- played. The churches set a good example on Sunday when from most of the pulpits of the town, the affinity of cleanlihess and godliness, and the importance of obeying the simple laws of health, were emphasised. Special afternoon services for men and women respectively were held under the auspices of the Church of England Bible Classes and the Free Church Council, and practical addresses on the individual and national aspects of the health question were delivered. At the day schools during the week, opportunity has been taken to instruct the scholars on hygienic sub- jects, the Education Committee having distributed among the teachers some excellent model summaries of lessons on health, c mpiled by the Agenda (Things to be done) Club, which must be credited with the initiation of a movement which, if followed out, should go far towards making England a happier, stronger and healthier nation. _ _

Although a great deal was done by some of the tradespeople to arrange a striking display of hygienic goods, we think more enterprise might usefully have been shown in thia direction. "Health Week ' pre- sented a magnificent opportunity of concentrating attenticn on quality and an energetic co-operative movement on the part of the tradespeople might have made the general effect much more impressive on the public mind. The most important feature of the local celebrations was the visit which the Mayor and members of the Corporation paid to some of the slum areas of War- rington on Wednesday afternoon. They saw scenes ieif squalor and hopelessness which made a meat impres- sion upon them and should lead to a determination to prosecute a housing campaign on strenuous and comprehensive lines. A large number of leaflets on health were distributed among the inhabitants of the courts and allyes. On Wednesday afternoon and evening the Mothers and Babies' Welcome, Academy-street, and the Cripples' Guild, Bold-street, invited visits fro-n the public and those who availed themselves of the opportunity of gaining first-hand acquaintance with the work of these deserving institutions were very favourably impressed with all they saw. On Wednesday evening the National Service League held a public meeting at which compulsory military training was considered from the health standpoint. At the Band of Hope festival on Wednesday and Thursday evening, several health characters—chit fly emphasising the value of wholesome food and exercise —were introduced

Yesterday afternoon, the sanitary works at Longford and Howley were open to the general public for inspection. Throughout the week some excellent health films have been exhibited at the Picturedrome. Exception- ally interesting and attractive sets of pictures depict a model diary farm, showing the methods adopted to ensure a scrupulr usly pure milk supply, and a "Baby rearing institution" where everything possible is done to ensure the rising generation a fair start in life. At the Town Hall last evening Dr. J. Coote Hibbert, medical officer of health, gave an interesting and instructive lecture on "Preventable diseases and how to prevent them." In the organization of the local programme valuable assistance was uiven by Mr. Wilfrid J. Rowland, secretary of the Guild of Help, who is also a member of the Agenda Club. MEN'S SERVICE AT THE PARISH CHURCH. " Appallingly Wicked Waste Among the Poor."

The Church of Englund Men's Bible Classes in War- rington held a united service at the Parish Church On Sunday afternoon. The Rev Lyndon Parkin, Vicar of Holy Trinity, Southport, was annonnced to preach but owing to a change in the train service, his place was taken at short notice by the Rev A J Bratt,senior curate at the Parish Church. In the course of his address he referred to the appallingly wicked waste among the poor He was not speaking of the thrifty, whe, considering all their chances' were a credit to the town. When the coal strike had been on about a fortnight he went into a house in his district on a warm afternoon and found an intensely poor widow who had six children. A great fire, almost large enough to roast an ox, was blazing up the chimney. The woman came to his house week after week for a conl or grocery ticket, and when he told her that he had to be careful with his coal and asked her why she was using so much, she had the effrontery to say " When this is gone I :shall be looked after. They won't let a poor widow starve." Two houses might be seen side by aide: One was always clean and tidy and like a 'little palace, although the man who lived in it received only 215., 22i., or 25a, a week ' • another house, although the tenant's wages reached 30s. or 355. a week, was like a pigstye, and dirt and everything which was disgusting predominated. We were weakening our men to-day and making some of them poor creatures. In many ways be did not think free education was a good thing, Free education might be necessary in certain cases, but in Fairfield and other wards parents could afford to pay a penny or twopence: yet they were given something for nothing to which they had no claim or title, and which tended to weaken their moral fibre and make them less manly and less womanly, Workers should have a living wage to enable them to live in decent habitations. But the lesson to be brought home to the people was that fresh air was a necessity and that there must be pure and wholesome food. The problem for the Health Committee and other bodies and the clergy was to bring home their duty to men and women. Whether they would have to make neglect criminal and impose a penalty be did not know. Men had said—and it would be so to the end—that they could not mike men sober by Act of Parliament. They could, however, help to make them sober. Let those who were organizing the health movement see that the message reached those for whom it was intended.

The Progress of*the Last Century. Preaching at St. Paul's Church on Sunday evening the Rev E E Peters asked the congregation to consider what a change in health administration had taken place during the past 100 years! A century ago there were open sewers, polluted drinking sources, pigstyes close to dwelling-houses, filthy bakehouses, and graves in the middle of large towns. The "Black Plague" and other plagues and the great fire of London removed a large number of insanitary dwellings, and caused other build- ings to be erected in their place, and it would be well in the present day if other insanitary dwellings in other parts of England were burnt down. The turning point in the history of public health was made in 157.5, when the first of a series of Public Health Acts was passed. Then the State for the first time began to take a real interest in the people, and then also rose up with their manifold activities and beneficial acts people to whom they owed a great deal of gratitude, notably the medical officer of health and the sanitary inspector. It was for that and other congregations to take a real interest in the affairs of the town and to age that so far as lay in their power Warrington was made clean and healthy, and even beautiful. " You are," said Mr. Peters, in conclusion, "your brother's keeper."
Rev... W.. Cooper , and the Housing Problem

At Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church the Rev. W. Cooper took for his text " No man ever yet hated his own flesh, but nourisheth and cberisheth it "and stated that the Old Testament code of laws for health and the New Testament example of Jesus Christ, left no room for the modern Church to ignore the laws of health. The sentiments of the text were essential to-day for the ordinary pursuits of life, for morality and for a robust Christianity. An ill-nourished physique was quite unequal to these demands in up-to-date activities. The legitimate methods for developing a healthy body were numerous and afforded wide scope for selection and be was glad that the Church regarded these with no unkindly eye. At the same time it was quite as essential to assist other members of the community in their efforts to attain health. The housing problem pressed for a solution. The preacher then instanced the kennels of a well known pack of hounds, built upon the most approved modern principles, but within 200 yards were homes inhabited by employees upon the same estate, in which the squire would scorn to house his hounds. This was a blot upon civilization. But in Warrington, it WRS not much better, for some of our slum property was a disgrace to our town. lie Wal glad to see that the week's programme in the interests of health included a Mayoral visit to some of this property. Another

welcome sign was that there was a desire to instal suittble persons in public office and be wished to re-echo the brave outspoken statement recently made to the Board of Guardians by a local clergyman. He urged his hearers to make this a christian duty of the first importance, first to attend te the laws of health in their own bodies, and then give P helping band to others who at in ignorance and need.

Services for Women. At St. Paul's Church on Sunday afternoon, a cervice for women was addressed by the Rev. Hendy-Cock, vice- principal of the Training College. A meeting arranged by the Free Church Council was held in Emmanuel Church, Bold-street, Mrs. Dodds presiding. An interesting and practical address was delivered by Mrs. Shilston Watkins, of Liverpool. At the Adult Schools.

At the three local Adult schools there were special addresses on health topics on Sunday. At the Academy Street school Mr. W. T. Flood, chief sanitary inspector, gave an interesting account of the sanitary administra- tion of the borough.—Early on Sunday mornings group of working men went round the Bewsev district "knocking up" members of the Adult School in Catherine-street, Bewsey-road, to enyble them to he in time for breakfast. At the conclusion of the meal, Mr Wilfred J Rowlaud, one of the local secretaries of the local celebration committee, gave a health talk on air, food, clothes, exercise and rest. An interest ng discus- sion followed.—Dr Naden spoke at the Sankey Bridges Adult School on housing, personal cleanliness, work and rest, some very useful and practical advice being given.

div.head: Rev. W. Reid and the Dignity of Humanity.
div.p: Rev. W. Reid and the Dignity of Humanity.

Preaching at St. John's Presbyterian Church on Sunday evening from 1 Cot. vi. 9-20 in connection With lir alth observance. the Rev. W. Reid spoke of the changed feeling which had come over the religious w rid in regard to the value of the human body. No longer a thing to be despised, tortured and punished, it was now coming into its own as an integral and indis- pensable part of the individual life. Christ had digni- fied fled exalted it, in constituting it a Temple of the Holy Ghost. The preacher told the story of Arch- bishop Wbately, who when dying revealed the pin he experienced in listening while his chaplain read the words of St. Paul as translated in cur Authorised Version : " Who shall change our vile body," and his satisfaction with the translation given in the Revised Version : "Who shall fashion anew the body of our humiliation." Nothing that God made was vile. It was because of theas expressions of God's regard for the body that we disliked to see the sloven, the boor and the fop. The man who could ba brought to regard the feelings of others in the expression of his manners. who could be induced to put his clothes on properly, and at the right time to exchange the scarf for a collar, bad gone some distance towards realizing that be was a temple of God's Spirit. In matters of temperance, said the preacher—and all forms cf intemperance were sin sgtinst the body—the man who atistained entirely from alcohol stood at a great advantage in the matter of health. Very earnestly did the preacher ask parents to wkely take into their confidence their b 035 and girls, when the right time came, as to God's mysterious processes for the propagation of life, rather than allow know- ledge corcerning these matters to come to them from less desirable quarters, impressing them with the fact that the body was the Temple of God's Holy Spirit, and that Satan sought continually to desecrate what , God had consecrated. While they might repair broken ' machinery, or re-light the extinguished candle, the flower that had been crushed could never, quite, be restored. The necessities of water, air, and sunshine were in turn referred to, and the fearful numbers of children in our schools, suffering from various bodily defects, drew from the preacher the remark that when we came to realize that these were consecrated temples, we would rise up and fight for their emancipation from every power of evil. His people were the onl3 body Christ now had on earth through which to minister ; therefore they mmt keep eyes open and keen, and muscles strong to work for Him," for ye are not your own, '43 are bought with a price," redeemed to serve.

div.head: FREE CHURCH COUNCIL
div.p: FREE CHURCH COUNCIL
MEETING FOR MEN AT BOLD-STREET.

Mr. C. E. Parker and Industrial Conditions. There was a fair attendance of risen at a special health meeting held in the Bold-street Wesleyan Church under the auspices of the Warrington Free Church Council. Dr .1 Bennett presided and he was supported by Alder- man Evans, Messrs C E Parker, E Wynne Jones and the Revs H Williamson and W Cooper. In his opening remarks, Dr. BENNKTT slid the object of the National Health Week was to make health the chief of topic concern during one week in the year. They all knew that a great deal was being done by health authorities, both Municipal and Parliamentary to diminish sickness and—what was perhaps more important to prevent it. They were all conscious of the fact that a great deal of sickness and a large number of deaths could be prevented. There were two classes of people who were responsible for the failure to make more rapid progress. There were those who did not help but

div.head: HINDERED SCIENTISTS
div.p: HINDERED SCIENTISTS

in their work—the anti-vivisectionists who would sacrifice thousands of human lives for the sake of not taking the life of the rabbit, etc. They were the most cruel section of the day. Then thore were those who seemed to obstruct thorn in their work and those who did not use the means already provided. There were also the anti-vaccinationists. Both those two belonged t 3 the "old woman" tspe, and were rightly termed antis." If the same proportion of deaths obtained now us throughout the 18th century, there wpuld be 130,000 deaths every sear from small-pox alone, whereas last year there were only _23 in Great Britain. Fortunately, in t, pite of

. TIIE CONSC I ENTIOUS OBJECTORS, the wisdom of the many ,counteracted the foolishness of the few whose only reason forl their action was ignorance of the awful history of smallpox. There were to-day three chief causes of death—alcohol, measles and phthisis. He dismissed the first cause in a word for they all knew the remedy to save 60,000 lives annually. There were 13,000 deaths from measles last year and the average deaths fromtbis source in Warring- ton for the last 10 years had been 50. In 1909 there were over 100. Those figures did not represent the evils which followed. There were ugly developments later in life which could be traced back to measles and they should do all they Gould to teach the people hoN to handle that diseade in its primary stages. The mortality was three times as great as from any other infectious disease. People treated measles with contempt and indifference and sometimes absolutely neglected it. In his opinion the chief cause of so many deaths from measles was smoke. He was sorry to say that the Town Council refused to let representatives go to the Smoke Abatement Covference a short time ago. He had never had a death from measles during his practice in the country districts. They became more frequent towards the centre of the town. If it was a question of housing, the town had the advantage, for the cpuntry cottage was less sanitary than a house in the town. Commercial prosperity attained at the expense of the community, was ill-gotten gain and false economy. They wanted a solution of the smoke nuisance and he felt sure that scientists could provide a substitute which would not be a loss to the manufacturer but would be a gain to the community. There were three main remedies for measles, a substitute for smoke, teaching the children to breathe through their noses, the prJvision of more open spaces (hear, hear)—and if possible to live in the open air. He specially
WELCOMED THE INSURANCE ACT

if only for the sanatoria benefits. They ought to do something for those who were suffering untold agonies from disease as well as afford protection for those on the sea. They should try to awaken the public conscience. The remedies for phthisis were fresh air and sunlight, absence of dust, physical development, wholesome food, and temperance was another matter which should be in the forefront of the remedies. If public opinion could be moved so that all citizens might become commissioners of health, they would find a solution to the housing and smoke question and thus help to prevent the burden of suffering which mankind was called upon to bear. (Applause). Mr. C. E. PARKER gave an interesting address, at the outset of which he said he wanted them to link that subject up wit'l the great Healer—Christ. The reason why Christ healed the sick seemed, to look upon them from every page of Sm.ipture. He thought it was because we had been so pre-occupied and had got such pre-conceived notions of the spiritual character of Christ's work that we had overlooked the simple lessons taught by His miracles. Christ healed the sick because they were sick and because they ought not to have been sick. It was an unnatural thing for them to be sick and that was why He healed them. Christ did not raise from the dead those who wtre old but those who were young and had no right to die Christ intended that we should live Gur full time. and it was part of .His gospel to bring health and holiness to the physical man as well as to the spiritual being. Christ had come into the world to redeem the whole man, body, soul and spirit. Every ill we suffered either as individuals or as a community was the result of some transgression of the laws of health. Probably most of those present enjoyed fairly good health. They were well circumstanced. Although there was stills great need for the whole community to know more about health, the question pressed most in con- nection with those at the poorer end of the social scale, those whom they thought of as living in the slums. Although he would not say that all who lived in the slums were unhealthy or that thoss who lived out of the slums were healthy, the former were generally the ones who needed more education in the matter or health. When they knew how so many who were living amongst them were injuring their health by alcohol and living poor stunted liver, and knew women whore interests in life and whose power to live healthy lives were very slight, and when they realised that ever so many children inherited the weaknesses of the parents, they must see how much there was to be done, and that out of town life there arose a great many serious ills they bad to tackle. In regard to infaat mortality, the speaker said a great number of deaths in the first year ef children's lives could be prevented if they only knew more about

health. (Hear, bear.) If they only lived up to what they knew, the mortality might be reduced from three to one. He was N ery glad that we were improving on the question of combatting consumption. He was I also pleased they had with them Alderman Evans, the chairman of the Health Committee, and that that com- mittee were taking the matter up with so much zeal and intelligence. In their work they wanted the moral support of the whole community. Without that help the work of the Committee would be very much I impaired. Better housing conditions had a great influ- ence on the question of morality. Probably they would all have heard of Letchworth which was a garden city and was progressing at a rapid rate. There the death rate for 190 S-10 was five per 1,000, and the death rate in Warrington for the sa • e time was 16. The infant morality rate of Letehworth for the three years showed that 47 per 1,000 children died in the first year of their existence and in Warrington it was 125 per thousand. In 1910 a record was made in Warrington. The people of Letch- worth were of the some class as those in Warrington and the conditions were tolerably ideal. There were, however, no licensed houses in Letchworth. They had public-houses, houses for public gatherings &G., but none licensed. How much that fact contributed to the health conditions he could not say but no doubt it was a very important contributory cause. There was a striking contrast between the infant morality rate in Warrington and in the Garden City. Unhappily the

div.head: INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION
div.p: INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION

which had been going on for 156 y-e-a;si'a hilst it had in many respects brought enrichment and C3M fort,had also created conditions in town life which were a disgrace to civilisation and we had been so busy trying to make money that we had not recognised the great evils which existed ultil recent years. To miss a great number of people together with no air space and surround them by factories and foul sir, produced the evil conditions , they were there to deplor3. It was for them all who ' believed in the power of the gospel to apply it in their own hearts and lives so that God's Kingdom might really be on earth as it was in Heaven. (Applause). Mr. E. WYNNE JUNES proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Parker for his excellent address and to Dr. Bennett for presiding, to Mr. Hickman the organist and Mr. Cook for his rendition of the solo " Lead Kindly Light." He thought they ought not t 3 leave the question of health for only one week in the year but to give it constant consideration. Dr. BENNETT in reply said they all felt the, were doing a public duty and they were glad to do it. For the young people to die was abhorent to God so that they need offer no apology for Inlling strz,h a meeting in His House.

div.head: Mothers' and Babies' Welcome.
div.p: Mothers' and Babies' Welcome.

An "At home " was held at the Mothers' and Pabies' Welcome, Academy-street, on Wednesday afternoon when many subscrioers and friends and lady helpers attended. A large number of the mothers also put in an appearance, bringing with them their babies which were, as usual,weighed to seo whether they were making satisfactory progress. Miss Pekes, inspector of rnidwiiei, gave a practical address on health. This was followed by a musical entertainment in which Mrs Townroe, Mrs Lloyd and Miss Jones (accompanist)took part. An excellent tea was served. A number of the helpers arranged to treat the mothers to a show at the Picturedrome, in order that they might see the special health pictures of baby culture:and a model milk supply.

The Cripples' The Cripples' Guild at Bold-street school was also thrown open to visitors on Wednesday evening and the public were able to see the cripples engaged in such work as mat making, basket work, drawing and fancy needle work. The Guild is contemplating extended action in the way of training afflicted members of the community to take a useful part in the battle of life.

div.head: NATIONAL SERVICE LEAGUE AND HEALTH.
div.p: NATIONAL SERVICE LEAGUE AND HEALTH.

On Wednesday evening a meeting was held in the Thewlis.street schools under the auspices of the National Service League. There was a fair attendance over which Mr. F. A. Frost presided. Be was supported by Mr It S P Poyntz (Oldham), and Mr B S Townroe. The meeting had been arranged to consider the follow- ing resolution "That National Service will be beneficial to the health of the nation."

The CHAIRMAN said be was deputising for Captain Crosfield who could not be present as he was serving the country in connection with the Territorial forces. They had met together owing to a movement which was on foot during this week in particular, to consider the health of the nation as a whole more particularly as it concerned the younger members, and those with the bulk of their life before them. There had been a lament- able amount of infant mortality which various towns and bodies were doing and had dons their best to combat. The National Service League was advocating that all youths of 18 years should have four months military training for the first year and two weeks every year afterwards, with the necessary drills in between. It had been suggested that the military training might be injurious to the health of the youth of 18. That meeting had been called to discuss the point with all its bearings as to whether the training would be injurious or advantageous to the youth going through that training, lie thought there was but little doubt but what it would be a decided advantage. (Hear, hear.) To take anyone from the slums, workshop or school, where they had been confined within four walls and possibly over-crowded at that, to take them and yut them in the open-air under healthy conditions with healthy food and recreation, and healthy discipline and work—he did not think that could do them any Injury. He understood that training would increase the chest measurement by two inches in the four months and that it would increase the lung capacity by 10 per cent. (Applause.) Mr Poyntz in proposing the resolution said some- thing must be done to improve the physical conditions of this country. For nothing could be more painfully obvious to those who moved about the great towns than the very low standard of physique which prevailed among the great masses of the population to-day. Other great powers of Europe took accurate statistics of the physique of all their young men of military age and so had a sort of national health barometer which showed them exactly where they stood and in fact enablr d them to take stock of their rising generation every year. We on the other hand did nothing of the kind, but went contentedly drifting along

div.head: VVN THE STREAM OF DECADENCE
div.p: VVN THE STREAM OF DECADENCE

with our hands folded on our laps, and our eyes -piously upturned to heaven in the sunny assurance that all must alwa3s be for the best in this best of all possible countries. "It's English, quite English, you know I " (Laughter.) There were a few facts familiar to all of them. Why was it that the height standard for the army had to be gradually reduced during the last forty years from 51t. Gin. to sft , and the chest measurement and weight, and even the tests of teeth and eyes be relaxed proportionately ? Why was It that our country bad been steadily losing ground in the last ten years in nearly every department of sport ? There were numerous other physical defects quite noticeable. It was a gloomy picture, but how could they Wonder at it all ? How could they expect, what right had they to expect, men to keep fit under our pre- sent industrial conditions—the crushing weight of com- petition, them d struggle for wealth. Penned up in those hideous centres working from morning till night in stuffy mills or ill-ventilated workshops how could they expect the great masses of our people to g3t enough fresh air and healthy out-door exercise to make them as fit as their forefathers on the soil. What was to be done? They of the National Service League had made up their mind. The sovereign remedy they proposed was a short course of military training for all young Englishmen without distinction of class or wealth to be preceded by a certain amount of simple military drill and miniature rifle shooting for every boy at school. (Applause). Mr. B. S. TowsnoE in seconding the resolution said ' he had been round that afternoon with the members of the Town Council and the Health Committee to visit slums. Some of them had not realised the filth and squalor in which some of their fellow-townsmen had to live. As they were proceeding through the courts all of them were asking : What is the remedy and what is the way out ? On listening to the conversation there bad seemed to him to be one common factor in all they , said. They feared the evil we had round us was so great and complicated that no one remedy was going to solve it and that it would not be done even by immediate legislation. They had all agreed that it was right to concentrate all efforts on the children---(hear, hear)—and that if they got the children strong enough they were making the next generation stronger. How would Nation a Service affect the children of the nation? They advocated compulsory military train- ing. Compulsory because compulsion was essential. If they had National Service to-day they would be able to put their finger on the weak points. With regard to the National Insurance Act be would say that a scheme of compulsory insurance always worked hand in hand with a system of military training. They recognised that it was not tight for tho State to do everything for the people and the people not to do something in return for the State. In conclusion he said that patriotism could he best shown both by ministers and miners, millionaires and poor men' by all using their thoughts and influences in seeing that other people were healthy and happy. The resolution was put to the meeting alrPclaarursieed. unanimously. Mr. BALL proposed, Mr. ASHWORTH seconded and Miss BROADBENT supported a hearty vote of thanks to all who Irtd taken part In the meeting.

11 Itu

Commons, Bradshaw was taking part in the buying of a very pretty piece of Bauble" for the town of Congleton. The Corporation Mace, still judged to be one of the finest in England, dates from that year, and it is said that Bradshaw chose for it the motto that can still be read "The ffredome of England by God's Blessing." The doings of the High Court are nitltters of familiar history and need not be repeated here. King Charles faced his Judges in the famous Hall of Westminster,John Bradshaw presiding. No one pretends that it was a trial in any ordinary and real sense. John Morley sums up the situation in a sentence. When King and Parliament went to war it was a contest of "Thy head or mine." The King lost and he paid the price. THE MYSTERY OF BRADSHAW'S DEATH.

The Restoration brought sore days for the enemies of the defeated King. The bodies of Ireton, Cromwell and Blake were dug up from Westminster and hung at Tyburn, the heads being stuck on poles. Estates were confis- cated and taken over by the King, among them that of Bradshaw. _ _ .

_ Mystery enshrouds the death and burial place of Bradshaw. It is said that like Crom- well he was laid to rest in the Abbey, and that two years later his mangled body was hung in chains at Tyburn. But none of these statements are confirmed.

In those days many strange things were done. To save men from the wrath of the second Charles, reports of their death were circulated and mock funerals made. Milton's funeral was thus announced and carried out, and the fiasco was so successful that his enemies ceased to look for him. Bradshaw died on November 1, 1659, and is said to have been buried with his wife (he married the daughter of John Marbury, of Marbuty, Knutsford) in the Abbey Yard. But there is no evidence for this, nor can we be sure that the minions of Charles 11. dug up the body to behead it. The mystery is heightened by a curious, and indeed extraordinary inscription that is engraven upon a cannon in Jamaica. This cannon stands as a monument at the top of a steep hill near Martha's Bay.

Stranger Ere thou pass, contemplate this Cannon nor regardless be told That near its base lies the dust of John 13; adshaw. Who nobly superirr to velfish regards Despising alike the pageantry of courtly splendour The blast of calumny And the terror of Royal Vengeance Presided over the illustrious band of flerces and Patriots, who openly and fairly adjudged Charles Stuart Tyrant of England to a public and exemplary death, thereby presenting to the amazed world and transmitting through applauding ages the meet glorious example of unshaken virtue, love and freedom, and impartial justice ever exhibited on the blood- stained theatre of human actions.

. _ Oh ! Reader pass not till thou lut,t blessed his memory and never never forget that rebellion against tyrants is obedience to God. Whether Bradshaw's body was carried to Jamaica, or whether the cannon has marked some English grave and been carried across the sea are questions to which we have not found an answer.

England might do worse than erect a memorial to John Bradshaw. Careful enquiry reveals a character marked by honesty and courage. He climbed the ladder of fame to find himself, apparently by no wish of his own, forced as a subject to sit in judgment upon his sovereign. We are slowly learning the worth of the great Puritans and the value of what they did for England. Westminster, Manchester, and Warrington have statues of Oliver Cromwell. St. Margaret's, Westminster, has a fine window to Blake. Why should not Congleton do itself the honour of a Bradshaw memorial? It is pitiable that the only memorial to his memory should be that lonely cannon reared upon the bleak hill-top of Jamaica. A.M.

div.head: CHILDREN'S CORNER, Conducted by UNCLE CALEB.
div.p: CHILDREN'S CORNER, Conducted by UNCLE CALEB.
SOME MORE HOWLERS.

I find that the list of schoolboy (and school- girl) blunders which I gave two or three weeks ago was very much appreciated. As I have a large collection (I never fail to put a really good howler in my note-book) a few more may be copied out for my readers to chuckle over. .

The Test Act of 1673 was passed to keep Roman Catholics out of public-houses. Henry I. died of eating palfreys. Louis XVI. was gelatined during the French Revolution. Gender shows whether a man is masculine, feminine, or neuter. James I. died from argue. An angle is a triangle with only two sides. Geometry teaches us how to bisex angles. Parallel lines are the same distance all the way, and do not meet unless you bend them. _ _ _

A parallelogram is a figure made of four parallel straight lines. Horse-power is the distance one horse can carry a pound of water in an hour. Gravitation is that which if there were none we should all fly away. A vacuum is a large empty space where the Pope lives.
--In India a man of cask may not marry a woman out of another cask. - - _
Thomas Becket used to wash the feet of leopards. Romulus obtained the first citizens for Rome by opening a lunatic asylum. The Rhine is bordered by wooden moun- tains. _ _ .

A renegade is a man who kills a king. The press to-day is the mouth organ of the people. A lie is an aversion to the truth. Women's suffrage is the state of suffering to which they were born. Tennyson write "In Memorandum." King Edward IV. had no claim by geological right to the English throne. George Eliot left a wife and children to mourn his genii. - THIS WEEK'S STORY. HE HAD BEEN THROUGH IT _ . _ •

The-s-treet-C-ricket match between 15a-r-adise Alley and Blower's-court had come to a sudden stop, for P.C. 24 had appeared on the score. The cricketers were lucky enough to escape with the exception of one little lad, who was pounced upon by the constable before he could get away. "Now then," said the policeman, trying not to smile "you're going to be punished, my lad. What's it to be—a summons or a hiding ?" "Gimme a hiding," said the youngster,wearily. "One more won't make any difference. I was the Umpire." A TRUE FABLE.

too! Next day a smile went beaming clown that very selfsame street.

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
THE TEE 1 11.

Sound teeth are not only essential to proper digestion, as noted in these columns last week ; ignorance respecting them, and neglect of ordinary dental precautions, are undoubtedly answerable for many other physical ailments. In days so enlightened that quite a number of municipalities have adopted the health week idea, such things as I have just indicated may almost be said to be axiomatic; but more useful facts are likely to be discovered as time goes on. That the condition of the month may adversely affect one's vision was a revelation to me, but that it is so has just been exemplified in a striking instance within my own experience. Readers will be aware that I have taken peculiar interest in the Royal Eye Hospital, Manchester. One of the latest cases coming under my observation there was that of a baker's apprentice who had developed a mysterious eye trouble. Dr. Bride, the resident house surgeon, attributed the cause to bad teeth, and recommended the patient to have the lot extracted. That was done with the result that he now bids fair to make a thoroughly good recovery. I mentioned the case to a medical man who rather prides himself on his know- ledge of such matters, and he admitted that Dr. Bride's diagnosis came as a new theory to him.

William Booth, as he then was, resided at Brighouse, in the West Riding and in one of the Halifax circuits. The head of the circuit was North Parade, Halifax,and the chapel-keeper, Hudson by name, was about the age of the preacher now in question. After his amazing organisation has achieved world-wide fame and right up to the old chapel-keeper's death (which occurred only a year cr two ago), General Booth never visited Halifax without going for a little friendly chat with Ur. Hudson. When I last repotted the General's lecture on "The work of the Salvation Army," I remarked how jealously the members of his staff guarded him. sparing no pains to ensure his comfort and anticipating his every want. Only in one slight particular, so far as I noticed, did any oversight occur. Prior"to the opening of the proceedings, I had inad- vertently hung my overcoat in an anti-room which was supposed to have been reserved for the General's private use. After the meeting I blundered into this apartment, supposing it to be unoccupied, and there was an officer at-ting aar valet to the wonderful old man—helping him to change his coat, indeed, the General being in his shirt sleeves at that moment. Of course, I seized my belongings and beat a hasty retreat ; but I could not help seeing that the old man's arms were extracrdinarily thin. Most absteinious of men, be strictly limits and regulates his diet according to the principles of the vegetarian cult ; and attributes to his simple and plain living his rare vigour and vitality which enable him to constantly preach and lecture here, there, and elsewhere, besides personally supervising the work of his vast organisation and attending to all sorts of details. His energy is apparently boundless. THE SALVATION ARMY. One may say the same of the whole of his system of religious effoit and social regeneration. According to the latest statistics which I happen to have at hand— and the figures I am about to quote were issued shorty after the General's characteristic doings in Australia, where he went two or three years ago to make arrangements for his scheme of emigration colonies so far as it applied to that continent—the Army is e&tablished in fifty-two countries, and for its
