PAIN AND THE SEXES. It was at that same hospital that I tested chat is set forth in the opening paragraph of last week's " Women's Chat," wherein Professor Claire's asser- tion in St. Bartholomew's Journal than women can tolerate pain and privation better that men is referred to with evident approval. I had myself previously suspected it to be so, and I put it to two or three nurses and a ward-woman of several years' experience. These concurred in the opinion that there was really no difference—that brave, uncomplaining sufferers, capable of enduring slow agony and of going to the operating theatre without a tremor or apparently an unworthy selfish thought, were common among both sexes, as likewise were the " soft," the querulous and the needlessly trcublesome. In face of such testimony, I for one consider it no longer safe or fair to dogmatise as to the point raised. IMMORT AL.

When I read last weeks paragraph on economics of infant mortality, I was tomehow reminded of an experience in an industrial town some 30 years ago. The registrar of births ard deaths there was an original sort of character. Ile invariably had ready an apt quotation for any situation, however suddenly created, and for whatever turn the conversation might take—until one chanced to mention the source of his income. Then w( uld his countenance immediately fall, and be would shake his head and sigh- "Surely there never were such times. This has been the worst year of all. People will not die ! Preachers may endeavour to assure them that death is simply the soul's change of residenoe ; but they cling most obstinately to the old roof tree. It is in vain that one cites Addison as holding that no frail man however great or high, can be concluded blest before he die ; they'll none of it. Old Fortunatus describes IDeath as a lean fellow who beats all conquerors ; but I I must say be takes his time about it in this part of the globe. I've only made a blessed half-crown or so this week up to now. It's a poor game to be on when one has to depend on folk that won't die ! 'A short life and a merry one,' say I—l mean for others; as it is is, how are such as I and the undertakers to make even a bare pittance? What the doctors are about, I can't make out ; they've no consideration nowadays for some of us whom they were supposed to work with formerly." INFANTILE DEATH-RATE. But to get back for a moment to that clamant ques- tion of infant mortality. Not so long ago Mr. Wedgevvood, M P., received from the President of the Local Government Board a return showing the aver- age infant death-rates in 1905 and 1910 in those county boroughs which have adopted the Notification of Births Act. Some striking reductions were shown as in Grimby, where the decline was from 174 deaths under one year of age per thousand births to 118 ; Ipswich from 144 to 92 ; Lincoln frcm 118 to 82; Merthyr Tydvil, from 193 to 143 ; Norwich from 174 to 119; Sheffield from 167 to 118; Stockport from 168 to 132 ; Birmingham from 154 to 134; Bradford from 144 to 116 ; and Stoke-on-Trent from 117 to 126. So that we appear to be getting on. A BAD MEMORY.

Large families are not fashionable in these times— these degenerate or advanced or wise times, according to the reader's point of view. It was not ever thus, as most of us have reason to know. My great grand- fathers on both sides bad many olive branches ; but, then, they were poor clergymen, one having a living in York, and the other being vicar of Fewston for upwards of 50 years. The latter baptised the Venerable Dr. Coßyer, of New York, and married that famous blacksmith-divine's parents. Not only did these earn the blessing pronounced upon him that bath his quiver full, but my grandparents likewise put a literal inter- pretation upon the ancient command to be faithful and multiply. One of them used jocularly to say that he was the father of three times thirteen children, and what time the uninitiated in his audience were figuring it out by mental arithmetic or with the aid of the multiplication table, the old man would confide to the one nearest to him the simple explanation : number 13 having died, another took the vacant place and that also expiring,a third succeeded to the position, making the third 13. But I have allowed myself to be drawn aside, for none of the foregoing had a bad memory when the number of the children was con- cerned though I think any of them might have been excused for losing count once in a while. What I set out to write when I penned my present sub-headline was that according to a certain district medical officer of my acquaintance, a resident, on being asked how many children she had, repli,d that she had only three living, and when a fourth came running into the house as they talked, threw tip her hands and exclaimed: " Well, I declare, I'd plump forgotten him! Ay, there's fosver on 'em." GENERAL BOOTH. When first I knew the G.O.M. of the Salvation Army, he was a minister in what was then the Methodist New Connexion, now merged with the Old Bible Christians and the United Methodist Free Churches in one United Methodist Church. The Rev.

work employs cicse upon 14,000 officers. The bare number, of stations and societies in working order reaches 1,243, and no small part of their work is to issue sixty-four periodicals in twenty-four languages, with a circulation of about 1,200,000 copies at each issue. As was remarked at the time, the side of the Salvation Army's activity that the public generally sees —the public street meetings and pro- ccs.tions with bands, and the reports of tours is comparatively speaking, but a small part of its work. What the public does not eee is the whole army of wotkers who are engaged in the conduct of institu- tions, Lome,, and houses to cope with every imagin- able form of poverty, misery and vice, but the General told of these things as much as possible in his addresses here on Sunday, especially in the lecture at the Elippedreme. As to the exclusively religious propaganda, the Army demands from all who would enter its ranks acceptance of a set of six "Articles of War," and insists on total abstinence from intoxicants as another prime necessity. These "articles " must be signed by all recruits before enrolment. This side of the work has been severely criecised by one and another, and I have copies of many of these adverse comments by me as I write; hut, although I am not myself a thick-and-thin supporter of the General and all his works, the present is not the time to introduce matter of that kind.

div.head: WORRIED ABOUT UNEMPLOYMENT.
div.p: WORRIED ABOUT UNEMPLOYMENT.
Labourer's Body Recovered from the Mersey.

Mr S Brighouse conducted an inquiry at the Warring- ton Coroners Court on Monday into the circumstances of tbe death of Walter Griffiths (58), general labourer who recently resided with his sister at 4, Leonard-street, who was found drowned in the Meray at Howley on Sunday. Mary Jane Lowe said deceased was her brother and he had resided with her for some eight weeks, fie was lame and suffered a great deal and worried a great deal about being unable to obtain work He was also concerned about his son, Thomas, who was in failing health. About eight o'clock on Saturday he went out and she had not seen him alive since. Mrs Griffiths. widow of the deceased, 8, Gas-street said that about nine months ago deceased broke up, the home in Pocket-street and went into the workhouse She went to live with her 80D. She hal noticed that deceased IN as worried about work. Thomas Griffiths (brother) 25, Greenall-street, said deceased seemed to dread having to go back to the Union hospital. Witness saw him at one o'clock on Saturday and gave him sixpence and promised him a pair of trousers. He then looked very depressed and worried about not being able to get work. Thomas Richardson, 31, Wellington-street, said that at seven o'clock on Sunday morning he was on the path leading from Howley Quay at Paddington Lock when he saw a body floating about 12ft. from the bank. He drew it to the side with a wire and sent for the police. Detective Holland said the water would be about Oft. deep. lie had examined the body and found no marks of violence. Th jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned."

div.head: MUSIC-HALL ARTISTE'S DEATH. Sad Case at Warrington.
div.p: MUSIC-HALL ARTISTE'S DEATH. Sad Case at Warrington.

At the Warrington Coroner's Court on Monday, Mr. S. Brighouse held an inquest on the body of Agnes Wilkes' a music-ball artiste, who was found dead in bed on Sunday morning at her fathers' house, 41, Bank- street by her blind brother. Thomas Burke, the father of the deceased said that up to three years ago his daughter was on the stage as a wire-jumper. She was married to Edward Wilkes, also a musio-ball artiste. She was 23 years of age and about two years ago was asked to undergo an operation but refused. She bad complained of her cheat being bad and had been subject to colds. She had been to Blackpool and returned home on the Saturday night. She had got some sweet nitre and asked for a cup of hot milk and went to bed. He knocked at her door about 7.45 On Sunday morning but got no answer and thinking that the milk and sweet nitre had made her sleep be did not try to waken her. He went to church and on corning home heard she had expired. Sarah Madden, 31, Bank-street, gave evidence to the effect that deceased had often complaned of having pains in the chest. She callad on her (witness) on Saturday, about eight o'clock and said she had come from Blackpool. She asked if her niece could go for a penny- worth of swest nitre. This was obtained and witness did not see her alive afterwards. Dr. Geary said he was called to the house about 10 30 on Sunday. He had known the deceased for some time. The Coroner : Is a pennyworth of sweet nitre a big dose ?—Yes it is a big dose for anyone suffering from heart affection. Witness added that deceased had died a natural death, heart failure being the probable cause. A verdict in accordance with the medical evidence , was returned.

• Kathleen'. O'Gorman (87), stepped In front of a Salford trarncar last Saturday morning in spite of the cry of the driver. Ile almost brought it to a standstill, but the front just struck her and knocked her down, and she died later in Salford Hospital. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned at the inquest.

div.head: GREAT INSURANCE ACT,
div.p: THE GREAT INSURANCE ACT,
HOW IT AFFECTS WOMEN.
BY H. B. LEES SMITH, M.P.

Women under the Insurance Act contri- bute 3d. a week—a penny less than men. To this the employer adds another 3d., and the Government adds the equivalent of 2d. In the normal case, therefore, the 3d. contribu- ted by a woman is transformed into Bd. when she is ill and in need. The benefits which women receive are:

(1) SICKNESS BENEFIT.-7s. 6d. A week. (2) DISABLEMENT BENEFIT. ss. a week until the sickness is cured. If it becomes permanent, so that she is no longer able to earn her living, she receives a pension of ss. until the age of seventy, when the Old-Age Pension begins. (3) SANATORIUM BENEFIT.

The Act initiates the first national cam- paign against the great white scourge. Every woman contributor has the right to whatever treatment will do most to help her. If necessary she will be sent to a sanatorium, and if she has a family or dependents her sick pay of 7s. 6d. a week can be ,used to help to keep the home together while she is away. The campaign against consumption, how- ever, must be waged not only on behalf of those who are insured, but on behalf of every man, woman, and child in the community. The Act, therefore, provides that if the County Council (or County Borough Council) in each locality will provide half the money to extend Sanatorium Benefit to the wives and children of insured men the Govern- ment will provide the other half. This will enable every public-spirited 1.5 cal authority in the country to make the provision for the treatment of consumption universal in its (4) MATERNITY BENEFIT. —No section of the Act will be more popular than that which provides for Maternity Benefit for in- sured women, the wives and children of in- sured men. Thirty shillings is payable when a child is born, and if the wife is insured as well as the husband there will be another payment of 305., amounting in all to £3. A million mothers will receive this benefit in a year. While an insured woman is receiv- ing her Maternity Benefit there are no con- tributions to be paid to the insurance funds, and no arrears counted when she returns to work. (5) ADDITIONAL EENEFITS.—The benefits described do not exhaust the list. The actu• aries upon whose calculations the Act is based state that a prudently-managed society will be able to pay these benefits and have a considerable amount of money left. The money saved may be used to give additional benefits, such as Old-Ago Pensions beginning at sixty-five instead of seventy, higher mater- nity pay, and a number of others from which a society may choose those which it prefers.

The most complicated clause in the Act is that which refers to married women. Insur- ance for women presents one- special diffi- culty. They will in most cases come into the scheme at the age of. sixteen. Being young, they will usually be strong. The sick- ness benefits that they receive will, there- fore, amount to considerably less than the contributions that they pay. Year by year their societies will make a profit out of them, and will accumulate what in friendly society finance is called a "transfer value" on their behalf. In the majority of cases women will after a few years get married, leave employ- ment, and pass out of insuranoe. This is the special difficulty which their position pre- sents. Unless special provisions were made they would lose their transfer value, and ob- tain no benefit from the contributions that they had been paying for years past. The provisions with regard to the transfer values are the starting-point of the very difficult clause which deals •with married women. If upon her marriage a woman leaves em- ployment she is entitled to her transfer value. First, however, a certain deduction must be made from it. If her husband dies and leaves her a widow she may be compelled to return to her employment. But here a. difficulty will arise. .Friendly societies cannot accept elderly 'widows as members, because since they are elderly their sickness is likely to be so frequent as to eat up more than the value of their contributions. One-third. therefore, of the transfer value is retained in order that, if she becomes a widow, societies may be compensated for giving her full benefits. This leaves two-thirds of her transfer value; it can be used in two ways:

(1) She may take it in direct benefite. The House of Commons, however, decided not to give it aa a cash grant on marriage, as much of it might be spent in "celebrating the occa- sion." It is, therefore, to be given either

- (i.) As a maternity grant of ss. a week dur- ing the four weeks of confinement. If her husband is insured this will be in addition to the ordinary maternity grant of 30s. Or (ii.) .ss. a week during any period of sick- ness or distress such as the unemployment of her husband. .

(2) She may continue as a voluntary con. tributor, and use the transfer value to in- crease her benefits. The ordinary voluntary rate of sickness a week is, however, so high that only a few women of the comfortable class could afford to pay it. Married women therefore are not allowed to become ordinary voluntary contributors, but a special Married Women's Voluntary Insurance scheme has been provided for them. In this the contribu- tion is SLR, week, to which the Stat 9 adds Id-

For fins rne•wuisen, wnen iney nee nt, receive medical attendance, with medicine, and sick- ness benefit of ss. a week for the first thirteen weeks and 3s. a week for the remainder of the illness. If the illness become permanent they receive a pension of 3s. a week until they are seventy, when the Old-Age Pension begins. The only other difficulty in the insurance of women was that connected with domestic ser- vants, nurses, and others who, in many cases, are already paid wages while they are ill. They need, therefore, not sickness benefit, but something to help them when they are getting too old to work. The Act meets their case. If they wish to give up sickness and disable- ment benefits they can join a society which gives superannuation allowance or other benefits to suit their own requirements. The great value of the Act to domestic ser- vants can be seen from these provisions. It has been generally acknowledged that the Act will be of the greatest value to ordinary women workers. The one large class on whose behalf an agitation against the Act has been raised are the domestic servants, yet there is no sec- tion of workers to whom the Act will be a greater boon than to them. Most of them get married; on marriage they will receive their transfer value, and will have something as well as themselves to take to their husbands. But of those who do not get married many find their way to the workhouse, because there is nothing to help them through the years when they are getting too old for service and are not yet qualified by age for the Old-Age Pension. The Act enables them, if they do not need sickness benefit or disablement benefit, to have a superannuation allowance to tide them over these dangerous years.

div.p: (The next article of this series will be b 7 Mr. H. Mamieid, M.P.] • WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. Mr. A. M Mitchell's Protest against a Tradition.

The annual metting of the Warrington Mir,' District C.uncil was held in Beasey Chambers on W.- oneaday afternoon. At the outset Mr J C Sutton (clerk), pre. sided and there were also present :—Meaars W Furness, J IV Knowles,P Longton,G Mather, .J 13a11,J Backnouse, W Houghton, C Brooks, the Rev A M Mitchell, Dr Murray, Dr Sephton (medical officer), B S Newcombe (surveyor), H Burnago (assistant surveyor) and F Kerfoot (inspector). ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN. Mr 3 BACKHOUSE in proposing the election of Mr G Mather as chairman said by his devotion to the Council be had deserved the honour they were oon- ferring upon him. Dr MURRAY, in seconding, said Mr Mather was a man who took a deep and untiring interest in the work of the Council. The Rev. A. M. MiTcYtEtt. said be did not know what the order was, whether it was a tradition or not to elect a new chairman every two years. If it was a tradition be thought it was a mistaken one and might be brokrn. He thought that seeing the members were elected for three years, they ought to have the same chairman for the whole of the time, lie was sorry that such an important council should hold such ideas. He proposed the re-election of Mr. Baekhouse.

Mr. BAC/MOUSE, however, declined and Mr Methyl' was unanimously elected. • Mr MATHER thanked them for having elected him and said with their assistance he hoped he would be able to conduct the affairs of the council as well as they had bcen conducted in the past.

VICE-CHAIRMAN. On the proposition of Mr BROOKS. seconded by Mr BALL, Mr W Furness was elected vice-chairman. hlr FURNESS, in response, thanked them for the honour they had conferred upon him, and added his eulogy to the worth of the Chairman. The various committees were re-elected en bloc. GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.

_ The minutes of the General Purposes Committee were read and confirmed. They contained the following resolution :—" On the motion of Mr Furness, seconded by Mr Mather, a cordial vote of thanks was passed to Mr Brooks as chairman and Dr Murray as vice-chairman of the committee for their services during the year:' SHOPS ACT. Mr. Houghton asked who were the local authorities to administer the new Shop flours Act. The Chairman pointed out that the Clerk had had no information on the subject.

A BID FOR A BRIDE
BY BLANCHE EARDLEY, Author of " Kitty Bell—Actress," "The Lady
Killer," &c.
CHAPTER XXIV. FACE TO FACE.

'When Paul Steinway was standing outside the elaborately-carved marble portico of Clifford Havvke's town house, his face fell into its old set and thoughtful expression. The last time he had seen the financier face to face had been on the day when he had refused to let him have an introduction to the diamond merchant who had been wanting a partner, and on that night had occurred the strange fire in his Claverton-streot rooms, which he now more than suspected had not been the accident it had been supposed at first. In answer to his ring the footman who opened the door said that Mr. Hawke was out, but would be back soon, if h,e would like to leave a mess. "No, I don't think I can do that, but -I will come and wait if I may, as my business is im- portant, and I can't come back. You may tell Mr. Hawke that Mr. Smith is waiting," he added. The man, seeing nothing remarkable in his request, for his master had many visitors come to him on business, took him into a small room that was neither a library nor a study, but a combination of the two. As he glanced curiously about him l'aul Steinway smiled grimly. It appealed to his sense of humour that he should have stormed the house of the man who was now congratu- lating himself upon having shaken off his old enemy. He gazed round the room with in- terested eyes, feeling the personality of the man whom he had beaten in spite of every- thing. An old bureau stood in one of the windows, and he saw that one of the drawers had been left a little open, and a scrap of paper was sticking out. A moment's hesita- tion, and then he opened the drawer and took up the little half-sheet of soiled paper and looked at it curiously. It would be amusing to learn something of his enemy's life, though he knew enough already. The next moment he gave a soft exclamation, and crushed the scrap of paper in his long, lean fingers. "The hand of Fate!" he muttered, "it can be nothing else, for I have only learnt it just in time!' The door- behind him opened quietly, and as he turned the man who stood on the threshold breathed deeply. "Well, so we meet again!" Paul Steinway said slowly; "it is a pleasure I feel sure you did not anticipate, Mr. Hawke! You recog- nised me in spite of my changed appear- ance?" Clifford Hawke came slowly into the room. His face, which had gone deathly pale, had shown no further sign of the great amaze- ment that had seized him, only his mouth twitched when he spoke. "So, you are not dead?" he said quietly. "I certainly had no idea that we should meet again, though, of course, I am delighted to see you looking so well and flourishing!" Paul Steinway smiled. "I am sure you are. The fire that was generally believed to have been the cause of my sudden and inexplicable end failed to accomplish what it was intended for, as I did not happen to be sleeping in the house that night!' "Ah!" Clifford Hawke answered. "You were indeed fortunate! I congratulate you! But I am interested to know why you should call on me." "Because I had a desire to talk to you again, to tell you one or two things that I hope, in consideration of the old days, you will make an effort to listen to. If you clonit," he went on, "I am afraid I shall have to make you listen." "You seem to be quite interesting," was the mocking reply. "I hope you will justify • your words and be as amusing as you pro- mise to be! I must warn you to be quick, though, because there is another man wait- ing to be interviewed; an feol of a footman had evidently given me his name and for- gotten yours!" 'I will be as brief as possible!" Steinway said gravely. "The last time we met, Clif- ford Hawke, you had the whip hand, and I had to obey, but now I think the positions are reversed, all the tricks are in my hands. I know what before I only suspected," he went on, "that you killed Nat Radbourne out in Tarragoola, and it was his claim that you 'jumped % and made a fortune out of! Clifford Hawke gave a contemptuous laugh. "Really! I don't see why you should refer to that old affair—more than twenty years old, is it not?" "It doesn't matter if it is twenty or a hun- dred years old," Steinway retorted quickl,y, "murder is murder, and poor Radbourne is not the only chap you have tried to hurry to a premature end," he went on, "there is my- self and Jaapar Tennant, your first wife's brother!" An ugly smile parted Clifford Hawke 's lips. "You seem to be pretty well acquainted with the picturesque side of my life!" he sneered. "May I be allowed to suggest that you are a little late with your startling evi- dence of my criminal career? There is such a thing as proof, you know, and your melo- dramatic statements are not very dangerous to me, since they lack any proof of the slightest degree!" "Don't be too sure!" Steinway replied quietly, "I have one man whom I can call as witness to the fact that you killed Nat Rad- bourne out Went, and as to the 'attempted' murders, it won't be difficult to bring them to your door!" Clifford Hawke broke into a short laugh. Now that he had recovered from the first shock of meeting his old enemy face to face, he began to put together the chain of evi- dence that he had obviously worked up against him, and didn't see much cause for fear, though he recognised that Steinway could make it very awkward for him in cer- tain quarters if he began to noise his suspi- cions abroad. "I don't suppose you came here to talk all that stuff without some good reasons," he said at last. "You have a price for your silence, I know of old—well, you have only to spit it out, and if it's fairly reasonable I might pay it, though you look sufficiently prosperous to make me doubt whether you need money!" he sneered. Steinway flushed to his forehead. "You are right. I don't need money. I have lifted myself out of that miserable con- , dition when I was willing to be silent for a consiaeration. Now my . Trial.- rC a heavier one "Really! Then I am afraid I cannot pay it !" was the swift retort, "and now I must, ask you to go, for I have to join my other' visitor, and as a parting word let me tell you that I am not afraid of you or your lately- acquired knowledge concerning wliat you are pleased to call my 'infamy'! You may do and say what you like, but you will find it AB difficult to hurt me now as you did before !" Steinway's eyes flashed suddenly. "Shall 17 Well, I am content to wait. I shall not have long now, for this is my day, Clifford Hawke—or John Ford, whatever your many names are, and the day of my re- venge is close—very close at hand!" "Your revenge!" Clifford Hawke's eyes grew sombre. 'So you prate of revenge like the hero of a penny novelette! You are amusing, Mr. Steinway! It would be inte- resting to hear how you propose to hurt me!" Paul Steinway leant forward, his fingers gripping the back of a chair in the intensity of his feelings. "To-night when I go back to my rooms I

have a chance. It will be looked upon as a form of blackmail by a needy adventurer, and you will find yourself in a cell!" "1 am not afraid," Steinway said slowly. His last outburst had cooled as suddenly as it had begun. "I am not afraid. I can prove my words, and as I have plenty of money I shall not be accused of blackmail. My City name is 'too well known for that! "

"Your City name !" Clifford netlike laughed scornfully. "You really are the most consummate scoundrel I have ever met! May I enquire what your City name is? I ihould like to know it before I ring the bell for this farce to be ended I" "My City name," he began slowly, "is quite an ordinary one—it is Smith, plain Smith." Clifford Hawke gave a queer strangled little sound in his throat that might have been surprise—fear—anything. "You are lying !" he said hoarsely, "you have taken that name because you have heard something in the City !" Paul Steinway did not immediately reply. He was fascinated by the almost magnificent courage and bluff of the man who had fought so long and bitter a battle. There seemed to be no way of cornering him nor of forcing him to admit anything. lie wondered curiously how his next "bomb" would be re- ceived, or whether that too was half-sus- pected!

"I once vowed that I would have my re- venge on you!" Paul Steinway said slowly, "I waited a long time for it, but all things come to those that wait, you know, and so has this. I made my plans so well, that no :Otte with whom I came in contact guessed that, I was anyone else but what I said I was—en American come to dabble on the English mar- ket. I took good care to find out everything concerning your financial deals, and learn- ing of your interests in a certain mine called the Sapphire Spring I gradually bided my time, and then began to buy—and now I have bought out all the other shareholders and only you and I remain, Clifford Hawke, and in a day or two you will be forced to sell out. I shall be the sole owner of all the shares in the Sapphire Spring, and you know what that means!" he concluded grimly. Clifford Hawke knew only too well what it meant for him to lose control of the Sapphire Spring. With it went the remaining rag of his credit and he would in all probability be "hammered,". disgraced, and made an ex- ample of! His father-in-law had already in- timated to him that he did not approve of his recent business transactions, and then he had upon his already Aurdened conscience the memory of a certain transfer which he had forged in Mr. Traine's name. He glanced up and met Paul Steinway's calm accusing eyes, and a red hot rage swept over his brain like the heat wave of a monsocß,in :the tropics. "Curse you!" he said thickly, "so „it's you, is it, you infernal blackmailer! ,You have accomplished your task of retaliation very well. I congratulate you upon your business acumen, which has served you very well. Even I am forced to admire you, which no doubt will please.your he sneered, "we are evidently equals in business!" "Even in that I have won the game," the other answered, "you see that I have kept my word, and ,you are no longer the great man you were "The fight is not yet over," Clifford Hawke replied with a grim smile. "Ile laughs best who laughs last, and I may yet win the odd trick in spite of your clever- ness."

Steinway shrugged his shoulders. "Then you had better hurry up, for by this time to-morrow you may not be the master of 'lour actions as you arc to-day. You've had a good run for your money; it's other people's turn flow! "You know that I have a second wife!" Hawke said slowly. "I am not pleading for her, but I should like you to remember that in trying to hurt me you do her a far greater hurt!" it is strange that you should think of her when you have never thought of the first woman you married, and who loved you, while your present wife has never been in love with you, and was married by a trick!" Paul Stein- way retorted coldly. A <NA, brick-red colour stained the dther's face, then faded, leaving it deathly pale. "Be careful!" he snarled, "don't go too far; I am not done yet, ,you know!" Steinway touchul his pocket significantly. "I have a protection now; I came prepared!" ulitford Hawke bit his. lip. There was something so impassive about the man whom he had so long hoped was out of his way, that almost insensibly he began to feel afraid of him, a sensation that he had never had before in all the shady undertakings of his life.

Suddenly he uttered an exclamation, and, following his gaze, Steinway saw gazing at them through the window the crafty Oriental ace of a Chinaman! For a moment only it stood there, and then vanished, and when he turned to look at Ma companion, Steinway saw that he had fallen into a chair with an expression of rage on his face that was strangely out of all proportion with the inci- dent.
Then 11. mtrange thought sprang into his mind. He remembered deeds that Orientals did for heavy payment, and who knew what link there was between Clifford Hawke and the evil-faced Chinaman !

"There is one thing I want to know," he said abruptly, "one question the answer to which matters more to me than all the rest of yliur N illainous deeds put together, and that is, where is the young girl who has been your wife's protegee all the time oi her marri- age r' Clifford Hawke drew a deep breath. He had regained his composure, and his watchful eyes had noted the expression of anxiety that

'Can I?" Hawke laughed insolently. All his old assurance had come back, and he looked once more his former successful self. "1 suppose you know that Lottie Bond is under age?" he said softly. Steinway nodded. "That is nothing to do with you,e' he said, "you are not her guar- dian

Clifford Hawke rose to his feet and lit a cigar with deliberate coolness, then he turned to Steinway and said slowly, "No, I am not bailie Bond's guardian. Shall I tell you what I am, though?" he added, his eyes rak- ing the other's grave face maliciously, "I stand in a relationship to her that gives me full control over her! Steinway started. "What go you mean? What fresh Beg are you telling?" he said roughly.. "No lies this time !" was the mocking re- tort. "What I tell you now is Gospel truth. Lottie Bond is my daughter, my child by Alys Tennant, and the law is on my side where she is concerned I"
(To be Coatinued.)

div.head: SCIENCE AND SENSE.
div.p: SCIENCE AND SENSE.

Foods should be associated in such a way as not to (fiend the appetite or burden the digestive powers. Thus say the men of science. And the same learned people are continually urging us to eat Currants, not occasionally, but regularly and often. Because they know that so many folk do not appreciate the value of Currants. There are those, for instance, who are not aware of the enormous amount of pure nutriment contained in currants. But when it is explained that the best of all foods is Nature's grape sugar, and that Currants are composed almost entirely of that constituent, then they appreciate why Sir Francis Laking (the King's physician) and other eminent men are so emphatic in their advice to every- body to eat Currants every day. Whoever takes the trouble to compare the values of the various foodstuffs must learn that Currants are four times as nutritious as lean beef. Surprising no doubt, yet scientifically correct and, therefote, literally true. They will also learn that Currants are in every way desirable, not only on account of their delicious flavour, but because of their great inherent value. Good plain food with Currants is the best of diet, and every hunaewife should make a point of studying Currant cookery in detail. The presence of Currants in the meal means a well-nourished family, therefore a healthy and happy family—and that is what everyone dealt., s.

div.head: CONTINENTAL GOLF.
div.p: CONTINENTAL GOLF.
Le Zoute-Knocke, In Belgium.

So much having been written and said about the magnificent 18 hole golf links of the Zonte-Knocke near Ostend during the past five years, that Massey's saying that " they are the finest golf links on the Continent" is pretty well known all over the United Kingdom to every lovs r of the health-giving game. But it is not only Knocke-Le Zoute itself, with its beautiful sandy beach and its picturesque hamlet that attracts countless tourists every sui mer ; there are quite unrivalled surroundings to this favourite summer resort by the sea. Quite tear by is Bruges, the old Venice of the North, an ancient city of very great historical interest, certainly after Ghent, the most beautiful of the Belgium medimval towns. Begians say that there is but one Bruges in the world ; every year thousands of tourists come to admire its striking architectural features, its picturesque sights, its numberless artistic treasures, precious relies of its former splendour. The Hotel de Ville, dating from 14th century, and the belfry, (1248) with its chime of 49 bells, immortalised by Longfellow, rank amongst the wonders of Europe. Bruges is thirty minutes by tram from Enocke. - _ .

A little further on is the wonderful city of Ghent, which will in 1913, be the seat of a great International Exhibition. The city of Ghent contains more monu- ments of first class interest than any other three towns in Belgium together. It is known as the city of flowers and ancient monuments, and no visitor to Belgium should leave without seeing Ghent in details. Close by is fashionable Ostend, too well known to need description. There are many pretty walks round Knocke. One Is the Sluice (l'Ecluse), a pretty little eld town, 20 minutes via Westcappelle by light railway. Plots of land are for sale, on the sea front, among the dunes in tbe woods and in the village. The condition, regarding style of building and hygiene are required of all intending purchases of land, as they form a guarantee tows rds the future development of the estate. A special office has been opened in London at I, Southampton Row, W.C., • for the distribution of booklets, prospects, etc.' concerning the Le Zonte golf • links and the hotels of the locality. These will be supplied gratis and post free on application.

div.head: WEARY OF MATERIALISM.
div.p: WEARY OF MATERIALISM.

A cbaptd erected at the Wigan Infirmary through the generosity of a benefactor, who preferred to remain anonymous, was opened on Monday by the Bishop of Liverpool. The Bishop observed that materialism, which lad so long reigned among tbern in certain quarters, but which now appeared to be on the wane, had wade its influence felt bath in the world of medicine and surgery as well as in the Church, and bad often led to the ignoring of the Spirit in the treatment of disease. The guardians of the poor, in their desire to benefit and uplift and brighten the lives of the inhabitants of the workhouses, had built commodious balls for concerts and entertainments, but regarded it as no incongruity to require that public worship, even the Holy Communion itself, should be celebrated in a building redolent with the odour cf a recent meal or associated in the minds of the worshippers with dramatic performances or the jests of a conjuror. It was Lecause that (impel was one sign among wany that the people of the land were sick and weary r f materialism, which could neither ennoble duty, gladden life, nor fill the future with the splendour of a great hope,that they bailed its epening that day,and launched it with a most thankful heart on its career of blessing to glorify God and to comfort and ennoble man.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Fewer American Visitore.—With the opening of the Royal Academy next week, the London season comes into full suing, but it appears likely that there will be fewen foreign vhitors thin umml this year. The leading hotels, which cater especially for An eric inn, report a considerable falling off in their bookings, for which various roosons are assigned. The main one, no doubt, lies in the fact that this is the Presidential election year vni all Americans nut want to be ,in the United Strifes In August. Then not a few wealthy families bare been placed in mourning by the sinning of the Titantic, whilst many Americans alio frequently come to this country on a summer visit have been made nervous by the Atlantic disan.t•r. That terrible affair, in addition to its immense direct loss, seems likely to considerably diminish the number of money-spending Americans on this aids of the Atlamic this year. Jane Austen.—Batb, where the memory of Jute Austen has been commemorated by Liao erection of a bronza butt in the Pump Room, was the home of the novelist from 180 l to 1805. Jane, tits daughter of a country clergyman, was twenty-fire when the family removed from Steventon to Bath, and after her father died in 1805, she resided In Hampshire until her death in 1817, and was buried in Winchester Cathedral. The six stories ft hich comprise Miss Austen' s chief contri- bution to English literature, have given Ipr a place among the classics. Macau'ey, Tannyzon, and Scott. were amongst her ereatest admirers, but denpite their encomiumns thtre are many who cannot understand why Jane Aust in is numbered among the roll of memor- able writers. Tee n ,vet render of to-day, outside the small band of the well-rend, kuows little or nothing of Jane Austen. She does not del in sensations, or enlarge upon improprieties. An el p unent is the most daring episode in all her writings and mild romance is rather out of touch with modern taste for realism and vicarions thrills.

Whist Drives.—The public whist drive is a form of entertainment which does not appeal to the fashionable world. It, is patronised almost exclusively by that class of society whiLh is spelt with a small s, and despite the threatening aspect of the law on the subject, quite a hundred or more of these progressive whit competitions have been held weekly in London through- out the winter. Now the High Court has decided that pul-lic whist drives, at which prizes ars given, are illegal. It was thong, t that if the value of the priz,s was announced beforehand, irrespective of what was taken at the doors, the law could not interfere, and this is still the opinion of leading ccuasel. But the law on gaming can be interpreted in many ways, and it seems there is Wit in force an Act of Henry VIII., which prohibits all and everyone from playing cards, except at Christmas time. That only shwa a nebulous state of things which r«pired to be put right. Upon the whole, whist drives are an inutosnt form of recreation. They have been taken up in countless neighbourhoods, by hostesses, church guilds, clubs, dc., and have at least served some useful purpose in releving the humdrum of social life in village and suburb.

The Advantage of Being Prepared.—The weather wise assure us ti-at time holds a glorious summer in store. I.Vhether their predictions will be verified or not, there will perforce be some spells of hot weather, and to prepare for these is the manifest duty of every woman who studies her comfort—and that of others—as well as her appearance. On a tropical day, the mere glance at a woman dressed in dark heavy garments, adds to one's personal discomfort, and mattes one feel hot and uncomfortable. The new fashions, and this season's new materials have been for some weeks on view, and nothing oan therefore be gained by delaying necessary purchases. On the contrary much may be lost, for dressmakers are not yet reshec., and have the time to give due attention to original ideas and individual designs. Then, the prettiest of the new materials are generally caught up by early shoppers, it theref) re behoves the wire woman to take time by the forelock in the flatter of summer clothes, as in most other things. Two-Colour Tailor Afades.— Different shades of one colour, m-re especially in the popular grey, are quite a feature Of the new fashions in tailor-modes. Pale shades are combined with steel and slate colours. Directoire styles are particularly attractive in two colours or sna des when intended for smart wear. Bolero coats in a modified form will be worn with Shantung and linen dresses for the summer. In some instances they are long, in otters short, and the former are by far the most becoming, because the gap at the back is absent. These little coats are generally cut away in front and finished with a wide frill of lace or lawn on the left side.

The Basqued Blouse.—The basqued blouse has "caught on " and in lace is a very attractive garment So too is the cuirass, ahich somewhat resemblas it, and suggests a use for an embroidered scarf, which may no longer be required for its original purpose. The scarf must be cut in two equal parts, sloped and fitted to the shoulders,rounded or cut square at the neck and trimmed to match the skirt with which it is worn—a belt keeps it in place. The basque has shown itself capable of great variety and already it is seen with long points with panels and with tabs. The effect of a coatee is obtained when the idea Is carried out in taffetas, thus it serves a double purpose, since it can be worn over a lingerie dress. Transparent lingerie blouses are mounted over flesh-coloured chiffon and those women who find dead white trying, will avail themselves of this really pretty notion. A striking combination of colour has been seen in a black and white voile blouse, which had a flat collar of scarlet satin. Blouses of net match the new tailor-made silk skirts and have no decoration beyond innumerable tucks. Crocheted Revers and Novel Neckwear.—Those woman who are clever with the crochet needle, can make of coarse tan-coloured cotton, most eff.ctive as well as the most fashionable colours for their tailor- rrades. Although used on materials of every hue, these trimmings are perhaps at their best on white or putty- coloured cloth, and the deep sailor collars and pointed culls are particularly attractive. Another appropriate trimming for tailor-mades is the wide draped revers in rich corded silk used with smart serge frocks. One piece dresses usually depend for individuality on the lovely lace collars that adorn them, and these are of the quaintest, oddest shap2s. Collars of shot taffetas are taking the place of feather boas. These are a variation of thick taffetas ruche with pinked or frayed edges. The silk is folded in the centre and the edges are bordered with feather trimming. Like the ruche with frayed ends, these collars fosten at the side, two pointed ends falling over the shoulders. Slaws of Fashion.—Men generally scorn till idea that they are slaves of fashion, but they are so' all the same almost as much as women. For the past two or three seasons, they have heel wearing straw hats, with narrow brims, rather an absurdity for summer headgear, hut one notices that this year they are to be permitted straw hats with wide brims. The" mere r..an " is also greatly affecting spats, a taste he has apparently acquired from the feminine fashion of wearing light coloured gaiters. We have long been accustomed to socks of vivid hues, but these will be largely hidden by the spats, of which the more noticeable are white and the less daring fawn, yellow and brown. Upon the whole however, blue appears to be the predominant hue in the colour scheme of the men's shops.

div.head: Padgate. Wesleyan " Mayflower " Bazaar.
div.p: Padgate. Wesleyan " Mayflower " Bazaar.

For a considerable time the Wesleyans of Padget* have been preparing for a bazaar, the object of which vsas to reduce the outstanding debt of £7CO upon the new school premises. On Thursday—favoured by beautiful weather—the opening ceremony took place, Mr Alderman Bennett presiding. After the hymn " Who givest all," the Rev II Williamson led in prayer. The Chairman then called on the Rev E Morgan to make a statement. In the course of a short, felicitous speech, the rev, gentleman referred to the happy inspiration which had suggested the name" The May- flower bazaar." "You sir," said be, turning to the Chairman," are our captain." Mrs Dodds is the lady who is to launch the vessel and instead of the pilgrim fathers of the original" M 53 flower " our ship is to be "manned "by the" Pilgrim mothers." Speaking of the illness of Mr and Mrs Wm.Bennett,which prevented Mr Bennett presiding at the opening ceremony as advertised Mr Morgan said he suggested that a message of sympathy be sent to cheer them under such trying conditions. . . .

In the course of his remarks the Chairman promised to convey to his parents the kind expressions of sympathy and goodwill voiced on behalf of those present by their pastor, He was pleased to be able to say that both Mr. and Mrs. Bennett were steadily improving in health and they sent by him affectionate greetings for those present, and as an evidence of their interest in the bazaar and its object, the sum of £2O. After incidentally congratulating Mr. Wright on the brief synopsis of the history of the church and school, the Alderman proceeded to speak in eulogistic terms of the personal worth and kindness of Mrs. Dodds and invited her to furmally open the bazaar. In a particularly appropriate and neat speech, In which not a word wag wasted, Mrs. Dodds referred to the pleasure it gave her to be present for the opening of the bazaar. She said she had recently come across a passage of Scripture which bad impressed upon her the lessons of neighbourliness and mutual help, and although she had always regarded the people of Padgate as being wealthy and self-reliant, she was glad when she was invited to be present. She emphasised the lessons taught by the Puritan pilgrim fathers who left England simply for freedom to worship God in their own way. She had great pleasure in declaring the bazaar open. At this juncture Mrs. Dodds was presented with a small bouquet of choice roses by Muter J. G. (Sonny) Bennett, and a similar compliment was made to the Chairman (in the form of a buttonhole) by Miss May Tunstall. A vote of thanks to Mrs Dodds and the Chairman was proposed by the Rey E Becket, seconded by Mr T B Duckworth and put by Rev It Morgan. This was carried with enthusiastic applause and the chairman replied in suitable terms. Besides those already mentioned on the platform were Messrs. Wright and L. Bennett, secretaries to the Bazaar Committee, and Mr S P Silcock, F.R.1.8.A., the architect of the new premises, while in the large audi- ence were the Rev John and Mrs Gunnell, Rev H and Mrs Middlewood, Mr Frank Harris (circuit steward) and Mrs Harris, Mr and Mrs G Weaver, Mrs Becket and Mrs. Gladding. The stalls were tastefully decorated and crammed with articles for sale. A special feature was the flower stall which occupied the centre of the room. It was formed by a rowing boat with mast and sails kindly lent for the occasion by Mr Platt of Warrington, and designed to represent the historic "Mayflower." The effect of the boat tilled with flowers and plants was very pretty. " Charming," seems to be the only word to describe the Quaker costumes worn by all the stall- holders and lady helpers. Did many of them but realise bow much this apparel enhanced their charms, we should doubtless hear and see less of those hideous and grotesque examples of sartorial art which ruthless fashion imposes from time to time upon the fair sex. The stalls and stallholders are as follows :—Congrega- tional Stall : Mrs Morgan, Mrs Dackworth, Mrs Brough, Mrs Cottrell, Mrs Lunt, Mrs fireball, Mrs Hughes, Miss Smith, Miss Morgan, Mother's Meeting Stall : Mrs Houghton, Mrs White, Mrs Thornton, Mrs John Smith, Mrs Newton, Mrs lizard, Mrs Ward, Mies Eaglesfleld, Miss James, Miss White, Sunday SchoJl and Guild Stall : Mrs Wright, Miss Bennett, Miss Richardson, Miss Edith Bennett, Mr Plinston, Mr Proffitt. Pound Stall: Miss Brough, Miss Wright, Miss Lillie Mellor, Miss Annie Ball. Penny Stall : Miss Lillie Sykes, Miss Harriet Cooper, Mica Annie Sutcliffe, Miss Clarrie Tunstall, Miss Gwen Bennett. Bran Tub: Miss May Dawson, Miss Elsie Fryer. Men's Bible Class Stall : Mr Leech, Mr Appleton. Mr Harold Tomlin, Mr Herbert Monks, Mr Woods. China Stall : Mrs Gandy, Mrs Arthur Bennett, Mrs Leonard Bennett, Miss Gandy. Market Stall : Mrs Tunstall, Mrs Dean, Mrs Frjer, Mrs E Andrews, Mrs Thomas Worrell, Mrs James Worrell, Miss Morton. Flower and Basket Stall: Miss Lillian Wright, Miss Elsie Bennett, Miss Marjorie Bennett, Mrs Howarth, Miss Nicholson Miss Muriel Bennett and Miss Howarth. Refreshment Stall : Mrs James Bennett, Mrs Proffitt, Mrs Plinston, Mrs Guest, Miss Andrews, Miss Mason, Miss E Mason, Miss Britch, Miss Appleton, Miss Duckworth, Miss Lunt, Miss Gilbert, Miss Mortimer, Miss Weaver.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.

There was a good attendance at the opening cere- mony yesterday (Friday), which was performed by Miss BeSble Dutton. Mr. Meldrum, of Moore, presided and after prayer had been offered by the Rev E Morgan, Mr Wright gave a report of the result of the previous days sale and thanked all those who had contributed towards the £255. (Applause.) He offered a hearty welcome to their chairman and to Miss Dutton who had been connected with the Sunday School for some years. Mr. Meldrum said he congratulated himself on acting along with Miss Dutton. He emphasised the need of good fellowship and co-operation in church life. Miss Dutton felt greatly pleased at being there that afternoon. Mr. Wright had spoken of her as being a Sunday School worker for a few years whereas fifty years of her life bad been devoted to that noble work. Continuing Miss Dutton referred to the friendliness of the members of the churches in the Warrington Wesleyan Circuit and the good fellowship and spirit of unity which existed in that circuit and the praiseworthy manner in which the work was being carried on. (Applause.) A beautiful bouquet was handed to the opener by Master Henry Ward and the chairman was neatly button holed by Miss Ruth Cottrrell. A vote of thanks was moved by Mr Proffitt seconded by Mrs Gladding and carried unanimously. Dr Bennett who should have moved the vote of thanks was away, his absence being attributed to his having overworked himself the previous day. Tbe sale was proceeded with in a brisk manner and entertainments were given at intervals in a creditable manner.

DEATH 07 MRS. ARTHUR WRIGHT.—It is with great regret that we have to report the death of Mrs, Arthur Wright, the matron at the Cottage Homes of the Warrington Union, which occurred' alter a protracted illness on Wednesday at the age of 51 years. For several years the deceased lady had suffered from cancer and she bad undergone many operations. Since ben advent into Pad gate, now many years:a go, Mrs. Wright had by her unvarying kindness and unselfish thought and consideration for others endeared herself to a large number of friends. The Board of Guardians bas lost a valuable servact, the officials a sympathetic colleague, and the children a veritable mother. The funeral is to take place this (Saturday) afternoon at Christ Church, Padgate.

div.head: PRICE OF COAL.
div.p: THE PRICE OF COAL.

The Mining Association of Great Britain met at Westminster on Wednesday, to discuss the financial effect of receit legislation, and it is understood that the owners agreed to endeavour t 3 obtain an increase of 2s. 6d. per ton on contract rates for coal.

The Commissioner of Immigration at Winnipeg states that the rush of American settlers to Canada will be far more heavy this year than kas previously been the case. The increase to March 15th was 80 per cent, over that of the same period last year. Large numbers are also arriving from England and the Continent. During the second fortnight in March 3,851 British and 1,930 Scandinavians and other Continentals arrived in Winnipeg. The 40 immigration halls throughout the West of Canada are in readiness to receive and care for new arrivals.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
NEW POSTMASTER AT RUNCORN.

The Postmaster-General has been pleased to approve of the promotion of Mr. G. H. Bradley, postmaster of Sandbach, to the postmaltership of Runcorn. Mr. Bradley commenced his official career at Newport, Salop. thirty years ago, and since his removal to Sand- bach in 1902 the work at that office has grown to a very great extent. For many 3ears prior to his promotion to the postmastership of Sandbach he acted in the important capacity of the chief clerk.
WIDNES CHEMICAL EXPLOSION. THE FIFTH VICTIM.

Widnes was visited with a works calamity last Tues- day week, resulting in four deaths within the space of twelve hours. The fifth death was reported on Wed- nesday, when W. Marsh, of Halebank, expired at the accident hospital from shocking burns. At tiro inquest, which was adjourned for a month, it was stated that Marsh was seriously ill,but there were hopes of both he and Haley attending the next hearing. The men comprised the handy gang employed at Messrs.'Muspratt's Chemical Works, and while they were lifting a huge drying rat by means of jacks a terrible explosion occurred, followed by a burst of flames many feet high. All the men were badly burned so much so that one named Groorce was burnt to death on the spot. _ . . . . .
It is theorised that friction caused by the weight on the jacks ignited some carbonaceous matter at the bottom of the driver, causing it to explode.
WARNING NEEDED.

div.head: JURY'S RECONINIENDATION AT WIDNES INQUEST.
div.p: JURY'S RECONINIENDATION AT WIDNES INQUEST.

At Widnes on Monday a verdict of "Accidental death" was returned at an inquiry into the circum- stances attending the death of an eighteen months old child of a chemical labourer named Thomas Ilindley, of Ann-street West, Widnes. The child stepped off the pavement in front of a large steam lurry belonging to Messrs J E C Lord, of Weaste, Manchester. The steerer noticed the child's danger and shouted to the driver. The latter shut off steam and reversed the engine, but the wheel knocked the child down and passed over both legs below the knees, crushing then. to pulp. Both legs were amputated at the Accident Hospital, and the child died from shock. A juryman who witnessed the occurrence said that the driver could not have saved the child if it had been his own. Th.' jury found that no blame attached to the driver, Thomas Edwards of Tintern-street, Salford. They, however, recommended that the °minty council be requested to place a warning notice near the spot in consequence of the close proximity of the school and the considerable vehicular traffic. NEW TECHNICAL SCHOOL POE WIDNES. TRIBUTE TO LANCASHIRR BOYS AND GIRLS.

A handsome extension to the Widuea Municipal Secondary and Technical School, costing £14,000, was opened on Monday by Sir Henry Ilibbert, chairman of the Lancashire Eduoation Committee. The school is now one of the best equipped in the administrative county. Sir Henry said that last year the county council spent £535,160 on secondary anOigher education and .C 145,000 on technological and evening classes, making a total of £6Bo,ooo—an infinitely greater amount than the revenue of many a German State. Of this amount £877,062 was provided out of the rater Widnes was annually absorbing something like £2,527. Lancashire urea a great place for evening schools. In the whole of the Palatine there were 23 per cent, of the entire number of evening students in England and Wales, while in the administrative smutty over which he presided there were considerably over 8 per cent, of the entire evening students in the United Kingdom. When the question of attendance at evening continua- tion school- being compulsory was before the Consulta- tive Committee of the Board of Education complaints were made from various parts of the country that it was too much to expect young boys to attend evening schools after they had done a hard day's work. He agreed that it was a hard day's work. He agreed that it was hard, but he instanced the case of Lancashire, with its 45,000 evening students, the greater bulk of them boys and girls who worked from six o'clock in the morning until half-pest five in the evening.

div.head: ---,--____. EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: ---,--____. EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
MR. J. A. SEDDON AND THE SHOP HOURS ACT.

Mr. J. A. Seddon, seen on Tuesday evening, said be believed the Shop Hours Act would be a magnificent success. Undoubtedly it bad some faults, but it was not like the law of the Medea and Persians, and could be amended so as to meet all reasonable requirements.

LORD WOLMER AND THE LABOUR PARTY. Speaking at the quarterly meeting of the Newton Division Conservative Association on Saturday, Lord Wolmer said that at the present time the freedom and independence of members of Parliament were being crushed out by the force of the party caucus. Home Rule was being supported by soores of Liberal members who hated it. That iniquitous measure Welsh disestab- lishment was carried on its first reading by a majority of 78 votes, and of those who voted for it 7G were Irish Nationalists and 30 were Scotch members. The bill affected cnly England and Wales, but if it bad not been for the Scottish and Irish membens it would have been rejected. These were instances of how all we held most honourable and most sacred was bargained about and sold to the highest bidder in the House of Commons. There were many reforms urgent and necessary in this country. We wanted social reform, Imperial reform, reform of the House of Lords, but we wanted reform of the House of Commons above everything else. Even the Labour party were not above entering into disgraceful corn- pants. They voted for Home Rule in a body although they had no interest in it, and although there were thousands of Protestant trade unionists in Ulster who %vete being betrayed by the Labour leaders, whom they helped to maintain. The Labour members were simply the hirelings of the Liberal party. Whenever there was a dirty piece of work to be done b; Mr. Asquith the Labour party were always ready to help.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
NO SUNDAY MUSIC IN ST. HELENS.

The St. Helens Parks Committtee has refused per. mission to the Nutgrove Prize Band to give two sacred concerts in aid of the Chief Constable's clothing fund on the first two Sondays in June in the Queen's Recreation Ground sod Victoria Park. The committee offer the band two Saturdays instead.

div.head: "KINDEST OF MAYORS. CHILDREN COMPLIMENT TO SIR JOSEPH BEECHAM. ,
div.p: "KINDEST OF MAYORS. CHILDREN COMPLIMENT TO SIR JOSEPH BEECHAM. ,

Sir Joseph Beecham, Mayor of St. Helens, received a charming compliment on Monday. The boys and girls of Holy Cross and St. Joseph Schools attended at the Town Hall to present a beautifully illuminated and bound address of thanks for the recent mayoral treat to the children of the town, who were all provided with free seats at the local theatre when the' Golden Land of Fairy Tales" was performed by the company from the Aldwych Theatre, London. The children who formed the deputation were Misses Mary Murray, E Harrison. Mary Turner, Doris Ashton, and Masters Thomas HOdgkinson, and Matthew Berrill. Father Baldwin, in introducing the children and their teacher (Miss Kilmartin), said that the children would have liked to have presented the souvenir on the Mayor's name day (St. Joseph's Day) btt as he was away from the town the presentation had to be deferred. Miss Mary Murphy read the address as follows : To the kindnest of Mayors—Alderman Sir Joseph Beecham, on the occasien of his name day, March 19, 1912, from some very grateful children, the boys and girls of Holy Cross and St. Joseph's Farr : " The Golden Land of Fairy Tales" revealed A heart of gold our Mayor would keep concealed That quicker beats at sound of merry voices, And at the sight of happy smiles rejoice ; A kindly heart that, spite of toilful dsye, Could leisure make to bring bright sunny rays Of joyous mirth to many a child for whom Youug life has oft too much of care and gloom.

Now we would tell you how we hope and pray That God will bless and:brighten your life's way, With those good gifts He keeps for such as love His little ones, nor shrink from cost to prove This love by personal deeds of grateful thought That to the hearts of thousands pleasure brought, Our priests and teachers join with us to-day And echo from their hearts the thoughts we say : For all you give to each of us they bold Is given to them thereby a thousandfold. The Mayor, in accepting the gift. said his little friends had given him a surprise by presenting him with that beautiful address and memento, illustrating some of the scenes from the "Golden Land of Fairy Tales." Although it. was very gratifying to him to receive that Iron' them, it was quite as gratifying to know that they all enjoyed the performances. He was sure all the children did, judging from the applause they bestowcd and the way they and the teachers showed their pleasure fie did not know of anything that would have given so much pleasure to so large a number of children, about 12,000 altogether. He thanked them most heartily for their kindness, and assured then t that he would value the address most highly,
BUFFALO CHASE IN LONDON STREETS. An Indian buffalo, which escaped from a drover, was chased by crowds through the London streets on Wed- nesday, and finally caught and thrown by a policenifin.

div.head: MR. VICTOR GRAYSON AT. WARRINGTON.
div.p: MR. VICTOR GRAYSON AT. WARRINGTON.
LESSONS OF THE "TITANIC."

Mr. Victor Grayson addressed a large meeting in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Saturday evening under the auspices of the Warrington branch of the British Social party. The ex-Member for Colne Valley has some claim to be regarded as the free lance and jester of the Socialist party and his address on this occasion, sparkling with witticisms and racy comments on topics of the day, was followed with great interest. To the question " Are you a Socialist ?" Mr. Grayson said one seldom received an intellectual answer, but an answer that belonged to prejudice. It usually took the form off' What about Victor Grayson at Belfast ?" (Laughterj. " What about Kier Hardie at Merthyr Tydvil ?" (Laughter). "Where did Tom Mann get his new bowler hat ?" (laughter)—or "Is ' it true that a certain prominent Soc;alist has more than one wife, being induced by a strong principle of imitation of Solomon." (Laughter). " If you ask me anything about the social question " continued Mr. Grayson " You have not to ass me any- thing about my moral character. You have to judge what I say on the basis of its logicalness and truth,and it won't matter whether I have one wife or sixteen, or none—which is my unfortunate plight—(laughter)— whether I am a burglar, or a pimp or a politician. (Laughter.) " He started out in the endeavour, pro- ceeded the speaLer, to prove first of all that there was A GREAT CRIME BEING PERPETUATED in society ; that that crime was capitalism, that the capitalists were not the perpetrators of it, that the workers could wipe out that crime with a great sponge whenever they chose to, and that the whole of humanity would be emancipated when the workers ohose to take that step. Nowadays we were all talking about the wreck of the "Titanic." The papers were gurgling and bubbling over with it. Some 1,600 had gone down with the ship and our marvellous publio conscience was suddenly shocked. If those 1,600 lives bad taken a year to go down, our imagination and sympathy would have taken a year to be roused up. (Applause.) Why was the "Titanic" spawned from the brain of the inventor? Why would it be possible if he were tsking a trip on that vessel to play a game of tennis in the afternoon and have a cold bath and a swim afterwards? The reason was very plain and simple—the "Titanic" was built cia kind of illustration of

div.head: POWER OF WEALTH.
div.p: THE POWER OF WEALTH.

He heard of a young lady—en American—who went to' her father and Eaid "Dad, give me some dollars quick.% He said" How many dollars?" she replied "Hundreds As many as you have got about you?" (Laughter). He asked "What do you want to do with them?" She said" I am talking to a chap from England and I want to dazzle him." (Laughter.) That bad been the whole motive for the building of "The Titanio" and other floating monsters. Safety, be maintained, ought to be the first consideration.

OPIr. Grayson rant on to say that the most important fact that the recent coal striLe has brought to the rather opaque notice of the public is that we eannot live without coal, and we have found out by the trans- port strike that we cannot live even with coal if we have nobody to transport it from the coal fields. We have found out also that the Government in power at the time—whether Liberal or Tory—is usually com- posed of landlords and capitalists whose interest it. is to get the workers baok to work on the minimum terms that they will accept. (Applause.) I es a Socialist say that if there is labonr unrest, I am happy to have had some part in the creation of it. (Applause.) 1501

div.head: OUT TO MAKE DISCONTENT.
div.p: OUT TO MAKE DISCONTENT.

When I find a workman striving, toiling, delving. digging, pinching and starving and yet contented, I feel like saying with John Stuart Mill "1 would rather be a man dissatisfied than a pig satisfied." (Applause.) I am out frankly, plainly and openly to make men and women dissatisfied with conditions of slavery. I Those who laboured on the raw material of nature create all that can be created, and are morally entitled to enjoy the product of their labour. (Applause). The worker had a right to demand that if his child was at sea and in danger it should stand as much chance of life as the first class child. (Applause.) He had a right to demand that, whether at sea or on land, bis child should intia!e as sweet air as the child of the superior class, that its clothing should be as good, pure and honest as the clothing of any other class. He had a right to demand, in general terms, that what that child created, it should enjoy.! To obtain their rights the workers must see that they returned to Parliament not lawyers, capitalists, brewers and other parasites whose interests were diametrically opposed to theirs, but men belonging to their own class—men who would tell the Cabinet what they thought of them.

WHAT WAS THE PROSPECT FACING THEN at present? They had just finished a great railway strike, followed by a great coal strike. They had had Mr Balfour,Rith philosophic moisture dimming his blue , eyes,Mr Asquith plunking tears on the Treasury table— (laughter)—and society thrown into a state of ecstatio hysteria because the miner would not mine. The miner had gone back to work and he had got his minimum wage, but the owners had got the schedule. The moment that happened, the Government had discovered that Ireland must have Home Rule and that the Church In Wales must be Disestablished. (Laughter.) For another two years at least, unless there was a providential act of God to prevent that infamy, they were going to be wrapped up in Home Rule and Welsh Disestabliahment and possibly another Bill that was being contemplated for the elimination of goosebery mildew and he wiping out of crinkles iron tripe. (Laughter.) It was the obvious duty of the Govern- ment to deal with the problem that was right under their very noses—the problem of the nationalization of the mines, land and every great national monopoly upon which the people dPpended for subsistence. (Applause.) Instead ,of that the Government and the rich classes were I organizing civilian forces Oxford and Cambridge undergraduates, young sprigs of the nobility, were preparing to go down and mine coal when the miners refused to work. (Laughter.) He had received as many as five circulars in a fortnight asking him to join certain civilian forces to be used in time of industrial dispute. That was the way the Government and the dominating class ale ays acted and this was the moment for the workers to gain a great victory. (Applause.) Referring to the " Syndicalist" prosecutions, Mr. Grayson said the paper bad a circulation of about 100 and be did not know of any member of the army who received a copy. Because that little paper said " Don't shoot," the Government intervened, locked up three men, arrested another and they were waiting to let him out of the backdoor if they could possibly get a way of letting him out. (Applause). At all events, they would not take him (Mr. Grayson) in at the front door. (Laughter.) There was hardly a soldier in the British army who was not acquainted with the fact to-day, owing to the Government's gratuitous action, that he should not shoot down his brethren in the time of industrial dispute. (Applause). The people, con- cluded Mr. Grayson, were facing an absolutely new epoch. There never had been a time in human history when there were so many vital issues just ready to he expressed. They wanted men and women of real back- bcne and he did not think it was undue optimism to hope that in the next ten years they would see the first few blows delivered that would finally destroy the enemy which they had fought for many lung centuries, Applause). Questions having been invited, Mr. R. G. Pierpoint said Mr Grayson had taken a long time and bad used some charming language, but be had not really said very much. (Laughter ) A manifesto issued by the local branch of the British Socialist party stated that •• Socialism does not consist in violently seizing upon the property of the rich and sharing it out among the poor." If they were going to make the poor richer and the rich no poorer, would Mr Grayson mind saying from what source the increased wealth was to come from? _ . .

Mr Gra3son, in reply, instanced the action of Count Tolstoi, who one day discovered that the land he owned did not belong to him and that he had no right to take t s fruits when those fruits were derived from the labour of the peasantry. Therefore Tolstoi, not being a Socialist, and not understanding the wisdom of the British Socialist Party's manifesto, made himself poorer by giving the land to the peasantry. By doing so, be was acting in an anarchistic and individualistic sense and he (Mr Grayson) was credibly informed that the land was in worse hands than Tolstoi's o mld ever have been Socialists did not propose that the rich should redishurse their richer. If he could get all the millions of the rich classes to-night and lay them at the feet of the working classes, be believed the workers would be worse off to-morrow than they were before. They did not want to make the rich poorer. They wanted to make them letter, cleaner and nobler—to concede to them the right to work. (Applause.) It was not their wealth they wanted, but the ownership by the people who worked of the means of production which they used in their industrial operations. They did not .vant to redisburse the plunder, but to atop it at its source. They wanted to democratise and socitilise the instru- ments of production so that nobody would be able to consume wealth who did not take some part in the production of it. (Applause) Answering a further question, Mr. Grayson said the present revolution would not accomplish Socialism,but it was a large step in that directicn. He believed that the next five years would see a greater advance in human development than the last fifty years bad realized (Applause).

CHEAPER G S AT MACCLESFIELD. The Macclesfield Town Council on Wednesday decided to reduce the price of gas by 3d. per LOCO feet to all clams of consumers. The present price for domestic use is 2s. 6d., with lower rate i for trade purposes.

div.head: EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
'` KICKING AGAINST" THE BOARD OF EDUCATION.
ALDERMAN BOLTON'S REPENTANCE.

Protests against the Board of Education's policy of penalising education authorities for the overcrowding of schools were forthcoming at the monthly meeting of the Warrington Education Committee OR Monday evenine. Councillor H Roberts presided and there were also present :—Mr A J Jolley (deputy chairman), Aldermen Bennett and Tinnion, Councillors Archer, Dellis°, Birtles, Dickenson, Jackson Holmes, Jenkins, Locker. Pemberton, Steel, Toole and Wilkinson, Revs James Davies and Canon Stevenson, Messrs R T Fair. dough, J Chrlmes, H Ringdon, E Plinston, C H Uneworth, J Upson, and G Walker, Mrs C Jackson Holmes ; Messrs J Vt Murray (director), It B Roberta (assistant director).

div.head: PENALIZED FOR OVER-CROWDING. NOT TO "TAKE IT LYING DOWN."
div.p: PENALIZED FOR OVER-CROWDING. NOT TO "TAKE IT LYING DOWN."

At a meeting of the School Attendance Committee • letter was submitted from the Board of Education, stating, in answer to the committee's appeal against the Board's action in making a deduction from the grant in respect of the Hamilton-street school in consequence of the continued overcrowding of that school, that the Board might be prepared to consider a renewed appeal I after the contract for the erection of the Oakwood. avenue Council school bad actually been signed,provided the necessary preliminary steps were taken without any undue delay. Mr. PLINSTON, in moving the adoption of the minute. which motion was agreed to, remarked that if the Sites and Buildings Committee would push along with the Oakwood-avenue school, there was a possibility that the deduction of grant would be remitted. Councillor WlLlotisoN _Are we to take a matter . . .

like this lying down ? Surely the Board of Education are fully aware that we are doing what we emu to find all the extra accommodation we can in Wsrrington by building new schools. We should not take such inter- ference quietly when we are doing our best. Councillor PBMBERTON was of the opinion that the committee took a great eeal too much lying down. It was time they kicked, and kicked hard and effectively. If they encouraged the school attendance officers to be lax, not a word about deduction of grant would be heard, but because the highest standard of atti ndence was insisted upon they were penalised by a diminution of grant. The Board was treating municipal bodi*s very shabbily indeed. It was a public scandal when education bad been forced on the country in the c‘ay it had been by Parliament, that the expense of it should be pushed on to the local taxpayer. The CKAIRNIAN thought they might take it as a word of comfort that the suggestion contained in the minute amounted practically to telling them to ask again for the return of the money. Mr. PLINSTON refuted the idea that the tra'ter of deduction from the grant had been taken lying down. He showed that everything possible had been done to place the case before the Board.. They had endeavoured to present the most pressing excuses, but they had got to that stage when excuses would be taken no longer. Mr. JOLLEY said it was desirable that kicking should be done with discretion, and with the thought in mind that it was a game at which two could play. The marvel was that the Board of Education had been go long-suffering. To say that everything possible had been done was simply stating what was not correct. The Board bad been very lenient indeed They had repeatedly threatened and warned them, and at last a small penalty had been inflicted. They should be very thankful that the penalty was not a much more severe one. Counzillor PRIME RTONT said that since 1903 when the schools were taken over, there were only 300 more scholars, while places had been provided for something

like 3,060. Mr. UrsoN said, as usual, they proposed to look the stable door after the steed had been stolen and to kick when kicking was of no avail. The kicking should have been done a few years ago, when the Board of Education raised the standard and diminished the accommodation in every one of the schools. The Board of Education should have been asked to stay its hand until sufficient accommodation had bezn pro- vided by the erection of new schools. Mr. PLINSTON pointed out that the matter had been going on for several years, and they had been threatened in connection with other schools in the same way. The matter then dropped. He hoped it would not be thought that he was shirking any unpleasant duty, but as a member of the Sites and Building Com- mittee, he could do what he ought to do for the rate- payers when the sub-committee submitted its reports.
