Wesleyan Cycling Club. Saturday, April 27th, to Runcorn Pier Head.— Eighteen members took part in this rather unusual ran, and were agreeably surprised to find not so much of interest, though not of rural beauty, at the ancient river pot. Mr. and Miss Stubbs, of the Runcorn Steam Laundry, met the party, and after tea had been enjoyed, well served at Riley's Restaurant in Bridge- street, they conducted the party through the maze of locks, gates, warehouses, arid docks that form that end of Brindley's great canal, to the Pier Head, and on to Weston Point. There all the materials for making and glazing the North Staffordshire ware are unloaded ready for transport by canal, and the shipping and the breezes from the wide estuary of the Mersey gave quite a feeling as of the river-side at Liverpool. A fine thiee-masted French sailing vestal lay in the big canal, and we could not help contrasting her beautiful lines with the severer aspect of the steamers Con- stantly passing at Warrington. Those cyclists who Possess a camera will do well to take this run, for pictorial subjects are endless. The return run was lengthened by Balton, Stockham, Dutton and Grims- ditch to Stratton and Stockton Heath, where the party began to separate after a very enjoyable afternoon.

div.head: CLOCKS.
div.p: THE CLOCKS.

Mr. Parker's Reply to Mr. Rylands. Sir,—ln Mr. Rylands' last letter he says "The whole point underlying the Tariff Reform pcsitiem lies in the answer to the question whether there is any industry which might be protected with advantage. Mr. Parker's answers to my question involve him in acquiescence in the view that the country would benefit from Protection in the clock industry." Before pursuing the main argument let me say how glad IDM to see the capital P to Protection. It has always seemed to me unfortunate that Protectionists adopted the vague term of Tariff Reform which may mean anything according to who uses it, and where it is used. Mr. Rylands Tariff Reform means Pro- tection and nothing else. He tolls us " that to his mind the taxation of corn forms no essential part of the policy of Tariff Reform " and again " For this reason I decline to attach any importance to the food tax question." I wonder what Alderman Bennett who gives no serious theught to Protection, and whose whole thought is on Colonial Preference, has to say to this tepid indifference of Mr Rylands towards the only aspect of the question which appeals to the Alderman. To my mind it was Tariff Reform when yr. Gladstone in 1860 abolished at one sweep protective duties on four hundred articles of commerce It was Tariff Reform when the Bostonians chucked the tea chests into the Boston Harbour, it was Tariff Reform when the tanners of Exeter let the unfortunate excise man who had fallen into a tan-pit nearly drown. It was called Tariff Reform when Bismarck to raise war funds started high protection in Germany, and gave as Lis reason that in such indirect taxation people would not know that they were taxed. In Ireland ;and in agricultural coastitu- encies Tariff Reform means a higher price for agricultural products. In Warrington it takes the form of higher prices for leather and the like, every- where and always it is higher prices—a raid upon the consumer. On the other hand in Germany and America Tariff Reform denotes an agitation to reduce tir abolish import taxes, it is the consumer in revolt who wants Tariff Reform. Protection in its vaiied career has adopted many °fleet's such as Fair Trade, Reciprocity, Tariff Reform. The last seems to be the most inappropriate and confusing. Now that Colonial Preference is considered as non-essential it clears the air, and we can get back to the term which everyone understands viz , Protection. There is nothing to be , ashamed of in the term, and I am glad Mr. Rylands ' frankly uses it and speaks of Protection in the clock industry. Now to return to the main issue. Why Mr. Rylands should say my answers involve an acquiescence with an idea that the country would benefit by Protection in the clock industry puzzles me. There is nothing in my answers which justifies such an inference. At the same time I am glad my answers satisfy Mr. Rylands. it is always pleasing to find common ground in matters of dispute, and it affords a better prospect of arriving at the truth. I freely acknowledged, and still do, that there is surplus capital being regularly created in this country which could be forced into, say the clock industry, and made remunerative to the makers at the expense of the users if the tax were ' made high enough to keep out foreign clocks. But I hold that such artificial methods of creating industries which do not naturally develop under Free Trade conditions would be a national less. It would divert labour from channels in which the product is exchanged for its natural value to channels into which part of the price, not the value, is artificially produced! by the tax. However much the home made article Is raised by means of the tax its utility is not enhanced one jot, and utility is the true measure of value. The effect of Protection is to cause something to be made at home which under a state of freedom would be procured by exchange from abroad for some- thing that bad cost less to make here. Hence Protection causes a waste of labour and labour wasted cannot he a source of wealth. Whatever employment is given by Protection must be given at the expense of others. Protection is thus only a form of legalized plunder ; the protected industries become tax gatherers from all who buy their products, they are essentially parasitic. The capital required for these tax-created industries would either be withdrawn from home industry in which it is naturally productive, or diverted from investment abroad. If the latter, as I suppose Mr. Rylands would claim, it would have the effect of reducing the home employment in the making of the goods, or giving of service, such as in shipping, by means of which capital can only be exported. This brings me to Mr. Rylands' illustration. He says "that I suggested that the imported clocks could be paid for by the sale of foreign securities, that is by the absolute exportation and alienation of capital, and Mr. Parker agrees that ..f.1,000 of imported clocks could be paid for by the exportation of £l,OOO American Railway Bonds." In this sentence Mr. Rylands suggests a confusion which appeared in his last letter and to which I drew attention. I mean his use of the word exportation of £l,OOO American Rail- way Bonds. When suppose Mr. Rylands sells these and the proceeds by the operation of excharge are balanced by the importation of German clocks—there is no exportation. In using this word Mr. Bylands may simply mean the paper certificate which he held as evidence that he owned part of the capital in the American railway and which he posts or exports to the American buyer, but the true exportation occurred when Mr. Rylands bolight these bonds. These would be paid for not directly by Mr. Rylands but in the processes of exchange by the exportation of goods of British make, they might be rails, engines, wire, or the like, to equip the American railway. As I poioted Oat last week the purchase by Mr. Rylands of the American railway stock only delayed the exchange, when he sells the stock the exchange is completed and the clocks, or some article of equal value to those exported, has to be imported. Mr. Rylands airily dismisses this aspect of the ques- tion as being " irrelevant." I claim it to be both relevant and important, confirming and illustrating the fact that the principle of exchange governs all international trade. Mr. Rylands, in a later sentence, seems to agree with me because he says " I must be content to express the opinion, and broadly speaking, an export compels payment in the form either of an import of commodities or the creation cf foreign obligations due to this country." This is exactly what I contend. I simply expressed it the other way round ; imports, clocks if you like, compel payment in the form of an export of commodities, or the creation of British obligations due to foreign countries. There appears therefore to be little differences between us as far as the principles of exchange are in question. This is a great gain, and if we could get Protectionists always to start from the poiut at which Mr. Rylands has arrived we should considerably curtail the field of difference. CHARLES E. PARKER.

div.head: Penketh, May '2, 1912.
div.p: Penketh, May '2, 1912.
Some Lessons of Health Week.

------ Sir,—lf you can spare me space in your paper, I should like to say a word or two about the excellent pictures (touching upon health) which have been shown at the " Pictuiedrome " this week. There is one showing the old fashioned, unsanitary farm, the general carelessness over little matters and the illness caused through the milk being impure. Then a transformation takes place, the old man becomes convinced at last that be is not working his farm on the best lines, and he alters his methods. We are next shown his beautifutly clean and airy cow sheds ; the cows being groomed by machinery, and above all the milk not being exposed to the air, some put into air-tight tins and some bottled. This picture might appear strange to many people, but I really have seen' a dairy farm like this at New Earswick, near York, and I was much impressed with it; and only wish we could have one in this neighbourhood. I don't think many of us realise the imprtance of taking me of the milk, even after we get it from our milkman. Some people pat milk into tall jugs, which is bad because it does not allow enough air to get to it. It should be either air- tight or in a vessel which allows a free flow of fresh air ever the surface of the milk. Basins are therefore preferable to jugs, atd they should be put in a cool place away from all smells, as milk takes up a smell very readily. One great fault the poorer Classes have, is untidiness. Whatever time of day one calls at a house the food is on the table and a general air of untidiness pervades the rooms. I do

ot say this without actual knowledge. I am a worker for the " Citizen's Guild of Help " and I visit heaps of houses, but I am glad to say they are not all so bad, though very many are. I have been pleased to find in several cases a marked improvement on my second visit. This is the great problem we have to solve, I think. How shall we make these people more tidy and thrifty ? If we can succeed in this we shall soon have a decrease in the present high rate of infant mortality. ' But one despairs sometimes, with one's inability to alter things. Picture a woman, who has not good health herself, a crowd of little children sunning about getting dirty, another expected shortly, and only a small weekly wage coming into the house, even though the husband is in regular wca k. How is one to blame that woman fez her failure to keep her house cleaner and her children more tiny ? She has already more than she can manage.. This is but one of many such cases. I am afraid I am taking up too much of your valuable space, but I am very earnest in the cause and I feel very strongly that much may be dcne by willing service on the part of women who have time and opportunity to visit the homes of the less fortunate of their sisters Another picture which was most interesting was the "Baby rearing institution." I am thinkirg that a great many of those little mites were very much happier there, than they would have been at their own homes. Then there was a picture called "The awakening if John Bond," showing the dangers of " Tuberculosis, " which I am sure a great many people do rot realise. I think picture palaces might do a deal of good if they showed pictures of this type oftener than they do, rather than the highly sensational pictures which wo sometimes see. _ _
I think our health week in Warrington bas been very successful, everybody seems t have entered into it heartily. I only hope we have done a little lasting good.--Yours &c., 2nd May, 1912.
MAY PERRIS.

div.head: Wire Tangle—and After.
div.p: The Wire Tangle—and After.

Sir,— This evening I received a telephonic com- munication from the " Guardian Office " refusing to print more than the first sentence uf my letter in reply to " Workman Jim. " To that, I refused to *Tree. After the scurtilous personal attack upon me, to which they gave full publicity. I must conclude that the journalism of " the new style " is no more to be commended than its " politics. " -nun truly. EDMUND OSBORNE.
3rd May. 1912.

Sir,—l am afraid Couneillor Broadhurst, or as .he prefers to sign himself" Workman Jim," has mistaken his man. Judging from the two letters which he has addressed to your contemporary (why they were not also sent to you, I do not know), he is a correspondent destitute of the common courtesies of debate, and even if I am the "son of an ironworker," I have still sufficient self-respect left to t c train from "splintering r a lance" with him. The nactives which prompted him to level abuse at me can only be known to him- self. So far as he is concerned, I have nothing further to add.

It is perfectly obvious, however, that the questions which I addressed to the member for Warrington are not to be answered. It is not by argument that "the new style" hopes t-s gain its ends. I have lived in Warrington practically all my life, but I do not remember a time when people were so sick of the word" pslitics," as applied locally, as they are to-day. It is alt-gether unaccountable, but true nevertheless, that there are political personages—who are respected by all in private life—who no sooner don the party colours and put on the party war-paint than they become positively monstrous in their manners and language. On the other hand, there are well-educated gentle- men, with a keen desire to serve their town, who would sooner think of chewing clay than o' offering themselves as " independent " representatives, simply and solely on account of the misrepresentations they would be subjected to at election time. Such a state of affairs cannot be conducive, surely, to the best interests of the community. Unfortunately, we appear to bs getting deeper into the mire. The virulence of party contention mocks at that which is best in us; and the sooner public attention is directed towards curbing such a dangerous political product, and a serious effort is made to prevent it from contaminating our literary, social and philanthropic sfforts, the better it will be for all.—Yours truly, EDMUND ORBORNE. 22, 80ld-street, Warrington. 2nd May, 1912.

div.head: Cheap Health Week.
div.p: A Cheap Health Week.

Sir, -The men's or demerits of a National Health Week can now be judged by experience, and it onli remains to pay the bills. Owing to the economical and businesslike management of his worship the Mayor and the Health Week Committee, the total expenses are less than five pounds. It is thought desirable not to ask one or two persons to subscribe the full amount, but to appeal to public spirited citizens, who appreciate the value of arousing public cpinion as the health question, to send their quota, either Is., 2s. Gd., or 53. to the fund. I shall be very glad to receive subscriptions at the address given below.—Yours, etc. 10. Winmarleigh-street, B. S. TO WNROE, Warrington. Hon. Treasurer. May 3rd, 1912.

div.head: Summer Nuisance.
div.p: A Summer Nuisance.

Sir,—May I venture to ask that the Health Com- mittee will consider one practical outcome of Health Week. While returning late last Saturday night from the theatre the noses of our party were all unpleasantly aware that a hot week had made the usual summer odour of Warrington streets appear before its due time. The pail closet system possesses certain merits, but unfortunately, unless emptied frequently during hot weather, the results of the system are not only vile to the sense of smell, but carry germs of disease into our bcdieq, and worse still into the bodies of the helpless babies of the town. The Health Authorities work nobly against tie difficulties which surround them, and no man can cast a stone against them. But I would ask our representatives on the Health Committee to consider whether it would be practical peitics for the pails to he emptied more frequently during the summer months. The extra expense and trouble involved vt ould be well spent if we could save only one baby's life, which tries to survive the fetid atmosphere.—Yours &c., "A RATEPAYER."

P S.—lam not sure that this matter comes under the control of the Health Committee, but at all events it is obvious that conditions affecting so intimately public health can best be governed by one authority.

div.p: The tixarriner. Saturctay, May 4, 1912.
A SLUMMING EXPEDITION. MAYOR AND CORPORATION IN DARK PLACES.

How often are we told that " one half the world does not know bow the other half lives." It is indeed such a truism, a commonplace of our modern civiliza- tion, that few realise what an obstacle to improvement this ignorance really is. Those who are comfortably placed can, in the ordinary course of events, have but little idea Lf the depressing and sordid conditions of life which obtain at the lower end of the social scale Like every great manufacturing lost', Warrington has its slum areas. It may not be as bad in this respect as some Lancashire centres of similar size, but the fact remains that many of the poverty stricken classes are living in environments which are a disgrace tu a professedly progressive municipality. The Town C_runcil pcssesses certain powers cumbrous and res'ricted they may be —to deal with the h...usirtg question, hu we cannot expect a sufficiently drastic use of tbr powers until our local rul.rs grin a first-baud acqu•iin- lance with the evils wh:ch cry for redre 39. Howeve imaginative a man may bc, he cannot c7njure up very vivid conception of the soul-deadening, disease- producing surroundings of slumd 'm until he ha actually be en brcught face to face with them :• •For this reason, we regard as the most important of tht Health Week ob,ervar ces ill Warrington, the flt•ia visit which membr•rs of the Corpiration and t,the•

div.head: Photo Burrell.
div.p: Photo Burrell.
COUNCILLORS SLUMMING UP DOLMAN'S LANE. In the group will be seen Alderman Bennett, C .urrillors Archer D:cken3on, Bellian, and Mr. W. T. Flood (sanitary inspector).

prominent townsmen paid to some of the local courts and back alleys on Wednesday evening. They saw houses into which the sunlight never penetrates, where the only prospect is a blank wall or another squalid dwelling confronting the householder within • a few feet of his doorstep ; streets and yards where the only object of the builder appears to have been to crowd as many cheap hones as possible into a given area ; people bereft of all hope or ambition and content merely to exist. Happily there were some bright exceptions to the latter category, and the visitors saw how character can assert itself even in the most unpromising setting,and how some dwellers in unlovely places do their best to keep their houses clean and to impart some degree of cheerfulness to therm

The party made a start from the Town Hall at 5 o'clock in the evening, under the leadership of the Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph), ar.d the chairman of the Health Committee (Alderman James Evans). There was a fairly good muster of memhers of the Couocil, although an even larger representation might have been looked for. Passing from Bridge-sure,t into the gloomy recesses of Dolman's-lane, one could not help being forcibly reminded of the Mayor's declara- tion—which seemed startling at the time that "flu idge- street is a whited sepulchre----a veneer of grandeur covering over a mass of squalor." Flktre we siw houses which can only be deicribed as hovels. One, which commands a rental of 2s. per week, had only two rooms—one upstairs and one down—and the only entrance was not more than 2 feet 6 inches horn the doorway of another dark and wret bed dwelling which faced it. One would conclude that the dwellers in such a stifling, dismal quarter were in the locieat depths of po7erty, but the visitors could not fail to notice that the ro f of one of the outbuildings was literally covered with large pieces of bread which, it was suggested, had been placed there for the birds. "Such waste" said one of the councillors " would not be tolerated at my house." One respectable-looking woman who occupies a 3s per week house of three storeys (one room on each for) told the Mayor that she had lived in the lane for. twenty-eight years. "Do you never feel you would like to get out of it?'' asked his Worship. "Yes," she replied, "but I have not the means." "Do you ever hear any of the others say they would like to get out of it? " _

"I do—n't mix with them ! " , Passing along the lane we saw property which I belongs to the Corporation. One block was closed, and we were told that after their condemnation these buildings were found to be so full of vermin that the workmen v.ho were sent to cleanse them refused to carry out the task. Alderman Evans recalled the fact that some years ago the Street Improvement Committee acquired property and brought forward a scheme for a new I street which would have eliminated the Dolman's-lane area. It was, however, defeated in the Cuuncil. The present conditions, he thought, showed that the Council ought to place confidence in the committees who were thoroughly conversant with the conditions they sought to remedy. A councillor was led to remark that the Corppration ought to have some organized scheme for clearing undesirable localities. It was useless to buy property and keep it on their hands for years. Not far from D lman's lane, we cams to Stoney Yard which has a more spacious appearance bat leaves much to be desired in the way of improvement. One block of houses bore the date 1770 and no doubt it had served its day end generation. We learned that in recent times one house had been demolished in order to provide an air passage between two others. A marked contrast in the appearance of one house as compared with those immediately adjoining it called attention to the fact that the habits of the people count for a great deal. This tenement had every indication of cleanliness and brightness while most of the others looked as deprtssing and repellent as could well be conceived.

"It is not altogether a question of the property but of the people' said one councillor. "Talk about educating them," said another "You would have a jib !" One particularly unsightly feature of this neighbour- hood was that the outhouses for all the property faced the front doors of a row of houses.

Through a narrow passage, the party pissed into Buttermarket-street and immediately made its way to James-street which branches off near the site of the old Bridewell. We were taken to a back passage which was the very embodiment of hideousness and squaltr. There was hardly room to turn round and it was little wonder that an alderman exclaimed " I don't know bow the people live here. They can haadly breathe." There was a row of heuses, opening immediately on to a wall— newly whitewashed and behind that more houses. Alderman Evans explained that if one batch of houses
" Do you like it? " he asked, but there was no answer.
" Cheap, I suppose" suggested his worship. "No, it is not that. It is being used to the place. We don't like to leave it."

Alderman Evans made a happy suggestion that the Guild of Help and other citizens who had the time and opportunity might visit such neighbourhoods as that on summer evenings and give little musical entertainments. The Mayor or he (Alderman Evans) could accompany them and say a few words to the people as to what might bs done for their betterment. Alderman Bennett pointed out that the Beautiful Warrington Society did work of that kind very successfully for two summers. Why it had been dropped, he did not know. Having negotiated some of the tortuous byways of Cockhedge the visitors experienced a sense ot relief on coming to an open space provided by the demolition of old property. In Back Dial-nreet wls seen a row of six houses, condemned and closed. Why they remained standing was not explained. We hear that the Mayor has at heart a scheme for the C ckbedge district by which much dilapidated property would be pulled down and model dwellings built in its place. One of the chief difficulties in effectually dealing with the housing question is : " What is to become of the slum dwellers who ate displaced by the demolition t f their homes? " In I most cases they are engaged in classes of labour which produce only a pittance in the way of wages, and they 'could not afford to remove to houses for which a higher rent is demanded. The Corporation has, however, power to erect dwellings on its own account but any ambitious effort in this direction would, of course, be faced with the ever-present bugbear of the rates.

Some of the party found themselves wondering whether it was only a mere coincidence that a certain works chimney which was belching forth dense volumes of black smoke on the appearance of the civic representatives, reduced its output in an incredibly short time to a light, filmy line of smoke to which the most ardent smoke reformer could take little exception. After the pictures of gloomy homes, grinding poverty and deadly ii.difference which had confronted the visitors in so many directions, it came as quite a pretty contrast, on turning into Brick-street, to see a little fairy proudly setting out in a cab for the Band of Hope festival at the Parr Hall. Through several streets and passages the deputation passed into Lythgoes-lane and Haydock-street. Some of the denizens of one court regarded with a tolerant smile what they would no doubt look upcn as the faddiness of one gentleman who, seeing a child con- tentedly munching some bread whichhad evidently been lying on the ground, tried to make the food look more palatable by removing acme of the dirt which had adhered to it. Haydock-street, as everyone knows, presents a monotonous succession of drab, cheerless cottages, but it did not suffer by coinparison with some courts previously visited. One of the yards had been improved during the past twelve months by the removal of some buildings, but wherever cne turned the houses looked stuffy and uninviting. In several windows were noticed the red sand-bags" once so generally used to keep out the draught, and the Mayor did not miss the oppor- tunity of telling the inhabitants of the foolishness, from a hygienic standpoint, of making use of such devices.

The tour was brought to a close with a visit to a yard off Winwick street, approached by one of the narrowest ai.d worst lighted passages imaginable This yard, although quite uniatractive ana indeed, ugly, was chiefly notable in that it provided what the Mayor described as an o Isis in a desert—a working- man's dwelling which bore marked evidences of licuse-pride. The living room was arranged with the best of . taste, the walls being decorated with many p:ctures and rlaques, and there was also a piano. Little fresh air could reach the place and cue marvelled that the tenant should be content to dwell in such uninspiring surroundings. He told the party that he might remove if his circumstances Improved, but he appeared quite contented and happy. Throughout the inspection one couid not help noticing bow the lady visitors from the health depart- ment were welcomed by the people. They had a cheery word and a smile for everyone and it was evideut that their systematic visitation of our courts and alleys is appreciated by this° whom they seek to help by sound advice. The visit had cccupied about two hours, and although in so short a time it was possible to make only a cursory inspection, the impression created by this walk through the haunts of the submerged tenth, will not readily be effaced from the memories of the party. If only it leads to a more resolute effort to grapple with an appallingly difficult problem, Health Week will not have been in vain.

Bef ore the deputation separated, the Mayor gave a short speech in which he expressed the hope that good results would accrue from this visit to the courts and alleys of Warrington. He felt convinced in his own mind that they had done some good that afternoon and he trusted it would be the beginning of real I progress in improving the lives of the people who lived in the poorer parts of the town. (Hear, hear.) Alderman JAMES EVAN 3 said he was anxious that every member of the Council should know just as much as the Health Committee about the work they had to do, and the difficulties they had to encounter. Their object was to improve the housing of the people and to bring about the test,possible conditions of life. He hoped that in the days to come, with the co-operation of evety member of the Council, they would realise if not ideal conditions, a substantial improvement on what had obtained in the town in days gone by. (Hear, hear).

could be Fulled down, t'm others could be made quite habitable, but the interests of the respective owners stood in the way of any such scheme —at least by mutual arrangement. " What are we as an authority to do?" asked the chairman of the Health Committee in hop,less tohei. _
" It is a standing disgrace to us" was the Miyor's tel se comment.

All the inhabitants of James-street turned out to see the invasion of their dein- in by such important visitors but there appeared to be no sense of resentment. If there had been, it would immeliately have been dis- pelled by Alderman Evans' remarks to one worker : "We are not here to find fdult with you people. We want to help you to mike your houses more comfortable."

"We cannot make everybody r.ch " added the Mayor. "I am sorry we cannot. You can, however, make the best of what you have gat. You are fellow- towr smen and the ciedit of the town is as much in ycur hands as in ours." div.head: PREVENTABLE DISEASES.
div.p: PREVENTABLE DISEASES.
DR. COOTE HIBBERT'S INTERESTING
LECTURE.
Sunlight and Fresh Air as Medicine.

In connection with the local 'celebrations of Health Week, Dr. J. Coote Hibbert, medical officer of health, gave a lecture at the Town Hall last evening on "Preventable diseases and how to prevent them." He pointed out that ignorance and neglect of the simple laws of health, as the Mayor had repeatedly stated, were the chief obstacle in the path of sanitary reform. The work of the health department was based on scientific principles and not on the fad or 'shim of the medical officer of health, as at least one of the leading citizens of this borough seemed to think. There were, from a health roint of view, definite reasons why our dwellings and schools should be well ventilated, why dampness should be avoided, and why sunlight should be sought. Science could demonstrate to us that clecnliness was essential for a healthy life in addition to its being necessary for our comfort and required by our 'ssnse of decency. The leoturer then showed how all the long list of the well- knovrnacute infectious diseases, many other diseases such as influenza inflammation of the lungs, 'bronchitis, sore throats, blood poisoning, anthrax, tetanus or lock-jaw, and of course consumption and the various forms of tuberculosis, were all due to the invasion of the body by disease germs Although the discase-producing germ was mostly to be found oit the living human tissues, it could also ex:st for a time at any rate outside the human body. It was then most likely to be found in warm, moist places and amid organic matter, schich really meant amidst dirt and filth. Dirty corners in warm, stuffy rooms, the warm, moist middenstead, and indeed any collection of animal or vegetable refuse formed the suitable tempo- rary habitation of disease germs while outside the living body. rbe moral," continued the doctor," is evident. Do not let these conditions exist in or near your dwellings, and thus you will not be supporting the germs until they find a suitable opportunity of pounc- ing upon you or some member of your family. Remem- ter above everything that direct sunlight kills them. Encourage these beneficent rays of the MID, and if possible allow them t) flood every corner of your house. If possible remove from sunless courts and shun a Etualees spot as a plague spot." The importance of boiling water or milk to ensure its purity and of keeping homes free from dust was also insisted upon. The lecturer next dwelt upon the invasion of the body by disease germs, pointing out that if the power of resistance in the body was great there would he no illness, but if the power of resist- ance was slight,illness would follow. It was therefore of great importance to build up our bodies in general health and the means of doing so might be summed up as

"LEADING THE SIMPLE LIFE." Simple, good, nourishing food was the first essential, and be often thought that much good could be done by giving the poor free lessors in simple cookery. The doctor also strongly advocated exercise —active participation and in games instead of gazing idly on the contests of professionals. It was also highly essential that we should get fresh air, not merely for an hour .or so during the the day when out for a short walk, but during every hour of the day or night. "If only," he continued those who close up the windows and doors of their dwellings and seal up every ventilator, crack and crevice as though to exclude every breath from outside, could experience for a few days the health-giving effects of living in the open fresh air, they would be tempted even to pull down the sides of their houses in their quest of this newly found remedy. The great mistake most people make when they open the windows is that they open thorn only to a slight extent and thus obtain a draught blowing on a small portion of their body and perhaps causing a stiff neck or other unplea‘ ant effect. Let the windows be opened to their full extent and there will be less troublesome draught and few complaints of local chill. Would that our schools wore better object lessons in this respect to the coming generation." The lecturer next showed how the germs in the body multiplied greatly and produced their spacial poisons or "toxins," causing symptoms of illness. On the other hand the body tissues produced antidotes or " anti- toxins " which tended to neutralise the poisons or toxins. A certain period must, however,' elapse after the first symptom of the disease before the manufacture of the antidote was complete and before it was avail- able for neutralizing the disease poisons. This fact had opened the way for scientific medicines and these "anti- toxins" were artificially produced in animals and made use of to cure disease in man in the early stages of the illness and before the patient's tissues could themsslves elaborate the cure. Referring to the anti-toxin treat- ment of diphtheria, the doctor said there was a great risk in neglecting a sore throat and it the cas3 should be one of diphtheria and there was delay, this wonderful remedy which, when given in time, had saved many a child's life, was of little avail. The lecturer then dealt in a lucid way with the vaccine treatment, instituted in order to protect persons against certain germ diseases such as small-pox. The method of inoculation was perfectly simple and, with modern precautions, practically free from danger. It was based on scientifle principle 3, although it was discovered and practised before its scientific explana- tion was known. It must be remembered that protec- tion lasted only for a certain number of years and that repeated vaccination was necesslry for complete protection against the disease. He urged his hearers not to neglect this most important safeguard against the horrors of unmodified small-pox. Finally the doctor alluded to two of the most fatal infectious diseases, measles and tuberculosis. Unfortunately measles was not looked on as being very serious by the general public. It was not included for certain reasons in the list of it.fectious diseases which had to ho notified under the Infectious Diseases Notification Act, and for that reason it was not considered to be dangerous by many people. Measles was chit fly fatal among children under live years of age, and if an attack could only be deferred till after that age, so much greater chance had the child of surviving it. Parents should not only try to shield their own children, but should also have more consideration for those of others, for it was by no means uncommon for children who were excluded from day schools because there was measles at their homes, to be allowed to go about and play with other children, to visit Picturedromes, and even to attend Sunday school. The chief human source of infection as regarded tuberculosis was the spit of a consumptive patient. As we were all possible consumptives, anyone who spat about in public, places should ba looked upon as a possible danger, and even if spitting was not prohibited by byelaws, the general feeling on the matter should be such that any person committing this offence should be suitably punished by his fellows. Nature gave freely her simple but poteat remedies for disarms, which were to a cert sin extent within the reach of all* Unfortunately those who dwelt in the centre of large towns, had oft-times great difficulty in obtaining a full supply of those remedies, because their dwellings were hemmed in and over- shadowed by other buildings which kept off to a great extent the fresh breezes, and blotted out the sunlight. Gradually, however, in this Borough, the work of the Health Committee was producing its effect, and be hoped the day was not far distant when every dwelling, even in the centre of the town, would be given its quota of fresh air and sunlight, and that those blessings will not be specially reserved for the more favoured garden city suburbs. (Applause).
